Position Paper: Towards Open Complex Human–AI Agents Collaboration System for Problem-Solving and Knowledge Management
A Hierarchical Exploration–Exploitation Net (HE2-Net) for Theory–Practice Dynamics

Ju Wu Affiliation: j-wu19@outlook.com; Ju.Wu@transgp.hk    Calvin K.L. Or Affiliation: Emails Affiliation: klor@hku.hk Affiliation: The University of Hong Kong
Abstract

This position paper critically surveys a broad spectrum of recent empirical developments on human-AI agents collaboration, highlighting both their technical achievements and persistent gaps. We observe a lack of a unifying theoretical framework that can coherently integrate these varied studies, especially when tackling open-ended, complex tasks. To address this, we propose a novel conceptual architecture: one that systematically interlinks the technical details of multi-agent coordination, knowledge management, cybernetic feedback loops, and higher-level control mechanisms. By mapping existing contributions, from symbolic AI techniques and connectionist LLM-based agents to hybrid organizational practices, onto this proposed framework (HE2-Net), our approach facilitates revision of legacy methods and inspires new work that fuses qualitative and quantitative paradigms. The paper’s structure allows it to be read from any section, serving equally as a critical review of technical implementations and as a forward-looking reference for designing or extending human-AI symbioses. Together, these insights offer a stepping stone toward deeper co-evolution of human cognition and AI capability.

Keywords: Human-AI Collaboration, Multi-Agent Coordination, Symbiosis and Co-Evolution, Meta-Synthesis, Theory-Practice Interplay, Knowledge Co-Construction, Hierarchical Exploration-Exploitation Net (HE2-Net), Complex Systems and Non-Equilibrium Dynamics, Cybernetic Feedback Loops, Symbolic-Connectionist Integration, Petri Net Modeling, Epistemic Justification and Validation, Organizational Design and Collective Intelligence, Tacit-Explicit Knowledge Management, Agentic Autonomy and Architectures.

1 Introduction

Empirical studies of human-AI agents collaboration, spanning specialized agentic frameworks, knowledge co-construction approaches, and organizationally oriented systems, have advanced in many directions without a unified conceptual basis. Viewed through the lenses of seminal pioneers in AI, systems theory, cybernetics, cognition, and organizational studies, including Wiener, Miller, Tsien, Pask, Maturana, Piaget, and Simon, these gaps become even more pronounced, and the task of reconciling symbolic AI’s explicit reasoning with connectionist, LLM-based inference remains an open challenge. In clinical settings, problems are high-stakes, time-critical, and characterized by dynamic, uncertain, and partially modeled variables, where erroneous or opaque collaboration between human and AI agents can harm patients and violate strict ethical and regulatory standards. Failures in this domain quickly expose weaknesses that may remain hidden in less safety-critical environments. For this reason, throughout our critical review medical use cases allow us to examine the skills that any domain-agnostic collaboration framework must ultimately support. Hence, this position paper offers a critical review of these efforts, identifying both their achievements and shortcomings, and then presents a formal conceptual framework that integrates them.

Two core parts: (1) a detailed critique of current methods and implementations, (2) our proposed multi-layered theoretical model, together illustrate how to organize, revise, and extend existing techniques. Readers may consult any section to find relevant references or design principles, as we summarize each subtopic’s key issues, highlight emergent synergies, and map them onto a higher-order perspective.

We conclude that such a unified view, anchored by active human engagement, could spur the fusion of symbolic and connectionist approaches while reinforcing the "theory-practice" interplay fundamental to knowledge management and practical problem solving. Ultimately, this position paper serves as a reference for future research to advance from loose collaboration protocols toward durable human-AI symbioses, in which adaptive co-evolution can take hold.

2 The Human-AI Nexus

A machine broadly refers to any engineered system performing mechanical or electronic tasks without inherent autonomy or reasoning capability.

The Cybernetic Partnership of Humans and Machines
Norbert Wiener’s seminal works [1], [2], along with his 1959 interview "Man and the Machine" [3], highlight both the parallels and differences between humans and machines. While both process information and execute tasks, humans stand apart with their moral responsibility, creativity, and adaptability in handling complex, uncertain situations. Machines, by contrast, excel in efficiency, leveraging robust feedback mechanisms to perform repetitive or data-heavy tasks with precision. However, Wiener stresses that machines rely on humans to define their objectives and provide ethical guidance, reinforcing the need for human oversight in addressing broader societal impacts. This dynamic, he argues, creates opportunities for humans and machines to work together, where machines complement human abilities while humans ensure technology is aligned with ethical and social priorities.

2.1 Human-AI Collaboration

AI extends the concept of machines by embedding cognitive functionalities such as learning, inference, and decision-making into computational systems, enabling machines to mimic human-like intelligence.

Defining Human-AI Collaboration and Its Modalities
Human-AI collaboration (HAIC) is an evolving process where humans and AI systems engage in reciprocal, goal-oriented partnership, leveraging differentiated yet complementary strengths, such as creative intuition and computational rigor, to achieve shared objectives through adaptive synergy. Unlike cooperation, which involves parallel efforts by largely autonomous entities, collaboration demands deeper integration, mutual influence, and synergy that surpasses the simple aggregation of individual contributions. While some use the term "collaboration" interchangeably with "teaming" or "hybrid intelligence," these constructs differ slightly by scope (e.g., collaboration may occur across individuals, teams, or organizations) and depth of interdependence [4]. Typical categories include decision-support setups (where AI offers recommendations and humans decide), co-creative processes (AI generates suggestions to spark human innovation), and fully interdependent partnerships (both agents adapt to each other’s insights in real time). Such arrangements carry both promise (e.g., augmenting human capacity) and risks (e.g., reliance on opaque algorithms), necessitating critical evaluation of trust, transparency, and synergy. Ethically, HAIC needs co-supervision and shared accountability, ensuring that both humans and AI mutually monitor each other’s actions, maintain transparency, and jointly uphold responsibility for the outcomes of their interactions [5].

Design Principles for Orchestrating Organizational Intelligence
Organizational intelligence is defined as the ability of collectives of intelligent human and digital actors to solve problems and adapt. [6] developed a conceptual and practice-oriented framework supported by six design principles, providing methodological guidelines for leaders aiming to orchestrate humans and AI effectively. Although the framework lacks empirical methods and evidence, these principles prescribe that adding more or higher-quality intelligence, whether human or digital, can boost overall intelligence. Additionally, tasks must be allocated to humans or AI based on their alignment with specific problem domains. When automation replaces people, the freed-up human capabilities should be redeployed to higher-value (non-automatable) tasks. A greater variety in the "actor pool" (including humans with diverse expertise and AI systems with different specializations) enhances the ability to solve complex or novel problems. Furthermore, humans and AI systems must develop collaborative skills and interfaces to ensure effective cooperation. It is essential for the entire workforce, including managerial personnel, to be trained in communicating with, questioning, and interpreting AI-generated outputs, collectively referred to as "fusion skills."

Leveraging Complementary Strengths for Complex Problem Solving
When humans and AI collaborate on complex problems, they can jointly address the very features that challenge solo attempts. AI can detect subtle patterns within large data sets to even inspire mathematical intuition [7] or rapidly model multiple scenarios, while humans supply contextual judgments, ethical considerations, and creative adaptation to unforeseen events. Still, mismatches in understanding, such as AI’s opacity or overreliance on computational heuristics, can hinder performance if not carefully managed. Critical attention to designing reciprocal interactions, clarifying responsibilities, and maintaining transparency is therefore key to leveraging hybrid intelligence effectively in high-stakes, dynamically evolving problems.

Existing Explorations in Human-AI Mutual Learning
A research paradigm for human-AI mutual learning was proposed to highlight the importance, possible quantitative and qualitative methods, and potential applications of preserving, exchanging, and improving knowledge during human-AI collaboration [8]. However, the paradigm is coarse and descriptive, lacking theoretical directions to guide the design, formal analysis, and implementation of such human-AI mutual learning systems.

Evaluating HAIC Systems Through Unified Metrics and Flexible Frameworks
A structured system has been introduced that categorizes the evaluation of HAIC into three overarching factors: ’goals’, ’interaction’, and ’task allocation’, each containing multiple subfactors and associated quantitative or qualitative metrics [9]. This system highlights the need to address not only performance indicators (e.g., accuracy, throughput) but also interaction quality (e.g., communication clarity, trust-building, user feedback) and flexible task assignment (e.g., complementarity, adaptability, overall acceptance). By folding these elements into a decision-tree approach, the methodology pinpoints which metrics matter most under a diversity of AI-Centric (AI leads decision-making; humans assist), Human-Centric (Humans lead; AI assists in data or repetitive aspects), or Symbiotic (AI and humans dynamically share control, learning from each other) modes of collaboration. The system further suggests the possibility of assigning weights to each metric so that an overall "HAIC effectiveness" score can be calculated, thereby aligning technical rigor (like error rates or resource efficiency) with more nuanced requirements (such as user trust or behavioral adaptation). Beyond unifying performance and interaction metrics, the framework formalizes a consistent means of applying the same fundamental factors across disparate domains. In healthcare, advanced interpretability and strict alignment with safety guidelines often outweigh raw model outputs, whereas finance typically requires dynamic risk modeling and robust anomaly detection in line with regulatory constraints. These domain-specific highlights integrate under a uniform, modular architecture, ensuring repeatable evaluations and easier cross-comparison of outcomes. This approach also anticipates the expansion into previously underexplored behavioral and ethical dimensions, allowing to further refine how trust, adaptivity, and fairness are measured and balanced in ongoing collaborations between humans and AI systems.

However, the three-factor taxonomy contains overlapping constructs, and its reliance on fixed collaboration modes, human-led, AI-led, or hybrid, does not adequately accommodate the evolving nature of human–AI synergy over time. In practice, a system’s mode can shift as tasks, objectives, and expertise develop, so a rule-based decision tree with static mode selection fails to address these time-dependent changes. Moreover, the proposed HAIC score, which relies on selected metrics that often incorporate qualitative feedback, remains largely conceptual and untested in real-world environments.

Emergent Abilities in Large Language Models as Spark of AGI
The emergent abilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) such as GPT-3 involve a phase transition in performance on certain tasks, becoming significantly above random only at a critical scale defined by training FLOPs, model parameters, and training dataset quality, with the intelligent abilities like multi-step reasoning, few-shot learning, and instruction following enabled by scaling and specialized prompting strategies [10]. GPT-4 sparks progress toward Artificial General Intelligence (AGI), by demonstrating multimodal integration, advanced reasoning, and interactive capabilities that enable human-like understanding, adaptability, and problem-solving across diverse real-world tasks [11].

Agentic AI and Holistic Intelligence as a Pathway to AGI
Recent work by [12] envisions an agentic AI framework that integrates perception, cognition, and action while unifying language, vision, and action prediction into a single foundational model for operation in physical, virtual, or mixed-reality environments. Although no concrete end-to-end system or implementation details are presented, the conceptual thrust of this approach is to enable cross-domain adaptability by interweaving learning, memory, and planning. By rejecting the narrow specialization of isolated sub-fields, the framework suggests that holistic intelligence emerges when these core capacities are jointly developed and updated in tandem.

Contrasting with methods that primarily scale language modeling, this agentic AI paradigm positions itself as a stepping stone toward AGI by emphasizing environment-grounded feedback loops. In other words, real-time perception and multi-stage reasoning feed directly into purposeful actions, be they physical or virtual, while memory and high-level planning inform subsequent decisions. Such a cohesive design, although proposed at a conceptual level, underscores the growing recognition that "intelligence" requires more than producing high-quality text alone; it must also exhibit the adaptability, autonomy, and integrative depth that can only arise from a system that evolves all of its key components together.

2.2 Human-AI Agents Collaboration: From Autonomy to Synergy

An AI agent specifically builds upon AI by operating autonomously within an environment, actively perceiving inputs, making decisions, and taking actions to achieve defined goals, thereby emphasizing purposeful interaction and adaptability beyond the static functionalities typical of conventional machines or passive AI systems. Importantly, AI agents have the potential to embed advanced, human-like meta-cognitive capabilities such as self-reflection, continuous learning, intrinsically generated intentions and desires, and goal-directed autonomy, enabling them to dynamically evolve their strategies and behaviors through internally driven motivations, experience, and introspective processes.

Historical Shift from Function Allocation to Collaborative Agents
The evolution of agent technology reflects a paradigm shift from early automation, which aimed simply to replace human tasks with faster, cheaper machines, to modern systems designed for dynamic collaboration. Initially, research in function allocation sought to delineate which tasks were best suited for humans versus machines. However, as early pioneers like McCarthy and Selfridge introduced the concept of an "agent" living and doing its business within the computer’s world (a "soft robot" capable of executing complex operations when given a goal and seeking advice actively when stuck), it implies that the agents should have the ability to operate independently in complex situations without constant human supervision, and it became clear that the static allocation model was insufficient [13]. The debate over what constitutes an "intelligent agent," a "smart object," or merely a "dumb program" has evolved over time, with different standards and criteria, which underscores the inherent complexity of this domain. While agents can perform tasks on a scale that entirely human-in-the-loop methods could never match, modern agents do much more than simply execute commands; they are engaging in collaborative systems with people that operate within a framework of mutual interaction, adapting their autonomy and behavior based on shared context, interdependent goals and responsibilities, and the fluid hand-offs nature of real-world tasks. This historical progression is critical, it reveals that the true challenge is not just replacing human action, but transforming tasks through an intricate balance of human insight and machine autonomy.

Dialectical Balance Between Agent Autonomy and Human Directability
Agent initiative embodies an agent’s capacity to act independently, taking proactive steps, making plans, and adapting strategies without constant human oversight, which is vital for efficiency and timely collaboration in dynamic environments. However, this autonomy exists in a dialectical relationship with human directing: while the agent must be confident enough to lead local decisions, it also needs to remain sufficiently directable to allow swift human intervention when conditions change [13]. Policy mechanisms serve a dual role here by enabling initiative in critical scenarios (such as triggering emergency protocols) while also constraining it to prevent deviations from overarching objectives. Striking this balance is essential, as it ensures that agents can operate autonomously to reduce micromanagement, yet still integrate seamlessly with human guidance.

2.2.1 Integrating Agent Autonomy with Cognitive and Creative Capabilities

Empirically, a human individual’s thinking can be categorized into three types: Conceptual and Logical Thinking, Imagistic and Intuitive Thinking, and Insightful and Inspirational Thinking. In any given cognitive activity, multiple types of thinking function simultaneously, with most cases involving a mixture of at least two, and sometimes all three. For instance, in innovative scientific research, pattern recognition thinking and epiphany-based thinking often complement logical reasoning, rather than being limited solely to conceptual thinking [14]. We are curious about whether LLM-based agents have the potential for human-level creativity. If they do, how can we integrate their creative abilities with the creativity of human experts? If they do not, how can human experts creativity be enhanced with the help of AI agents? Such a combination could have a significant impact on the design of synergistic human-agent collaborations.

A Holistic Framework for Evaluating Creativity
Margaret Boden’s criteria define creativity as the capacity to produce outputs that are new, surprising, and valuable, where "value" refers to an artifact’s utility and societal acceptance, "novelty" captures its originality relative to prior works (both psychologically and historically), and "surprise" measures the extent to which the output defies conventional expectations. The creativity is framed through four interconnected dimensions [15]: the "product," which is the final creative artifact; the "process," referring to the specific methods and steps taken to generate the work; the "press," indicating the external, environmental factors that influence creative expression; and the "person," which encompasses the unique attributes and characteristics of the creator. This holistic perspective suggests that true creativity emerges not solely from the finished work but from a dynamic interplay between the creative techniques employed, the context in which the work is produced, and the personal qualities of the individual behind it.

Assessing the Creative Horizons of LLM-Based Agents
There are observations that RLHF-enhanced LLMs can achieve strong performance in producing valuable and surprising outputs within the bounds of their training data, and generating combinatorial novelty by combining learned patterns in new ways, yet exhibit constraints when seeking transformational creativity or surprises that would fundamentally alter conceptual paradigms or frameworks [15], and It is the absence of self-motivation, intentionality to deviate significantly from learned distributions, self-awareness, and robust self-evaluation loops in LLMs, coupled with their immutability once trained, that restricts their current capacity for a multi-iterative creative process and prevents them from satisfying the deeper process- or person-related criteria of creativity. In other words, current AI agents operate without a self-feedback loop: rather than continuously refining their outputs autonomously and intentionally, they "wake up" anew with each prompt, re-collecting relevant information without integrating previous experiences. This corresponds to the fact that they lack human-like adaptability spatio-temporal uniqueness and do not engage in the kind of continuous, reciprocal information-matter-energy exchanges with the environment that characterize human creative processes.

2.2.2 Designing Joint Activity and Shared Understanding in Human-Agent Systems

The success of human agents interaction depends significantly on coactive design, where agents dynamically share roles, responsibilities, and maintain ongoing communication to facilitate interdependent teamwork. Establishing and sustaining a common ground, i.e., mutually understood knowledge, beliefs, and assumptions, is equally critical for effective coordination and mutual predictability between humans and AI agents.

Coactive Design as a Framework for Dynamic Interdependent Teamwork
Coactive design represents a novel approach that redefines the architecture of human-agent interaction by centering on interdependence and reciprocal constraints. Unlike traditional models focused solely on function allocation or mixed-initiative planning, coactive design treats joint activity as a dynamic process in which both human and agent share roles, responsibilities, and regulatory obligations [13]. In this framework, agents, whether human or artificial, are envisioned not only to be autonomous but also to exhibit several key characteristics: a good agent knows its limits, taking initiative when appropriate and deferring when necessary; it respects policy-based constraints yet remains flexible enough to consider exceptions and workarounds. Moreover, a good agent is predictable and dependable, performing its part consistently and is attuned to the requirement of progress appraisal—ensuring that others are continuously informed about the status of its tasks and that potential trouble spots are identified early. It is also directable across all phases of the ’sense-plan-act’ cycle, enabling it to be re-tasked swiftly by a recognized authority whenever circumstances demand. Such agents are also selective, helping to focus attention on what is most important in the current context, and coordinated, adept at communicating, managing, and de-conflicting dependencies among activities, knowledge, and resources to maintain common ground. Additionally, they must maintain mutual affordances, ensuring that their internal states, limitations, and intentions are transparent to human collaborators, while also being equipped to negotiate both "hard" dependencies (such as critical, sequential task handoffs) and "soft" dependencies (informal cues that facilitate teamwork).

This construction underlines a critical insight: successful interaction depends on a system’s ability to dynamically integrate human and machine inputs, an endeavor that is as much social and organizational as it is technical. While promising in its potential to overcome the limitations of isolated automation, the practical implementation of coactive design remains a complex challenge, requiring sophisticated models of shared context and real-time coordination.

Maintaining Common Ground for Effective Coordination and Mutual Intelligibility
It needs to be highlighted that the common ground is defined as the pertinent mutual knowledge, beliefs, and assumptions that support interdependent actions in a joint activity by [13]. It emphasizes that common ground as information space, includes not only pre-existing shared understandings but also the evolving mutual knowledge of history and current state that is acquired during the interaction. This definition captures the cognitive and digital aspects of collaboration by ensuring that all participants can make accurate assumptions about what others know, a critical factor for effective coordination. A robust common ground also ensures that any agents’ creative deviations, exhibiting agents initiative, triggered by a sudden equipment failure, an unforeseen user request, or the emergence of a better solution path, remain intelligible and acceptable. Note that the human cognition is richly nuanced and deeply contextual, incorporating social norms and unwritten rules, while agents rely on formal representations that simplify this complexity. This inherent representation gap is compounded by the necessity to continuously update the common information space over time, ensuring that both human and agent beliefs remain aligned; failure to do so leads to divergent understandings and undermines effective coordination.

However, it does not explicitly delineate the physical environment as a component of common ground. The tangible, situational conditions under which interactions occur are only implicitly suggested, leaving ambiguity about how these physical contexts and common environments are formally integrated into the construct of common ground. To build and maintain such common ground, not only must agents be informative and transparent, as mentioned above, but humans also need to provide timely feedback and corrections. However, there is an inherent tension between overwhelming the human with excessive detail and depriving them of essential updates.

2.2.3 Norms and Policies for Coordinating Human-Agent Collaboration

Policy and norm when coordinating human and agents
To enable both resilient and responsive human-agent system codesign, norms and policies are needed to play complementary yet distinct roles [13]. Norms are emergent, context-sensitive rules developed from repeated interactions; they empower agents to adapt, improvise, and coordinate flexibly, much like the unwritten social codes that guide human teamwork. In contrast, policies are explicitly defined and enforced constraints that ensure predictable, safe behavior; they can be dynamically activated or relaxed to meet changing conditions. While policies guarantee strict adherence to predetermined operational guidelines, crucial in high-stakes environments, they can also restrict an agent’s capacity for innovation by stifling initiative. Together, these mechanisms create a balanced framework that blends human-like adaptability with machine-like reliability, driving robust and agile collaboration.

2.3 HAIC in Healthcare: Navigating Complexity, Risk, and Uncertainty

Medical environments pose unique challenges for HAIC, marked by dynamic uncertainty, high stakes, and stringent time sensitivity. Complex tasks in the medical scenarios involving numerous variables with nonlinear, interdependent relationships demand deep synergy between human expertise and AI capabilities, calling for meticulously orchestrated trust-building, clearly defined actor roles and interaction models, and adaptive mechanisms for task allocation and coordination. Effective collaboration requires continuous knowledge exchange, appropriate integration of real-time context, and careful management of variables’ complexity, including discrete-continuous distinctions, nonlinear relationships, and highly interconnected causal networks [4]. Such environments underscore the critical necessity of robust theoretical frameworks, stakeholder-sensitive designs, transparency, explainability, and real-time adaptability to ensure trust and performance in collaborative decision-making scenarios.

Expanding Stakeholder Considerations and Theoretical Foundations
Critical issues in the current landscape of HAIC within healthcare are identified in [16], notably the limited consideration of stakeholders, as existing research predominantly examines pairwise interactions between AI systems and healthcare professionals. This narrow focus overlooks the multifaceted roles essential in medical environments, such as patients and clinical researchers, thereby restricting the comprehensive understanding of collaborative dynamics. Furthermore, the critical need for theory-based studies is highlighted to understand the mechanisms that facilitate effective HAIC in such safety-critical domains, evaluate the outcomes of these interactions, and identify the key factors that drive their success.

Iterative Decision Support for Mitigating Uncertainty in Real-Time
An integrated sepsis diagnosis framework demonstrates how a human-centered AI system can focus on intermediate decision-making stages, rather than providing a single final output [17]. Tackling with clinicians’ reluctance to trust purely model-driven predictions, the presence of insufficient information early in sepsis cases, and the urgency to make decisions with partial data, a practice-oriented loop emerges in which uncertainty can be iteratively mitigated, by suggesting which laboratory tests to gather next. This process aligns with clinicians’ domain knowledge and reasoning workflow, thereby cultivating trust and bridging the gap between AI-driven insights and human expertise. Observations indicate that such a synergy transcends the traditional human-AI "competition" dynamic, instead fostering multi-round collaboration in which physicians remain the ultimate decision-makers but rely on actionable, real-time feedback from the algorithm. This framework underscores the importance of aligning AI outputs with clinicians’ cognitive processes and demonstrates how AI systems can actively guide the experimental collection of critical data to reduce uncertainty and enhance decision quality in high-stakes settings, suggesting broader applicability in domains that require iterative data acquisition and informed decision-making.

Enhancing Trust through Explainability and Iterative Feedback
In a pilot trial conducted under time constraints designed to mirror real-world medical decision-making pressures, radiologists evaluated chest X-ray images to determine the presence or absence of lung lesions with the help of AI decisions [18]. The study compared explainable AI (XAI), providing both a heatmap that localizes suspicious lung-lesion areas and a probability score indicating the likelihood that a lesion is absent, with black-box AI, which offered only the probability score. The results demonstrated that having an "explainable" version of the AI’s decisions helped professionals trust correct AI outputs more often and override incorrect AI outputs more effectively, showing better balanced accuracy and precision. However, although medical staff benefit from the additional rationale provided by XAI when making decisions, the dynamic interplay between the AI decision-maker and the medical staff was not explored. Moreover, since the study only involved a single medical diagnosis task (lung lesion detection), its methodological generalizability is limited. Apart from directly informing a professional’s decision making [18], the learner model’s explanation can be evaluated by a critic model, rather than a human, to determine whether the explanation alone conveys sufficient information to solve the task. This feedback, mirroring the "criticize-reflect" mechanism, is then used iteratively to refine the learner’s ability to capture the essential reasoning behind each prediction by aligning its training with the critic’s feedback, such as by combining its base loss with an "explanation alignment" loss [19].

These empirical evidences highlight that integrating explainability and iterative feedback in AI-assisted decision-making not only improves human oversight of AI outputs but also facilitates effective intervention when needed. However, fully realizing these benefits requires deeper investigation into the real-time dynamic interactions between AI and medical professionals across diverse clinical tasks.

Human-Centered Criteria for AI Adoption in Clinical Decision-Making
An inquiry is designed to address the limited understanding of how AI might become a ’coequal’ team member in decision-making by shifting the focus from purely technical adoption criteria to a human-centered perspective [20]. Through semi-structured interviews with domain experts in healthcare, the approach identifies factors shaping adoption in high-stake and time-sensitive clinical scenarios: complementarity, mutual learning, user adaptiveness, decision transparency, time efficiency, and human agency. In pursuit of performance surpassing what either human or AI can achieve alone, clinicians often embrace an AI "second opinion" for borderline or complex cases, while algorithms iteratively refine themselves based on clinician-curated inputs. Role-specific interfaces foster acceptance across diverse medical teams, transparent and interpretable outputs build trust, time-conscious workflows preserve efficiency, and legal and ethical considerations ultimately reinforce the physician’s final decision authority.

3 LLM-Based AI Agents

LLM-based AI agents have significantly advanced their reasoning, learning, and action capabilities by leveraging specialized prompting strategies, such as chain-of-thought (CoT) and tree-of-thoughts (ToT), fine-tuning, and other in-context learning. Techniques like test time inference via self-consistency (SC) and outputs re-ranking, planning and tasks decomposition, structured function-calling, and external tool integration via a lightweight, context-aware interface and a robust communication protocol, empower LLMs to handle complex, multi-step tasks; however, these advances also reveal fundamental challenges regarding model coherence, consistency, explainability, and computational efficiency.

Improving Reasoning via Chain-of-Thought Prompting
CoT prompting enhances LLM reasoning by eliciting intermediate natural language steps, which allows models to decompose complex problems into sequential, interpretable sub-tasks [21]. CoTs can be implemented in various forms, tailored to diverse tasks, such as detailed arithmetic breakdowns, symbolic manipulation steps, or natural language rationales, and are typically introduced as few-shot exemplars that guide the model’s generation process. This method substantially improves performance on arithmetic, commonsense, and symbolic reasoning tasks, especially in very large models where such emergent abilities appear, although its effectiveness depends on model scale and prompt design, and it does not always guarantee fully accurate or coherent outputs.

Structured Exploration through Tree-of-Thoughts Reasoning
ToT transforms language model reasoning by replacing the traditional token-level, left-to-right generation with a structured, tree-based exploration of discrete "thoughts." Unlike CoT prompting, which produces a single, linear sequence of intermediate reasoning steps, ToT decomposes the process into well-defined units that represent coherent steps [22]. Its design hinges on four technical components: defining and structuring intermediate thought steps at an optimal granularity; generating multiple candidate thoughts through either independent sampling or sequential proposals; evaluating these candidates via self-assessment heuristics that assign scores or employ voting schemes; and integrating search algorithms, such as breadth-first and depth-first search, that facilitate look-ahead, backtracking, and systematic pruning of the combinatorial reasoning space. This approach aims to bridge rapid associative generation with more deliberate, evaluative reasoning akin to "System 2" processing. Essentially, ToT employs a ’critic-reflect’ mechanism by generating diverse candidate thoughts and then using self-assessment heuristics—such as scalar scoring or voting—to critically evaluate and reflect on each intermediate step, dynamically guiding the search toward the most promising branch.

However, this enhanced mechanism comes with notable limitations. The tree-based search incurs significant computational overhead, demanding careful balancing between exploration breadth and depth to manage resource costs effectively. Moreover, the reliance on the language model itself for self-evaluation introduces sensitivity to prompt design, its heuristics may require further refinement to consistently discern promising reasoning paths, underscoring an ongoing need for improved integration of deliberate planning within language model inference.

Enhancing Self-Taught Reasoning via Iterative Self-Explanation and Worked-Example Fine-Tuning
To bootstrap chain-of-thought generation without relying on large, human-annotated rationale datasets, the Self-Taught Reasoner (STaR) approach begins with a small, curated set of question-answer pairs that include detailed rationales as few-shot examples [23]. These examples provide the model with explicit reasoning steps. Alongside this, a large dataset of questions without rationales exposes the model to diverse scenarios. By iteratively generating rationales, comparing them to correct answers, and fine-tuning on the successful ones, the model gradually internalizes effective CoT reasoning patterns.

However, because STaR only checks whether the final answers are correct, it naturally treats any biased patterns that reliably yield those answers as "helpful." Coupled with rationalization, these biases can get even stronger because the model is prompted to produce plausible-sounding explanations that lock in or amplify problematic reasoning patterns, failing to generalize fairly or accurately in real-world contexts. Also since STaR trains on its own automatically accepted rationales, there is a risk of letting logically shaky or biased explanations slip in if they lead to correct final answers by coincidence. Although STaR motivates the creation of step-by-step rationales that lead to correct answers, it is challenging to ensure that these explanations are truly ’faithful’, that is, that they genuinely represent the model’s internal reasoning process. In practice, the model might simply choose an answer quickly and then generate a rationale afterward as a justification, rather than reflecting the actual thought process used to arrive at that answer.

The STaR approach functions like an iterative self-explanation process. First, through "rationalization," the model is given a question and the correct ("golden") answer, prompting it to reverse-engineer a rationale or CoTs. Next, it uses these worked-out examples (the rationales plus the original questions and answers) for fine-tuning, allowing the model to "learn by explaining." As a result, the model’s newly integrated knowledge from each round of rationalization and fine-tuning can further refine its reasoning on subsequent iterations.

3.1 Selected Methods of Test-Time Inference for LLM-Based AI Agents

LLM-Based AI Agents may generate inconsistent responses over multiple runs due to fluctuations in model parameters, environmental conditions, or problem states. This variability becomes especially pronounced in smaller, more complex test sets, where random differences can exert a greater impact on outcomes [24].

At inference time, sophisticated test-time strategies enable LLM-based AI agents to produce robust and reliable outputs by systematically evaluating multiple candidate responses. Techniques such as self-consistency aggregation and equilibrium-based re-ranking explicitly leverage repeated sampling, majority voting, and game-theoretic equilibrium selection, thus addressing the inherent variability and inconsistency of LLM-generated predictions; however, their effectiveness remains context-sensitive, requiring careful consideration of task characteristics, context length, and initial sampling quality.

In our discussion, we use the acronym "SC" exclusively to refer to a simple test-time inference strategy, one that samples multiple candidate outputs from a language model and selects the most consistent one to enhance reasoning accuracy. In contrast, when we employ the full term "self-consistency," we are invoking a broader conceptual framework rooted in logic, semantics, and rhetorical methodologies, where it denotes principles of internal coherence and methodological rigor. This distinction is crucial to avoid ambiguity: "SC" is a concise label for a specific, operational technique in model inference, whereas "self-consistency" in its full form may encompass a wide range of theoretical and interdisciplinary approaches.

3.1.1 Self-Consistency for Robust Aggregation of LLM Outputs

SC substantially enhances the performance of greedily decoded CoTs reasoning across a broad range of tasks. Typical self-consistency operates by sampling multiple CoTs responses as reasoning paths from an LLM for a given input and then extracting a discrete final answer, typically via rule-based parsing, for each response. These discrete answers are aggregated through a majority vote, where the answer that appears most frequently is selected as final. This method is highly effective for tasks with unambiguous, closed-form answers with a discrete, easily "vote-able" format (e.g., numerical solutions in math problems), but its reliance on exact matching limits its applicability to tasks where the answer can be succinctly represented.

Universal SC via Semantic Aggregation for Open-Ended Tasks
Universal self-consistency (USC) generalizes this approach by re-prompting the same LLM with a concatenated set of candidate responses and an instruction to select the one that is most consistent with the others, principally not involving rearranging, merging, or integrating components from different responses to form a new, hybrid answer, without any additional labeled training data nor an external reranking model such as consensus achieving algorithm used in [25]. Instead of performing explicit answer extraction and majority voting, USC leverages the LLM’s internal semantic reasoning to implicitly assess pair-wise similarity among the free-form outputs [26]. By employing a holistic evaluation that prompts the LLM to assess all responses together, USC eliminates the need for computationally expensive pair-wise comparisons while leveraging the model’s contextual and semantic understanding to capture nuances that explicit similarity metrics often miss, thereby ensuring broad applicability across diverse tasks. This process enables robust handling of open-ended tasks in real-world, such as summarization, creative question answering, and code generation, where answers can’t be trivially matched or grouped by exact string comparison. USC achieves performance comparable to standard self-consistency for math tasks and execution-based voting (where code snippets with identical runtime outputs get grouped) for code generation, without requiring explicit answer extraction or code execution, by leveraging the LLM’s semantic reasoning to compare candidate responses. Practically, USC exhibits robust performance, as randomizing candidate response order rarely affects the selected answer, indicating stable internal evaluation. Additionally, tailoring the final instruction (e.g., emphasizing detail or conciseness) allows customization of the selection process for specific tasks.

However, USC introduces challenges such as context-length constraints and potential biases (position bias, self-favor bias, over-trusting certain text styles) inherent in the LLM’s self-evaluation, highlighting a trade-off between its broad applicability and the precision offered by traditional SC in tasks amenable to discrete answer extraction. Moreover, standard SC’s majority vote implicitly gives a measure of how many solutions agreed on one final output, but USC’s final single choice lacks a straightforward numeric confidence measure (e.g., "we’re X% sure"). Internal consistency can be formally defined as the absence of conflicts or contradictions among all the points within an answer, ensuring harmonious alignment throughout the reasoning path. SC and USC, in their conventional form, rely exclusively on the model’s self-generated responses for verification, do not guarantee the ’internal consistency’ or ’logical coherence’ within the selected answer, without incorporating any external epistemic validation to ensure that its outputs are grounded in real-world facts, which means if the model is systematically biased or exhibits rationalization errors, the "most consistent" result could still be factually wrong. In the future, for human-AI agents collaboration system (HAACS), a calibration mechanism needs to be developed to perform epistemic check, output clustering and pairwise self-consistency explicitly.

Measuring and Ensuring Logical Consistency through Prompt Transformations
In real multi-step tasks, it often needs to refer back to what the model "already said." If the model cannot replicate its own sub-results consistently, it can’t reliably chain reasoning steps. And many problems are solved by combining sub-solutions. If the sub-solution changes or is applied incorrectly, we get logically contradictory answers. Thus two central forms of self-consistency are defined for LLMs, namely hypothetical consistency and compositional consistency [27]. The first requires that responses match across direct prompts and re-asked hypothetical prompts (e.g., "What would you say if…"), capturing the model’s ability to replicate its own outputs instead of contradicting prior statements. The second involves multi-step reasoning tasks in which sub-expressions are replaced with the model’s own previously generated answers, and the final composed result must remain stable. A formal framework delineates how to measure semantic equivalence between prompts and between outputs, along with procedures for creating new prompts and verifying whether the LLM’s responses maintain internal coherence.

In [27], self-consistency is formally defined using semantic equivalence. Given a specific set of prompt templates for string transformation, where each template contains exactly one placeholder that is substituted with a string, two strings are considered semantically equivalent if and only if, after substituting them into every prompt template in the set, the resulting strings remain semantically equivalent; in other words, a self-consistent model gives semantically-equivalent responses to semantically equivalent prompts. Internal coherence refers to an LLM’s ability to produce logically and semantically consistent outputs across variations of a prompt, such that rephrasing or decomposing a prompt (via hypothetical or compositional transformations) does not lead to contradictory or diverging answers. The procedures to test this involve creating new prompts by either rephrasing the original query (asking, for instance, "what would you say to…") for hypothetical consistency testing or by replacing sub-expressions in multi-step tasks with the model’s own prior responses for compositional consistency testing, and then verifying that the resulting outputs are semantically equivalent through structured evaluation methods such as multiple-choice selection or direct equivalence checks. However, these "consistency checks" relying on certain heuristics (e.g., multiple-choice or checking sub-parses) sometimes only measure an upper or lower bound of the true "logical equivalence", and the tasks to solve are somewhat simplified compared to the real-world multi-step tasks, which need more nuanced consistency hypothesis and testing procedure.

Experiments show that smaller GPT-3 variants exhibit near-random accuracy in recognizing their own prior completions when prompted hypothetically, and even larger models, including GPT-4, demonstrate persistent failures in compositional consistency, especially on arithmetic tasks, though both consistency rates improve somewhat when more in-context few-shot examples are given. While scaling improves these metrics to a degree, it is apparent that correctness and consistency only partially correlate, such that a correct sub-step may still be contradicted in the integrated response. These findings highlight the necessity of novel training or decoding strategies aimed at logically binding sub-solutions with final outputs, which ensure internal coherence, thereby enhancing trustworthiness in high-stakes, chain-of-thought tasks. It needs to highlight that the existing prevalent decoding methods like greedy decoding, beam search, or sampling still allow for significant self-contradictions in multi-step reasoning chains. Although the method reveals that new types of prompt transformations can break model consistency, it has not "solved" these observed issues but have laid the groundwork (formal definitions, test harnesses), and indicate the promising factors that call for attention like the decoding and training strategies for future improvements.

Identifying Limitations of Self-Consistency in Long-Context Tasks
Self-consistency, taking the method of aggregating multiple output samples, was examined in the long-context settings where transformers tend to exhibit position bias [28]. Self-consistency generates multiple responses by sampling the model n times with a non-zero temperature and then aggregates these outputs via majority voting to select the final answer or document. The analysis employed question answering (QA) and text retrieval (TR) tasks using both narrative-style passages and factual documents, each extended to thousands of tokens. In these tasks, models must distill precise answers from extensive narrative or factual texts for QA while accurately pinpointing the specific documents containing the necessary evidence for TR, highlighting the challenge of isolating key information in voluminous contexts. The design included systematically shifting the location of gold evidence (beginning, middle, end) and varying the number of distractor segments to observe whether repeatedly sampling model outputs and applying majority-vote aggregation, which are typical for self-consistency mechanism, could mitigate attention degradation across the entire context window. Results indicate that with self-consistency, only marginal gains in certain short-answer scenarios and, more often, performance drops. In particular, text retrieval tasks suffered from amplified position bias under majority voting, suggesting that repeated sampling and aggregation do not alleviate the model’s inherent difficulty in identifying middle or late-occurring evidence. This failure appears tied to correlated errors across the multiple samples, thereby reinforcing rather than correcting the model’s misalignment with long input segments. A key methodological takeaway from the study, which can be transferred to our HAACS designs, is that techniques successful in short contexts must undergo rigorous empirical validation before being applied to long contexts, as their effectiveness may not generalize.

Further technical scrutiny reveals that self-consistency does not sufficiently diversify the model’s reasoning paths when context length increases. The sampling mechanism amplifies pre-existing biases, favoring the front or back of the context relatively while neglecting other sections based on the results of texts retrieval, echoing the recent research findings that LLMs exhibit marked position biases in long contexts, displaying both primacy and recency effects and a U-shaped performance curve where mid-context information is underutilized. Overall, self-consistency’s performance depends on context length, position bias, and model scale while remaining largely insensitive to prompt design (whether the question is at the start or repeated at the end) or task type, exposing intrinsic limitations in long-context comprehension (i.e., needle-in-the-haystack scenario). The findings imply that architectural modifications beyond inference-time techniques like self-consistency, are needed to address position bias and to manage data more efficiently in scenarios where context length is substantially greater than conventional model windows. However, this study is limited to long-context QA and retrieval tasks with a basic self-consistency implementation, in need for future work to explore additional task types in the real-world (e.g., summarization or multi-steps reasoning tasks) and alternative aggregation strategies beyond simple majority voting to better address context position effects. In plain words, as input lengths for LLMs increase, the attention mechanisms become diluted, self-consistency, by simply re-sampling from the same biased distribution, fails to recover the subtle, relevant signals lost in long contexts. Therefore, practically for effective use of self-consistency in long-context tasks, apply a moderate temperature (e.g., 0.7-1.0) with a sufficient number of samples (around 8), while monitoring for diminishing returns, and consider segmenting large texts or employing external retrieval systems (e.g., a database or a vector store) before applying SC. Moreover, relying solely on prompt engineering to mitigate position bias is insufficient.

3.1.2 Game-Theoretic Equilibrium Re-ranking for Optimal Answer Selection

LLMs can either generate answers by sampling from their probability distribution or produce discriminative judgments by scoring candidate answers. These two modes can conflict, i.e., an LLM might generate one answer as most likely yet, when prompted differently, judge that same answer as incorrect. Such inconsistency leads to confusion about which output best represents the model’s "true" belief, determined by its parameterized knowledge. To solve these inconsistencies, [25] proposes a game theory based decoding algorithm to complement the ’self-consistency’ mechanism by equilibrium seeking to select the most promising output as answer for a given question. This approach models decoding as a regularized imperfect-information sequential signaling game, in which a "generator" selects candidate strings under either "correct" or "incorrect" modes, and a "discriminator" identifies each string’s true label. By leveraging KL-regularization to keep both their policies close to the base LM’s initial behavior, the final game solution is ensured to remain consistent with the model’s underlying probabilities. In plain words, the goal for this cooperative game is to find a pair of strategies, i.e., the discriminator’s objective is to correctly infer the hidden "correctness" label from the generator’s output; by contrast, the generator is incentivized to produce signals that clearly and unambiguously communicate that hidden label (i.e., correctness intent), until neither player can unilaterally improve their performance. Implementation is strictly prompt-based, no fine-tuning or training of the LM is performed. A small set of candidate answers is generated (either the given multiple-choice options or samples from open-ended text), and probabilities are collected under "correct" and "incorrect" prompts, as well as direct correctness classification prompts. These probabilities are then fed into a numerical no-regret algorithm (unrelated to neural computation), which iteratively updates each policy until they converge on a stable and sensible equilibrium, and pick the best candidate answer as consensus. Such equilibrium-ranking mechanism can be viewed as a variant of this multi-agent debate. This procedure resolves contradictory outputs by an equilibrium ranking of answers compared to other straightforward ranking heuristics, and consistently boosts accuracy in diverse question-answering tasks. However, only if the number of candidates is small (like 4 in multiple-choice QA), will the answers re-ranking method’s overhead be practically negligible, and for free-form QA, a finite set of candidates need to be sampled from the LM at first using top-k or nucleus sampling, and the quality and diversity of the sampled candidates heavily influence the solution searching space; if the initial samples distribution is biased or sampling a truly correct candidate set fails in the open-ended tasks, no amount of equilibrium refinement helps; even if the initial distribution is ideal, the game can not guarantee the locally optimal Nash equilibrium.

3.2 Tool Integration and Coordination in LLM-Based AI Agents

Effective utilization of external tools significantly enhances LLM-based AI agents’ capabilities, enabling them to handle complex, real-world tasks through dynamic integration of specialized functions and domain knowledge. Methods such as structured tool invocation, retriever-aware fine-tuning, and standardized communication protocols provide mechanisms for coherent and scalable agent-tool interactions; yet, the limitations in real-time feedback incorporation, static reasoning plans, external dependency reliability, and integration complexity remain critical challenges that need addressing for robust deployments.

Structured Tool Integration via Abstract Reasoning Plans
A novel training method separates logical reasoning from domain-specific data retrieval by having a language model first generate an abstract CoT using placeholders and then, in a distinct second phase, reify these placeholders via specialized external tools [29]. In other words, it uses a two-phase, one-shot process to separate the decision-making process (i.e., when a tool is needed) from the actual execution (i.e., how to retrieve the specific information), by first generating an abstract reasoning chain with placeholders. Then, specialized tools (which are implicitly chosen based on the type of sub-task, such as a math solver or a factual retriever) fill in these placeholders in parallel, thereby optimizing both the timing and the selection of tools used. The approach constructs fine-tuning data by rewriting existing step-by-step solutions into an abstract format, verified automatically with domain tools.

A key limitation is that the abstract reasoning plan is generated in a single pass without incorporating feedback from subsequent tool outputs, which means the plan remains static even if errors or unforeseen dependencies arise and it can not handle interactive problem solving. And it assumes that interdependent placeholders can be solved in parallel, which may be limiting in tasks with highly interwoven dependencies. Moreover, reliance on high-quality external tools introduces an external variable affecting performance, and the full-model fine-tuning required remains computationally intensive, suggesting that future work could explore parameter-efficient adaptations to extend the approach’s practical applicability.

Retriever-Augmented Fine-tuning for Accurate API Invocation
Gorilla addresses the challenge of generating accurate API calls by fine-tuning the LLaMA-7B model on a comprehensive dataset (APIBench) constructed from TorchHub, TensorFlow Hub, and HuggingFace APIs [30]. The approach relies on self-instructed instruction generation to produce a large and diverse training set of 10 instruction-API pairs for each of the 1,700+ APIs. This setup enables the model to learn various usage patterns and domain-specific constraints. A key advancement is retriever-aware training, which appends dynamically retrieved API documentation to the prompt during both training and inference, helping the model adapt to evolving or newly introduced APIs. Accuracy is measured via an AST sub-tree matching technique that pinpoints correct function calls structurally rather than by simple string matching. Ongoing dependencies on retriever quality, domain-specific data, and the complexities introduced by retriever integration are central considerations for future expansion, especially for tasks beyond machine learning APIs or in contexts where retrieval coverage may be incomplete.

Standardized Protocol for Secure and Scalable Tool Coordination
Model Context Protocol (MCP) offers a standardized, modular framework that replaces brittle, ad-hoc prompt engineering with a persistent JSON-RPC protocol for secure, stateful, and auditable tool invocation, ensuring every action is logged and subject to explicit human approval when needed [31]. By bridging the "last mile" problem for AI deployment, it eliminates the need for one-off custom integrations, solving the N×M integration challenge by enabling each tool to be implemented once as an MCP server that can be accessed by any number of agents via a standardized MCP client. This unified approach, with dynamic tool discovery, transport-agnostic communications, and context scoping, simplifies maintenance and scaling while enhancing consistency, interoperability, and human governance by empowering supervisors to monitor, govern, and intervene in AI agent actions as required.

3.3 Advanced Planning Strategies in LLM-Based AI Agents

For LLM-based AI agents managing complex, dynamic tasks, effective planning is indispensable. Recent research has established a comprehensive taxonomy of planning components that encompasses task decomposition, multi-plan selection, external planning support, reflection, and memory augmentation. In tandem, innovative systems such as HuggingGPT demonstrate a structured pipeline that orchestrates multimodal task execution using standardized templates and dynamic dependency management.

Taxonomy of LLM Planning and Decomposition
Planning is formally defined as generating a sequence of actions based on a given environment, goal, and specific parameters. Based on this formulation, the taxonomy in the survey [32] divides planning into five distinct yet interconnected components: task decomposition, multi-plan selection, external planner-aided planning, reflection and refinement, and memory-augmented planning. In task decomposition, two strategies are delineated: one that establishes sub-goals prior to planning (decomposition-first) and another that interleaves task breakdown with sub-task planning to adapt dynamically. Sub-goaling in mean-end analysis (MEA) can be seen as an adaptive process where planning and decomposition work in tandem. In this view, the planning component generates actions that reduce the gap between the current state and the goal, essentially serving as a difference-reduction mechanism, while the decompose (or sub-goaling) component dynamically breaks down the task into manageable sub-goals that address any remaining discrepancies. Systematic evaluations across interactive gaming, retrieval, and programming benchmarks reveal a trade-off between enhanced planning capabilities and increased computational overhead; improved performance is often accompanied by higher token consumption and more elaborate reasoning processes. Additionally, the survey critically identifies several challenges, including the propensity for hallucinations in LLM outputs, difficulties in adhering to complex constraints, inefficiencies in plan generation, limitations in processing multi-modal feedback, and the scarcity of fine-grained evaluation metrics.

HuggingGPT Pipeline for Coordinated Task Execution
HuggingGPT introduces a systematic pipeline where a LLM functions as a central controller to decompose complex, multimodal (i.e., crossing language, vision, speech, etc.) requests into a structured sequence of sub-tasks, each defined by a unique identifier, dependencies, and explicit input arguments [33]. This pipeline is partitioned into four distinct stages: task planning, model selection, task execution, and response generation. This process begins with a global planning stage, where the controller LLM parses the user input into a JSON-formatted list of tasks, each defined by a specific task type, unique identifier, dependency information, and required arguments. By enforcing a standardized slot-filling template (comprising "task," "id," "dep," and "args") and incorporating demonstration-based parsing within the prompt, the system guarantees consistent and precise task decomposition. Notably, unlike methods that simply batch all external tool calls without explicit coordination [29], HuggingGPT leverages its dependency metadata to orchestrate both sequential and parallel task execution, ensuring that tasks requiring outputs from prior steps are processed in the correct order. The resource dependencies are managed using symbolic placeholders (e.g., ‘<resource>-task_id‘), which are later dynamically replaced with actual outputs, ensuring that inter-task data flows are accurately maintained across the workflow. The subsequent stages further refine this algorithmic planning approach by dynamically assigning expert models to each task based on textual descriptions and popularity-based filtering, thereby bridging the gap between general-purpose reasoning and specialized model execution. This in-context task-model assignment minimizes token usage. While the global planning method efficiently produces a complete task graph in a single query, it also raises challenges regarding optimality and error management as task complexity increases. The design effectively addresses the challenge of integrating diverse model functionalities by treating language as a universal interface, yet it also underscores critical issues such as dependency reliability, execution overhead, and the absence of robust error-recovery mechanisms.

3.4 Cybernetic Perspectives on Goal-Seeking Adaptive Agency

Cybernetic-inspired approaches emphasize the iterative, adaptive interplay between AI agents and their environment through structured feedback loops. Recent developments integrate reflection mechanisms, long-term memory management, and explicit environmental verification into language-model workflows, creating goal-seeking agents capable of dynamic learning and self-adjustment. These methods combine internal and external feedback to progressively refine behavior, highlighting essential concepts from cybernetics, such as closed-loop control, evaluative reflection, and semantic gradient optimization, thereby enabling agents to robustly navigate complex, uncertain problem spaces.

3.4.1 Reflective Iteration through Internal and External Criticism

An iterative "critique-refine" cycle, mirroring the "critic-reflect" mechanism, allows language models to autonomously generate outputs, self-evaluate, and incrementally improve their results. Recent advancements have refined this loop by grounding critiques in external, real-world evidence, effectively addressing limitations associated with purely internal self-reflection methods, such as hallucinations or inadequate reasoning coherence. These augmented criticize-reflect cycles enhance both correctness and robustness in multi-step reasoning, particularly benefiting high-stakes scenarios.

Autonomous Iterative Refinement via Prompt-Driven Self-Critique
An iterative framework SELF-REFINE enables a LLM to generate an initial draft, autonomously critique it, and then refine its output, all within a single pass that leverages carefully designed few-shot prompts [34]. It formulates the process as follows: given an input (e.g., question), an initial output y0y_{0} is generated via a prompt pgenp_{\text{gen}}; then, a feedback step uses a prompt pf​bp_{fb} to produce actionable and specific critiques ftf^{t} for the current output yty_{t}; finally, a refinement step utilizes another prompt prefinep_{\text{refine}} that incorporates both the previous output and its corresponding feedback, yielding a revised output yt+1y_{t+1}. This process is repeated until a stopping criterion is met, with the model maintaining a history of outputs and feedback to avoid repeating earlier mistakes.

Special issues addressed include the challenge of refining "draft-able" solutions in tasks with complex or multi-dimensional objectives and managing potential non-monotonic improvements by tracking quality scores across iterations. However, the method critically depends on the intrinsic self-critique ability of the language model and careful prompt engineering, and may face context window constraints when incorporating extensive feedback history.

Externally Anchored Reflection for Robust Error Correction
CRITIC extends a standard "criticize-reflect" approach by anchoring the reflection step in evidence retrieved from external tools, rather than relying solely on the model’s internal reasoning. Like a typical "draft → critique → refine" loop, it starts with an LLM output (draft), but immediately verifies that output against real-world signals such as search results or code execution logs [35]. This verification then produces a grounded critique, which the LLM applies to correct or refine its original text. By integrating the external environment, be it a search API, interpreter, or toxicity evaluator, CRITIC goes beyond conventional self-reflection diagrams, providing more robust error detection and actionable feedback.

Specifically, the framework follows a formal "verify → critique → correct" pipeline, reminiscent of a fixed-point iteration. After a first pass, the LLM inspects the newly surfaced tool-based evidence to identify specific flaws, then merges that critique back into the generation process. This design addresses the limitations of purely internal self-checking, often riddled with unsubstantiated "hallucinations", by systematically introducing external checks that can reveal factual inconsistencies, code bugs, or toxic expressions. In doing so, CRITIC refines the "criticize-reflect" concept into a more comprehensive feedback loop, lowering the likelihood of overlooked errors and enabling robust, iterative improvements in a black-box LLM setting.

3.4.2 Structured Memory and Extended ReAct-Style Adaptations

ReAct and its variants structure an LLM’s reasoning by cycling through thought, action, and observation. Extended frameworks like RAISE and Reflexion integrate external memory modules, evaluation signals, or additional controllers to handle multi-turn dialogues, domain-specific constraints, and even iterative online adaptation. Together, these methods demonstrate how careful orchestration of short-term and long-term memory, along with external oversight, can tackle increasingly complex tasks.

ReAct and RAISE—Balancing Transparency with Memory Efficiency
ReAct [36] uses a unified sequence of "Thought-Action-Observation" at each turn, retaining all prior reasoning and actions directly in the prompt. Structurally, this design offers transparency, i.e., each new turn is supplied with the entire chain of events from before, allowing the model to see its own reasoning history in full. However, this single memory track can lead to unwieldy prompts in longer dialogues, since every intermediate step is replayed regardless of whether it remains relevant. RAISE, on the other hand, refines this structure by splitting memory into two components, a Scratchpad (short-term) and an Examples Retrieval mechanism (long-term) [37]. Specifically, the Scratchpad works as a transient buffer, capturing relevant details from recent dialogue turns and tool outputs so that only the most immediately necessary facts are carried into the next step. Meanwhile, the Examples module reaches into a long-term store of curated Q-A pairs that illustrate ideal agent responses in similar scenarios, thus reinforcing domain-specific behaviors without cluttering the prompt with every prior reasoning step. This architectural dual-memory system is further integrated into a comprehensive working memory (including conversation history, system prompt, and task trajectory) and a controller with the preset trigger conditions that orchestrates their interplay. When a new query arrives, the controller updates the Scratchpad with fresh observations or partial results, selectively recalls matching examples from the long-term memory, and generates a structured prompt that the LLM uses to plan its next actions. This layering ensures the agent remains focused on key information, seamlessly incorporates any necessary domain knowledge, and avoids replaying an exhaustive history of "Thought-Action-Observation" sequences. Moreover, by pairing the Scratchpad and Examples retrieval with a systematic fine-tuning pipeline, RAISE enables smooth integration of new domain rules and constraints from a high-quality, domain-specific dataset constructed by GPT-4 enhanced real-world dialogues based on specific criteria.

While ReAct often assumes a single query defined at the outset, RAISE addresses more real-world, multi-turn conversations that may include multiple objectives over time. Nonetheless, both frameworks rely on an autonomous loop with limited on-the-fly adaptability: RAISE’s Scratchpad updates and Examples retrieval, for instance, are governed by predefined rule-based triggers tailored to specific domains, which can reduce flexibility if conversation patterns deviate from the domain behavior logic unexpectedly. Moreover, neither ReAct nor RAISE incorporates active external oversight from either humans or other models to evaluate intermediate results or feedback rewards sporadically nor to help update the examples in the long-term memory dynamically during the online dialogue itself, potentially leading to less dynamic rectification of reasoning process.

Reflexion—Reward-Guided Memory Buffers for Iterative Learning
To better accumulate insights from interaction signals between environment and the agent during online trials, the external modules, external Evaluator and Self-Reflection process feedback from observations and provide informative verbal feedback to the long-term memories of LLM agent as Actor [38]. Each trial produces a trajectory, a reward signal, and a self-reflection, which is appended to a memory buffer. In the standard formulation, Reflexion treats each full trajectory (i.e., an entire attempt from start to finish) as the unit of evaluation before generating a self-reflection. The Evaluator observes all action-observation pairs within that trajectory, then provides a reward or diagnostic signal (possibly informed by heuristics or the LLM’s own analysis). The Self-Reflection model subsequently uses those action-observation pairs (along with the reward signal) to produce verbal feedback, which is stored in a long-term memory buffer. That feedback is then included as additional context when the agent attempts the task again. While the paper’s algorithm focuses on trajectory-level evaluation and reflection, one could in principle implement finer-grained intervals (e.g., reflecting mid-trajectory), but the core experiments reflect at the completion of each full trial.

A potential limitation of Reflexion is its reliance on the inherent self-evaluation capabilities of the LLM, or on heuristically defined evaluators, to generate the verbal feedback used for guiding subsequent actions. This dependency can lead to variability in the quality of the feedback, and without formal convergence guarantees, there is no assurance that the iterative self-reflection process will consistently steer the Actor toward correct outcomes. Compared to RAISE, which relies on pre-built offline examples and expensive fine-tuning [37], Reflexion actively updates its Actor memories with tailored insights gained from online trials via external modules to inform the future attempts.

From cybernetic perspective, the workflow in [38] is still ReAct-like closed-loop control feedback system but with additional modules to process the raw sparse reward signal, such as a binary success status (success/fail) and then inform the long-term episodic memories of Actor agent by amplifying the evaluation signals to more explicit and interpretable experience summaries. This mechanism is designed to handle long trajectories, localize points of failure, and provide verbal feedback as "semantic gradient" optimization signals through natural language rather than numeric rewards. However the verbal reflection might keep reinforcing a suboptimal path if the reflection does not pinpoint the real cause. Reflexion operates in an iterative manner, where the agent continually updates its text-based memory between trials without modifying model weights. This design is amenable to online adaptation as long as the environment or task allows repeated trials or partial resets, which are usually not the cases for open-world or high-exploration tasks unfortunately. Because the framework only requires (1) generating actions, (2) receiving feedback, and (3) storing self-reflections in memory for subsequent attempts, it can be applied in real-world scenarios where each "round" of interaction provides new data for reflection. The memory-based approach does not rely on gradient-based training loops, so it can feasibly integrate new insights on the fly, as long as a suitable source of feedback (environment signals or internal checks) is available in each iteration. [39] used a similar Evaluator module as a critic to provide insights into the current configuration of the multi-agent network structure, thereby informing the subsequent reflection to improve its organizational design. This design constrains complexity by retaining a manageable memory window of critical reflections while preserving an interpretable record of the policy’s evolution over iterative attempts. The future memory component of Reflexion can be extended with more advanced structures such as a sliding-window to handle the growing contexts, symbolic and non-symbolic knowledge bases, vector embedding databases or traditional SQL databases.

Multi-modal Integration through Actionable Reasoning
MM-REACT builds on the core principles of the ReAct framework by leveraging a chain-of-thought approach that interleaves reasoning with actionable outputs, but it extends this paradigm into the multimodal domain [40]. However, MM-REACT differentiates itself by parsing the chain-of-thought output from ChatGPT into distinct segments for model selection and pure reasoning, effectively creating a reasoning-action-reasoning loop. In this loop, ChatGPT issues explicit action commands to invoke specialized vision models (e.g., for image captioning, OCR, or object tagging) and then integrates their standardized textual outputs back into the dialogue to refine subsequent reasoning steps. The architecture circumvents the need for resource-intensive joint finetuning by orchestrating separate, pre-trained models through prompt engineering, thus enabling advanced tasks like visual math reasoning, spatial understanding, multi-image aggregation, and multi-hop document analysis. Key technical contributions include dynamic tool allocation, iterative observation integration, and standardized output formats that ensure interoperability between distinct modalities. Although competitive zero-shot performance is achieved when compared with jointly trained multimodal models, challenges remain due to prompt dependency, context window limitations, and potential error propagation from the integrated vision experts
