Implicature, Epistemic Reasoning, and Limitations in Human-AI Agent Teams
Implicature-based strategies succeed well in self-play (AI-vs-AI), significantly outperforming the entropy-based baseline and boosting perceived human-likeness by 71% in user studies, demonstrating enhanced human synergy. This approach explicitly acknowledges that effective collaboration depends not just on what an agent knows, but also critically on understanding what its partner might know or not know. However, no real performance boost is observed in actual human-AI Agent teams (with game performance similar to state-of-the-art methods) due to the non-adaptive approach and varied play styles of human participants.

This human synergy relies heavily on both partners sharing the same reasoning logic. If a human partner does not interpret single-card hints in the "correct" way, the AI agents cannot gracefully recover or shift strategy, causing miscommunications. Thus, a more generalizable strategy is needed to allow AI agents to continuously update how their human partner interprets or gives hints. Moreover, the system only partially addresses the full breadth of Gricean maxims, which are the cooperative principles outlining how, in everyday social interactions, speakers and listeners work together and assume mutual understanding to achieve effective communication. Humans often flout or manipulate multiple maxims flexibly, while the AI focuses narrowly on single-card hints as stylized "implicature signals.

4.6 Situated Collaboration between Human and LLM-Driven Agents in Cyberspace

By merging LLMs with GUI parsing, modern systems dynamically interpret interfaces and generate multi-step action plans, obviating the need for manual scripts. This approach has proven valuable for complex software tasks, yet it also highlights how human cognitive constraints differ significantly from agent-to-agent communication, necessitating interfaces that preserve human oversight and clarity.

Large Action Models and GUI-Based Automation
LLM-driven GUI agents combine LLMs with screenshot-based interface parsing to automate software interactions. To create a specialized Large Action Model (LAM) for these agents, user prompts, matching screenshots, widget trees, and multi-step action sequences are gathered, cleaned, and annotated as training data, which is then used to fine-tune a broad LLM (e.g., GPT-4 or open-source Qwen-VL) on this domain-specific dataset. By integrating computer vision models to detect and classify GUI elements in the cyberspace, such as buttons, text fields, or menus, these agents construct a semantically rich state representation of the current UI. LAMs then generate action sequences aligned with the user’s instruction and the inferred screen context, relying on short- or long-term memory for multi-step tasks. This approach reduces manual scripting requirements, allowing for dynamic planning and goal-directed navigation. It has been applied across web, mobile, and desktop applications to handle tasks like end-to-end testing, cross-application automation, and user assistance [65].

Such systems seek to address key limitations found in earlier script-based or rule-driven tools. They predict likely paths through complex workflows by referencing learned mappings, user instructions, and multi-step planning algorithms, rather than relying on guesswork. Self-reflection loops, error detection, and fallback mechanisms further improve resilience and accuracy. Although challenges remain, particularly around speed, privacy, coverage in dynamic or specialized applications, handling ambiguous instructions without human clarification loop, ensuring reliability in highly dynamic interfaces, these agents stand poised to transform both routine automation and larger-scale business processes.

Designing Interfaces Sensitive to Human Cognitive Constraints

4.7 Epistemological Foundations and Iterative Design for Human-Machine Systems

An epistemological framework grounded in systematically defined ontological elements, i.e., structure, function, context, resources, and knowledge, provides a robust foundation for iterative system design that seamlessly integrates human and machine components, including AI agents. Through iterative performance modeling, human-in-the-loop simulations, and the digital twin, and active documentation, this methodology actively accommodates emergent behaviors and dynamic complexity. However, contemporary advancements in AI agents, especially those powered by LLMs, necessitate revisiting these epistemological foundations and their iterative design processes to accommodate the heightened autonomy, reasoning capabilities, and multi-agent coordination that increasingly challenge traditional human-machine system (HMS) paradigms.

Unified Ontological Foundation for Iterative System Design
An epistemological framework for human-machine (including AI technique) system is built on carefully defined axioms and a systematic ontology, unifying disparate concepts, i.e., structure (the physical or cognitive makeup), function (the operational role), context (the environmental conditions and situational variables), resources (the supporting subsystems or assets), and knowledge (integrating both procedural "know-how" and declarative "know-what"), introducing the notion of a system-of-systems (SoS) with triple (role, a context of validity, and resources) that shapes how tasks turn into actual activities [66].

This unified framework serves as the backbone for an iterative design process that not only formalizes the initial system requirements but also robustly accommodates emergent behaviors. Emergence is addressed by enabling the system to shift from rigid, predefined procedures to dynamic, goal-driven problem solving, ensuring that unexpected functions are identified and integrated as the system evolves.

Iterative Modeling with Human-in-the-Loop and Digital Twins
The iterative design procedure, weaves these ontological elements together in a systematic cycle: First, a task analysis is performed using flowchart methods to capture the procedural, step-by-step operations. Next, a function analysis elicits the declarative dimensions by defining roles, resources, and constraints. The results from task and function analysis as well as feedback from human-in-the-loop simulations are merged into an iterative performance model that quantifies high-level metrics, such as safety, workload, and trust, where human-in-the-loop simulations reveal the gap between prescribed tasks and actual activities. The integration of digital twin technology, divided into predictive and explanatory models, provides a dynamic, evolving representation that supports early design validation, agile iteration, and emergent behavior identification, thereby ensuring that human factors are embedded throughout the system’s life cycle.

Subsequent activity analyses then expose emergent behaviors, prompting refinements that lead to updated performance evaluations. This cycle repeats until the system converges on a stable, acceptable configuration, while maintaining an Active Design Document (ADD) for traceability, thereby ensuring that the human-machine system design solution remains flexible and responsive to emergent problem-solving demands. The ADD can be regarded as a mirror of common ground, as described in [13].

Adapting Epistemological Frameworks to Advanced AI Agent Autonomy
Although the framework successfully synthesizes constructivist and realist perspectives, grounding human systems integration in both empirical evidence and abstract theory through a unified ontology and foundational axioms for both human and machine, it does not explicitly address the emerging role of AI agents powered by LLMs. These AI agents increasingly demonstrate reasoning abilities on par with, or even exceeding, those of human experts, coupled with autonomy enabled by advanced cybernetic design and multi-agent coordination.

While the framework does emphasize knowledge evolution and emergence handling through iterative design, leveraging human-in-the-loop simulations and digital twin techniques to continuously update models and capture emergent behaviors, in effect, the revolutionary capabilities of these AI agents on the whole may lead to a critical qualitative shift, where this system design paradigms are challenged by AI teams capable of autonomously organizing, planning, and reconfiguring tasks.

Rethinking Task Coordination for Synergistic HAACS
To fully harness the potential of real human-AI agent collaboration, task decomposition and assignment must be rethought. This involves not only exploiting known physical, digital and cognitive resources but also actively exploring the unknowns mainly through guided practices for collective problem solving and knowledge management. Each element within a system should be regarded as an independent agent that integrates both physical and cognitive components for effective reasoning and tool usage.

4.8 Human-Centered Interfaces for Concurrent and Load-Sensitive Collaboration

Real-world collaboration rarely unfolds in neatly synchronized steps. As AI-driven systems grow more capable of processing large, rapidly updated state information, collaborative interfaces must be designed to meet human cognitive constraints and preserve intuitive oversight. This calls for new mechanisms that time or filter communication flow, preventing overload while enabling meaningful human-agent coordination.

Bridging Simulation and Reality with Adaptive Interfaces Previous studies (e.g., [45], [39],[60]) mostly have humans control virtual agents to collaborate with other agents in a simulated environment. These trials are synchronous and step-based, which conflicts with the concurrent nature of real-world human-agent coordination.

Tailoring Collaborative Interfaces to Human Cognitive Constraints
The current implementations also lack a mechanism to ensure that coordination with AI agents, information communication and demonstration fit within human cognitive loads and constraints. The limits on an human’s ability to employ efficient strategies arise from the very small capacity of the short-term memory structure (approximately seven chunks) and the relatively long time (around 8 seconds) required to transfer a chunk from short-term to long-term memory. The capacity of short-term memory is defined by the number of chunks it can hold and the time required to transfer an item or chunk into long-term memory. In other words, short-term capacity and fixation parameters are the principal and almost sole characteristics of an information processing system [46].

Under time constraints, there may be a large volume of observation and communication data that is easy for an AI agent to process, but this can overwhelm human cognitive loads in the real world. We need to allow agents to "intervene" in real-world scenarios with novel human-AI agent collaboration interfaces, tailored to human information processing systems.

4.9 Comparative Analysis and Selection Criteria for Single and Multi-Agent Architectures

The choice between single-agent and multi-agent configurations significantly impacts the effectiveness, concurrency, and flexibility of HAAC. While single-agent systems excel under clear task definitions, well-structured feedback, and sequential decision pipelines, multi-agent setups offer inherent parallelism and agility in dynamically evolving environments. Additionally, reconsidering agent boundaries through controllability and coupling criteria clarifies when an internal system component transitions into a cooperative, external entity, helping to strategically delineate and select appropriate architectures based on task complexity and coordination demands.

Conditional Selection of Single-Agent versus Multi-Agent Methods
In contexts where complex reasoning and effective tool usage are essential, both single- and multi-agent methods can yield high performance [24]. Single-agent approaches excel when they are provided with a well-defined persona, an appropriate tool set, avenues for human feedback, and a mechanism for iterative improvement. For collaborative efforts on more intricate goals, leveraging at least one of these strategies enhances performance: establishing clear leadership, incorporating structured planning phases with refinement opportunities, implementing selective message filtering, and assembling dynamic teams that match specific skill sets to relevant sub-tasks. Employing any of these elements often outperforms both straightforward single-agent solutions and multi-agent approaches lacking such features.

Asynchrony and Parallelism in Single versus Multi-Agent Configurations
From one standpoint, single-agent systems can issue asynchronous requests yet ultimately rely on a sequential decision-making pipeline, thus limiting the degree of true parallelism. Although the single agent can manage multiple tasks in an overlapping fashion, a single agent must still progress through tasks sequentially, pausing for each set of asynchronous operations to finish before assessing outcomes and moving on, introducing latency and reducing its capacity for concurrent operations [24].

From another standpoint, multi-agent architectures distribute responsibilities among independent entities, each of which can execute tasks simultaneously across different domains or objectives and proceed without waiting for global synchronization. This division of labor fosters a higher degree of actual parallel task handling and agility, as each agent can adapt its plan without being constrained by the status of tasks managed elsewhere. The potential trade-off lies in the increased coordination overhead inherent in multi-agent systems, balanced against the benefits of true parallel execution that mitigate bottlenecks observed in sequential approaches.

Rethinking Agent Boundaries based on Controllability and Coupling
Regarding the question on the boundary between an agent and its environment, a critical resolution lies in framing boundaries through controllability and coupling [51]. For example, a publicly modifiable Wikipedia database is external, while an offline, agent-controlled version qualifies as internal memory. Likewise, code execution on an internal virtual environment is considered an internal reasoning action, contrasting with external grounding when executed on an external machine with potential security vulnerabilities. Tightly coupled components, such as interdependent proposal and evaluation prompts, are best regarded as part of a single agent, whereas independently useful processes may support a multi-agent perspective. From Simon’s perspective, a goal-seeking adaptive system as an artefact has an interface, which separates its inner environment from the outer environment [46]. The interface serves a crucial function by linking the internal mechanics of the system with external factors, ensuring that the system operates effectively within its context. This distinction between the inner and outer environments is central to understanding how systems adapt to their surroundings and how the outer environment interacts with and influences the system. The agent can be regarded as an artefact, and its interface configuration determines how it interacts with the external environment and other agents.

The approach in [51] can also be interpreted from a cybernetic perspective, i.e., dynamic system control, where an agent’s "controllability permissions" align with the idea of a control matrix, and "coupling" parallels the system matrix used in dynamic system decomposition. This viewpoint helps generalize how we determine what is internal or external for an agent, and help examine when and under which conditions the agent maintains sufficient independence. As an analogy, a quadrotor’s dynamics can only be decomposed into four interdependent sub-systems under certain state conditions, and similarly, an agent’s boundary between internal and external elements remains fluid based on the requirements and constraints that preserve the agent’s autonomy and keep necessary cooperation.

5 Openness and Complexity in a Systems-Theoretic Framework

Systems exist along continuums of scale (small, large, giant) and complexity (simple, multi-layered, dynamically adaptive). The degree of openness, i.e., how freely matter, energy, and information traverse system boundaries, further shapes the emergence of new behaviors and organizational structures. Living systems theory (LST), synergetics, non-equilibrium dynamics, and cybernetics each contribute foundational ideas for analyzing these open complex systems. When we extend these principles to HAACS, we observe parallel themes: the interplay of diverse agents, flows of energy and information, and emergent coordination patterns. This section synthesizes these perspectives, illustrating how open complex systems principles serve as a lens for designing and evaluating robust, self-organizing HAACS.

5.1 Complexity, Openness, and Hierarchy in Systems

Systems exhibit diverse structures and behaviors depending on how many parts they contain (scale), how these parts interrelate (complexity), and whether they exchange information, energy, or matter with their surroundings (openness). Equally important is the role of hierarchical arrangements, in which subsystems are nearly decomposable yet collectively give rise to emergent dynamics. Understanding these foundational principles clarifies how systems, from small and simple setups to vast, open, and complex multi-agent networks, adapt, evolve, and coordinate across different levels of organization.

5.1.1 From Simple to Complex and the Emergence of Non-Linear Dynamics

As systems grow in scale and diversity, they shift from small, easily modeled constructs to large or even "giant" configurations that demand statistical methods to handle innumerable interactions. Complexity emerges through both structural interconnections and context-dependent interactions, introducing non-linear behaviors and adaptive responses that cannot be understood by summing individual parts.

Progression from Small to Giant Systems
Systems can be categorized based on their complexity, hierarchical levels, and openness. At the most fundamental level, simple systems consist of relatively few subsystems with straightforward interactions, allowing for direct analysis and synthesis of their dynamics. As the number of subsystems increases, small systems become large systems, still amenable to direct computational modeling, albeit requiring significant processing power. Beyond this threshold, giant systems arise, where the sheer scale of subsystems (ranging from thousands to trillions) makes direct modeling infeasible, necessitating statistical methods to generalize behaviors while disregarding microscopic details. When such giant systems incorporate a high diversity of subsystems with intricate hierarchical structures and dynamic interrelations, they evolve into complex giant systems, characterized by emergent properties, adaptability, and non-linearity. Thus, as the number of subsystems increases, a system can be categorized as small, large, or giant. Meanwhile, as the complexity of interactions among subsystems and the diversity of subsystem types increase, the system transitions from simple to complex.

Multifaceted Nature of Complexity
Complexity is conceived as a multifaceted phenomenon emerging from both the structural interconnections of physical and cognitive system components and the dynamic, context-dependent interactions among them [66]. It is characterized by a dense network of nodes and links, where each node represents a subsystem (human or machine) whose interactions can lead to emergent behaviors that cannot be reduced to the sum of individual parts. Moreover, complexity is intimately tied to situational awareness, the need to continuously interpret, adapt to, and integrate multiple contextual variables (such as time, state history, and environmental conditions) that affect system performance.

5.1.2 Openness and the Formation of Open Complex Systems

The extent to which a system exchanges matter, energy, and information with its environment shapes its adaptation and evolution. Fully open systems, especially at a massive scale, manifest a high degree of unpredictability, calling for interdisciplinary approaches that surpass reductionist analysis.

Closed vs. Open Dynamics
The degree of openness further distinguishes systems: closed systems function in isolation with impermeable boundaries that completely prevent the transmission of matter, energy, or any form of information [67], whereas open systems continuously exchange information, energy, and matter with their environment, shaping their structure and evolution over time. The most intricate category encompasses open complex giant systems [56], where subsystems exhibit many varieties, diverse knowledge representation, acquisition, and learning mechanisms, multi-modal communication, and evolving structures, rendering them unpredictable and beyond the reach of traditional computational models.

Recursiveness in Open Systems and the Need for Interdisciplinary Perspectives
An open complex system is inherently recursive. A human being, as an individual, is an open complex system, continuously exchanging energy, information, and matter with the environment, and to gain knowledge by learning and interacting with the outsides world. Similarly, society such as the internet that connects users, composed of numerous interconnected individuals, is also an open complex system, evolving dynamically through collective interactions and knowledge acquisition. Understanding such systems demands interdisciplinary approaches that go beyond reductionist analysis, since there are numerous and unknown meso-levels between the observable whole and its subsystems.

5.1.3 Hierarchical Structures and Multi-Level Interactions

Hierarchy describes how subsystems nest within larger wholes, each performing sub-functions that contribute to overall objectives. In nearly decomposable systems, local interactions dominate in the short run, while longer-run global effects gradually propagate through the hierarchy, balancing autonomy with interdependence and often accelerating evolutionary adaptation.

Defining Hierarchy and Functional Subdivisions
Hierarchy refers to the structure of all complex systems that can be analyzed into successive sets of subsystems. In such a hierarchical arrangement, each component performs particular "sub-functions" contributing to the overall function. Just as the "inner environment" of a whole adaptive system can be described by specifying its functions rather than detailing its mechanisms, each subsystem can likewise be defined by its sub-functions without requiring precise specifications of how those functions are implemented.

Adopting this function-oriented view encourages the design and modeling of multi-agent systems in a way that is independent of the mechanisms carrying out the functions. In practical terms, this leads to a form of task decomposition in which a complete design is broken into functional components—a process that is not unique. For organizations, work may be divided by sub-functions, processes, areas, or other criteria, meaning that organizational theory often deals with multiple "alternative decompositions" of a collection of interrelated tasks. A generator-test cycle (referred to in some publications as "propose-evaluate" [51]) is then used to generate possible alternatives and test them against requirements and constraints.

Multi-Scale Temporal Dynamics and Near Decomposability in Hierarchical Systems
In hierarchical systems, evolution occurs more rapidly than in non-hierarchical systems due to selectivity from environment. Interactions in hierarchical systems occur among and within subsystems that operate at different rates of change, i.e., higher-frequency dynamics occur within subsystems, while lower-frequency dynamics emerge at the macro-level of the system. Similarly, a designed multi-agent framework can be categorized into fast- and slow-changing levels, both within and among agents. Such systems share common properties that are "independent" of specific content; hierarchy is not confined to "authority" structures because real systems involve numerous "inter-parts" relations.

The term "nearly decomposable" means that interactions among subsystem components are relatively weak, though not insignificant. In hierarchical systems characterized by nearly decomposable interactions, the short-run behavior of each subsystem is approximately independent of that of others. This independence allows individual subsystems to be examined in detail without accounting for slower, inter-system interactions. Over the long run, however, the behavior of any component depends on that of other components in an aggregate way. Additionally, executives situated higher in the hierarchy tend to have longer planning horizons and greater intervals between interactions, reflecting the higher average duration of interaction associated with top-tier positions.

5.2 Living Systems Theory as a Meta-Framework for Multi-Level Systems

Living Systems Theory (LST) conceptualizes biological and social entities as dynamic, open organizations of matter, energy, and information sustained by specialized subsystems working in concert. By positing multiple hierarchical levels and core functional processes, it offers a wide-ranging lens to interpret how complex living structures emerge, maintain homeostasis, and evolve. While originally focused on biological systems, LST’s core propositions can serve as a powerful guiding framework for analyzing and designing multi-layered HMS and HAACS in modern contexts.

5.2.1 Definition and Core Composition of Living Systems

Living systems are open, self-regulating organizations that balance matter-energy flows with information processing. Each subsystem fulfills distinct functions, reflecting the physical constraints of energy conversion and the need for coordinated control. This section outlines the essential building blocks and hierarchical arrangements fundamental to LST.

Characterizing Living Systems as Open and Self-Regulating Entities
A living system, as Miller describes, is an open, self-regulating developing, reproducing organization of matter and energy constantly shaped and sustained by information flows that coordinate its critical subsystems in a region in physical space-time, such as ingestor, distributor, and decider, so it can maintain homeostasis and respond to the environment’s demands with purposes and goals respectively [67].

Physical Reality of Matter and Energy Conversions
Each of these subsystems, tackles essential processes (e.g., nutrient uptake, waste removal, information transfer, control the entire system and synchronizes its components) that cannot be fulfilled by a single all-purpose "algorithm" because the physical reality of matter-energy conversions imposes distinct structures for specialized tasks.

Hierarchical Levels and Critical Subsystems
Complex structures conducting can be identified at seven hierarchical levels (cell, organ, organism, group, organization, society and supranational systems), and the systems at each of the seven levels have the same 19 types of critical subsystems [68], i.e., Reproducer, Boundary, Ingestor, Distributor, Converter, Producer, Matter-Energy Storage, Extruder, Motor, Supporter, Input Transducer, Internal Transducer, Channel, Net, Associator, Memory, Decider, Encoder, Output Transducer. Later on, an additional Timer module extended the number of critical subsystems to 20 types (see [61]).

Analogously, we observe that the vertical and horizontal structures for collaborative decision-making among multi-agents in [42] can be regarded as the instances of the subsystem of channel and net at the group level of the living systems [68].

5.2.2 Information-Energy-Matter and Progressive Differentiation

Living systems exhibit a continual interplay of matter, energy, and information flows. The resulting differentiation of subsystems, guided by feedback loops and evolving "blueprints," underpins their adaptive capacities. Here, we explore how these elements unify to maintain low entropy and foster increasingly sophisticated structures over multiple scales.

Synergistic Roles of Information and Matter-Energy
Rather than being a mere bundle of ad hoc functional modules, living systems rely on enduring, specialized subsystems collaborating in parallel, whose differentiation reflects both the physics of energy and matter (e.g., converter, producer, motor) and the functionalities of information processing (e.g., input, output and internal transducer, channel and net, associators, deciders, encoder, memory).

Evolutionary Principles and Progressive Specialization
They possess a DNA-like charter, serving as the foundational template, the original ’blueprint’ or ’program’—that dictates their structure and process from inception. This structural and functional process diversity allows the system to handle diverse inputs, maintain low entropy (survives the trend of entropy increase by absorbing negative entropy and expelling high-entropy byproducts) through negative feedback. And the structure and processes of a given subsystem are more complex at a more advanced level than at the less advanced ones, exemplifying the evolutionary principles of ’shred-out’ as a process of progressive labor division, differentiation, and function specialization for each subsystem [68].

Level-Specific Propositions and Cross-Level Identities
The hypothesized cross-level formal identities form the core of General Living Systems Theory, with propositions that are demonstrably applicable to multiple levels of living systems, and many more can be incorporated with ease. However, propositions relevant only to specific levels pertain to emergent structures and processes that do not exist at lower levels. Conversely, some hypotheses or propositions apply solely to structures and processes characteristic of lower-level systems, which are absent at higher levels.

5.2.3 Applicability, Practical Value, and Limitations in Modern Contexts

While LST provides a foundational road-map for analyzing multi-tiered entities, it also presents certain constraints when extended to AI-based systems. Intelligent machines can function with relative autonomy, challenging the classic notion of "nonliving artifacts." This section addresses how LST can serve as a heuristic for HAACS, along with its boundaries and potential updates.

Essential Functional Categories for Homeostasis
LST, originally formulated as a parsimonious framework of basic concepts through empirical observations of plants, animals, and social organizations of multi-scales, provides a set of essential functional categories to explain how living systems maintain homeostasis, going counter to the current of increasing entropy.

Reframing Nonliving Artifacts in Higher-Level Systems
In this framework, machines and computers are viewed as nonliving artifacts rather than independent living entities, serving as structural or functional components that enhance or supplement the information and matter-energy processes of higher-level living systems (e.g., groups, organizations, societies).

Heuristic Guidance and Meta-Theoretical Utility
However, for intelligent agents or general AI systems endowed with increasingly sophisticated reasoning and tool usage capabilities, capable of functioning autonomously as human-like subjects alongside humans, there is a notable gap within LST. Although LST acknowledges adjustment processes within living systems to handle excesses or deficits of essential information-matter-energy inputs [67], it does not explicitly nor analytically address how these principles extend to human AI agents collaborations (HAACs), specifically, how they should coordinate, evolve, and self-organize to achieve goals, sustain communication, and explore and adapt to changing environments.

Consequently, while these AI agents extend beyond the traditional confines of purely biological organisms, LST remains valuable as a heuristic or guiding conceptual framework. It can help practitioners systematically verify whether the designed HAACS account for vital considerations such as managing information and energy flows, maintaining boundaries and internal stability, providing feedback loops, adjusting to external demands, ensuring redundancy, etc.

5.3 Synergetics, Self-Organization and Non-Equilibrium Dynamics in HAACS

By drawing on Haken’s synergetics, human-AI agents collaborative networks can achieve self-organized coherence through nonlinear interactions. These emergent patterns often parallel phenomena observed in non-equilibrium systems, where continuous input of energy or information prompts innovative adaptations. This section examines how attractor-based design, slaving principles, and dissipative structures come together to shape collective behaviors, highlighting both theoretical underpinnings and practical examples from multi-agent scenarios.

5.3.1 Self-Organization and Coherent Outcomes in Collaborative Design

Inspired by Haken’s synergetics, heterogeneous agents can spontaneously form cohesive "macroscopic" patterns without centralized direction. Nonlinear feedback mechanisms and coupling guide emergent order, but preventing chaos requires careful attention to stable attractors. This sub-section explores how designing with self-organization in mind can channel disorder into purposeful coordination.

Emergence of Coherent Patterns from Nonlinear Interactions
Inspired by Haken’s synergetics, a human-AI collaborative system, comprised of heterogeneous interacting subsystems can form spatial, temporal, or functional structures via self-organization, that is, they spontaneously generate coherent "macroscopic" patterns without explicit external nor central "control" telling it to. The key to this process is nonlinear interactions, such as feedback and multiplicative coupling, which drive mechanisms of cooperation or competition [69].

Designing Collaborative Networks as Stable Attractors
By designing the collaborative network so that the desired patterns correspond to stable attractors, the system can automatically "solve" for these patterns, even if the initial state is messy or partially random, each module or subsystem can be designed to update its state based on local rules in combination with global coupling, running synergy-based algorithms iteratively until they converge on a coherent and emergent outcome. During self-organization system design, controlling and stabilizing emergent behavior is essential to prevent chaotic or unwanted patterns, making the solidification of these stable states a critical factor in system design.

5.3.2 Order Parameters, Slaving Principles, and Observed Multi-Agent Behaviors

Under synergetics, a few dominant parameters govern significant structural changes by "enslaving" other degrees of freedom, enabling large-scale coordination from small influences. This section illustrates how tuning these parameters aligns actual multi-agent systems with predicted synergy-based patterns, confirming the applicability of order parameters and slaving principles in practice.

Dominant Order Parameters and the Slaving Principle
In synergetics, complex systems that experience qualitative macroscopic changes are governed by a few dominant order parameters, particularly near critical transitions where the system shifts from disorder to a stable pattern, such that the evolving structures or patterns can be calculated quantitatively. This "slaving principle" implies that these key parameters effectively absorb all other degrees of freedom and they can steer the macro patterns of the system as prescribed and desired.

Empirical Insights from Synergetic Multi-Agent Systems
Previous studies have demonstrated that, with careful tuning of high-level hyper-parameters and settings in multi-agent systems, the observed behaviors subtly align with the predictions of a synergetic design framework: by running the closed-loop feedback group problem solving simulation in multiple rounds with the prescribed collaborative decision-making configuration, the human-like behavior patterns (volunteer, destructive and conformity) emerge [42]. With the Critic-Reflect mechanism to refine the organizational structure prompt dynamically, the novel communication patterns (dual-leader, dynamic leadership, etc.) and the three types of cooperative behaviors (information sharing, leadership & assistance, and request for guidance) emerge among the agents [39]; multiple specialized agents make independent location guesses that are cross-checked by peers, and connections are reviewed and adapted over time, reinforcing reliable judgments and diminishing weaker ones, so that each task iteration increasingly relies on the most accurate contributors [70].

5.3.3 Non-Equilibrium Dynamics, Improvisation, and External Energy Flows

When a system departs from equilibrium, fluctuations spark creative, adaptive responses, a theme mirrored in improvisational human-agent behaviors. In both contexts, new structures emerge as energy inputs drive self-organization, ultimately leading to novel equilibrium states. This sub-section unpacks how continuous energy flow sustains and reshapes these far-from-equilibrium conditions.

Instability as a Catalyst for Adaptive Innovation
We can notice that non-equilibrium dynamics shares notable similarities with improvisation in human-agent collaboration. Both arise when a system is far from its stable, balanced state, triggering fluctuations and creative, adaptive responses. In human-agent systems, improvisation occurs when existing norms and policies are insufficient to address unexpected challenges, prompting agents to explore novel solutions and strategies. Similarly, in non-equilibrium dynamics, systems exhibit spontaneous order and reconfiguration as they search for a new equilibrium. In both contexts, the departure from stability serves as a catalyst for innovation and the eventual establishment of a new, coordinated state.

Dissipative Structures and Sustained Self-Organization
External energy flow plays a dual role in dissipative structures emerging in non-equilibrium: it not only triggers the departure from a stable equilibrium by injecting disturbances and creating instabilities, but it also sustains the non-equilibrium state necessary for self-organization. In this dynamic process, continuous energy input causes fluctuations that lead to the emergence of organized patterns, which, maintained by ongoing energy dissipation, eventually evolve into a new equilibrium state. Thus, energy determines both when and how a system transitions from equilibrium to non-equilibrium and, ultimately, to a new stable configuration.

6 Human-AI Agents Collaborative Problem Solving

6.1 Means-End Analysis as a General Problem-Solving Framework

Means-end analysis (MEA) has long been recognized as a powerful heuristic for systematically narrowing the gap between a current state and a desired goal. Originating in classic artificial intelligence and human problem-solving research, MEA’s core mechanism of identifying significant differences and setting subgoals has influenced a variety of architectures and frameworks. While rooted in symbolic rule-based approaches, it also aligns well with broader theories of learning—especially those emphasizing meaningful rather than rote acquisition of knowledge. In this section, we explore MEA’s foundational concepts, implementations in cognitive architectures, and analogies in recent multi-agent problem-solving processes.

6.1.1 Conceptual Foundations and Human Problem-Solving Dimensions

Means-end analysis has been studied extensively as a guiding paradigm for both machine-based and human problem-solving. This subsection highlights its historical definition, relevance to human cognition, and the iterative nature of resource-constrained search strategies.

Definition and Historical Background
MEA is a classic heuristic that systematically bridges the gap between a current state and a goal state by comparing them, identifying the most significant difference, and then selecting an operator to reduce that gap, often generating sub-goals when the operator’s prerequisites are unmet. Introduced by Newell and Simon within the General Problem Solver [71], this iterative process demonstrated how symbolic rules and sub-goal formation can decompose complex tasks into manageable subproblems until the overall objective is reached.

MEA as the Conceptual Foundation of Human Problem Solving
Human problem-solving can be viewed as a form of MEA that systematically explores processes leading from a given initial state to a "desired" goal [46]. Much like the way scientists search for a differential equation to explain certain natural phenomena based on observed behaviors, MEA involves identifying and refining the rules or steps that reduce the gap between the current situation and the target objectives. This focus on narrowing differences also ties into the distinction between rote and meaningful learning: whereas rote learning simply stores data in forms that may not be readily integrated or applied, meaningful learning encodes knowledge as accessible and reconfigurable procedures. In other words, once individuals grasp how a process works, it becomes indexed to relevant contexts, robust enough to be reconstructed even when partially forgotten, and stored in ways that can be flexibly applied by general problem-solving routines.

Parallel and Iterative Exploration with Strategic Resource Allocation
Crucially, because any single step to reduce differences can inadvertently introduce new ones—or fail to resolve them completely—real-world problem-solving and design efforts rarely progress in a single, linear chain of actions. Instead, problem solvers deploy a heuristic-based "search" across multiple, tentative paths, switching focus when a once-promising route proves less viable. This iterative approach requires strategic resource allocation deciding when to concentrate on a given line of inquiry versus reassigning resources to alternative or emerging directions.

Since the goal is typically to find "sufficient" rather than strictly "necessary" actions, exploring these paths in parallel or near-parallel modes (i.e., factorizing differences into more manageable components) is often the most effective strategy. By cycling through possible solutions and refining their methods with each iteration, problem solvers gather valuable insights into the underlying structure of the challenge, honing representations and procedures to arrive at a robust and adaptable solution.

6.1.2 Empirical Perspectives in Cognitive Architectures

This subsection reviews how established cognitive architectures integrate MEA principles, illustrating the versatility of the framework in various rule-based and flexible reasoning systems.

MEA in Soar and ACT-R
Both Soar and ACT-R incorporate MEA in rule-based form. Soar adopts MEA principles through its universal subgoaling: whenever a conflict arises, it creates a subgoal and later encodes that solution path as a new production (chunk) [54]. ACT-R can similarly implement MEA by encoding goal-state differences in the conditions of production rules, so that multiple operators capable of reducing the gap may match a given situation [55]. Sub-symbolic activation parameters, derived from factors like recency, frequency, and past success, serve as heuristics to estimate each rule’s effectiveness in gap reduction, thereby implicitly guiding the selection of the most promising goal-reaching operator.

Flexible Heuristic Integration in CoALA
CoALA [51], while not providing a built-in MEA routine, supports flexible integration of such a strategy through its reasoning loops. Its "propose-evaluate" steps during the planning phase of the decision-making loop can be instantiated to implement MEA. In practice, the system first proposes difference reduction operations based on preset heuristics and then evaluates these proposals using additional heuristics that predict their effectiveness in reducing differences. An agent can treat any shortfall (e.g., lacking facts) as a "difference" and invoke retrieval or other internal actions accordingly. while CoALA remains neutral about which heuristic is used, allowing MEA or alternative methods, to be woven into its text-based decision-making framework.

6.1.3 Analogies in LLM-Based Agent Problem-Solving Processes

Dynamic Means-End Reduction with Deliberate Search Strategies in ToT
Tree-of-Thoughts (ToTs) in [22] parallels MEA by systematically using two prompt-based heuristics to first generate "operators" (candidate sub-rationales) and then self-assess the effectiveness of the partial solving processes as the "operator" chains at narrowing the gap from the current state to a target solution, much as MEA iteratively attempts to reduce differences; at the same time, BFS and DFS guide the solving process toward promising branches of "operator" chains, although ToT doesn’t explicitly partition the overall problem into predetermined sub-goals or dynamically construct formal sub-goaling steps.

Prompt-Based Feedback Mechanisms in AGENTVERSE
In the AGENTVERSE group problem-solving process, the system compares the current state of the environment with the desired outcome to produce feedback for the next iteration [42]. This mechanism resembles means-end analysis (where discrepancies between "what is" and "what should be" drive problem-solving steps), but AGENTVERSE relies on prompt-based feedback loops rather than following explicit, rule-based means-end procedures.

6.2 Preliminary Comparisons of Complex Problem-Solving by Humans and Agents

Complex challenges often involve dynamic, uncertain environments and interdependent variables that evolve over time. Human cognition provides mechanisms, both conscious and subconscious—for adapting to these nonlinear demands. Meanwhile, AI agents can bring specialized expertise, continuous processing, and scalable coordination. By uniting these complementary capabilities, a collaborative framework emerges that is poised to tackle the multifaceted nature of modern problem-solving.

Core Attributes of Complex Problems
According to [4], complex problems are distinguished by multi-faceted goals, dynamic or uncertain contexts, and tightly interdependent variables that unfold over time. These features can include time variance (the environment changes regardless of an agent’s actions), opacity (not all information is observable) such the partial observations in [39], and nonlinearity (small changes can have disproportionate effects), need for creativity, empathy, and domain knowledge.

Subconscious Catalysts of Creative Insight in Complex Problem Solving
During the complex problem solving process in humans, the so-called inspiration phenomenon may stem from the central nervous system’s reprocessing of certain perceived information, without the individual’s subjective awareness of it. This is analogous to the idea of "multiple selves," where some selves operate beyond conscious perception yet continue to function in the background [14].

We can hypothesize that when an individual persistently engages with a difficult problem, particularly an open-ended scientific question, it undergoes subconscious processing [52]. When the subconscious processes of different selves reach conclusions ahead of conscious awareness and then communicate their results to it, the resulting insight is what we recognize as inspiration, even though the underlying cognitive steps remain unknown.

Leveraging Collective Intelligence for Synergistic Solutions
This mechanism, defined as a dynamic orchestration of latent cognitive agents that yields emergent creative insight, can be simulated through multiple intelligent agents working asynchronously, mimicking the interplay between conscious and subconscious cognition. At the individual level, when faced with a complex problem, an appropriate set of specialized agent systems can be dynamically recruited to address and solve it efficiently.

At a higher level, much like the synergistic collaboration within human society, AI agents from different domains and disciplines, each encoding expertise, practical experience, and knowledge from human experts, can be coordinated to work as humans’ copilots collaboratively within a unified and general framework. As complexity rises, conventional problem-solving methods struggle to capture the webs of causality and delayed feedback, calling for more adaptive, integrative strategies, calling for human-AI agents collaborative problem-solving in synergetic way.

6.3 LLM-Based Multi-Agent Simulation for Social Science Research and Problem Solving

Multi-agent simulation offers a promising alternative for investigating complex social phenomena, allowing researchers to automate hypothesis formulation, data collection, and analysis within a controlled computational environment. By leveraging LLMs and structural causal models, these simulations replicate the core empirical research cycle as open-ended problem solving processes, i.e., hypothesis, experiment, and analysis, without direct reliance on human subjects. This method expands the toolkit of social science by enabling systematic experimentation on domains such as bargaining, auctions, and judicial decisions, and showcases how AI-driven agent interactions can reveal insights that might otherwise remain undiscovered.

6.3.1 Structured Simulation Workflows and Key Features

A carefully orchestrated pipeline underpins multi-agent simulations in social science, integrating LLM-based dialogue generation, causal modeling, and automated statistical analysis. This subsection highlights the principal components of that workflow and examines how they replicate or extend traditional research methods.

Modular Steps in Simulation-Based Social Science
A conventional research workflow for social science topics typically involves selecting a domain of interest, defining outcomes and plausible causal factors, designing experiments to isolate and measure those factors, recruiting participants, gathering data, and applying statistical models for estimation. A structured mechanism is provided for simulating social scenarios by combining LLMs and Structural Causal Models in a way that automates hypothesis formulation, in-silico hypothesis testing, exogenous variable manipulation, conversation-based outcome measurement, and subsequent statistical analysis of results such that all the researchers and subjects are simulated by AI agents [72]; it then programmatically instantiates agents whose attributes represent randomized treatments, runs scripted interactions to generate text-based "data," and conducts automated regression on the resulting measurements.

Replicating and Extending the Empirical Cycle
This pipeline synthesizes "hypothesize-experiment-analyze" phases entirely within a computational environment, reproducing a core empirical research cycle without reliance on real human subjects. It establishes predefined turn-taking routines, includes a coordinator role for more complex interactions, and captures partial internal "memory" to store dialogue history like buffers. These design features enable systematic experimentation on socially relevant topics such as bargaining, auctions, and judicial decisions. This approach proves that multi-agents role-playing interaction simulations can obtain the verified insights and findings of social science not ex-ante available to the LLM purely through direct elicitation, in other words the LLM knows more than it can immediately tell (when being used as production system [51]).

6.3.2 Limitations and Broader Implications

While multi-agent simulations offer significant benefits for social science research, they also face inherent constraints. This subsection addresses the rigidity of current interaction protocols and discusses the possible biases arising from LLM-based agent behavior, shedding light on the broader implications for modeling real-world complexity.

Restricted Dynamics and Interaction Fidelity
A key limitation is the lack of fine-grained, contextually adaptive controls for the interpersonal dynamics among virtual agents. Interaction protocols rely on rigid turn-taking sequences that do not account for overlaps, interruptions, or subtle emotional cues, thereby reducing the fidelity of simulated conversations. Individual-level emotional states, motivation, non-verbal signals, and multi-modal inputs remain largely unmodeled, constraining the capacity to replicate the spontaneous emergence of complex behaviors that often surface in real societies.

The scope of these simulations is limited to interactions among human-like agents and does not extend to modeling the interactions between human users and designed prototypes like physical objects and interfaces. What is more, the system is still strongly reliant on prompting, the cost of scaling up can be high, and there is no formal method to determine when to stop the simulations, unlike the explicit stopping criteria employed when forming group consensus (see Section 3.6.1-3.6.2 for examples).

Core Assumptions Underpinning LLM-Based Social Science Simulations
One foundational assumption in [72] is that certain governing aspects of human cognition and behavior can be approximated by LLMs, enabling them to act as both "researchers" and "subjects" in controlled, text-based simulations, drawing on human-like common sense for macro-level individual or small-group decision-making on average, but there may be potential systematic biases if the latest real-human data diverges from LLM’s outdated world knowledge. Because the simulations follow scripted sequences rather than parallel or stochastic processes, they primarily yield outcome measures that reflect predetermined agent roles and conversations rather than fully emergent group-level behaviors in the open world.

6.3.3 Reproducibility Gains and Qualitative Knowledge Generation

Despite these limitations, multi-agent simulations excel in providing repeatable and extensible platforms for exploring theoretical constructs. This subsection examines how parallel "universes" enable reproducible experimentation and outlines how these workflows can be generalized to advance qualitative social-science inquiry.

Parallel Universes for Experimental Consistency
It is the unique advantage of the multi-agent setup to allow the system to run multiple simulated conversations (each with different exogenous variable assignments) in parallel or in quick succession, so that all possible treatment combinations can be explored under identical scripted conditions. This approach [72] effectively replicates the notion of "parallel universes", overcoming the real-world challenge of irreproducibility, where reverting to exactly the same initial state is practically impossible. By systematically manipulating only certain parameters and rerunning the interactions from scratch, the system can isolate how each change in a causal factor affects the outcome, providing a form of experimental repeatability that would be very difficult to achieve with physical human subjects.

Generalizing to Qualitative Knowledge Workflows
This kind of research workflow can be further generalized to generate and validate the qualitative knowledge. The typical qualitative knowledge-generation workflow, mirroring standard social science procedures, can be generalized to: defining a clear research domain and its boundary; identifying the governing parameters and factors; specifying variables of interest; building conceptual, functional and computational models or theoretical frameworks; formulating hypotheses; systematically collecting relevant evidence (e.g., from historical data, simulations, and real experiments); and then rigorously assessing that evidence to validate the qualitative knowledge from the hypothesis under a specific condition and within a limited scope of applicability. In practice, some or all of these steps may require multiple iterations.

6.4 AI Scientist for Open-Ended Scientific Problem Solving

Open-ended scientific inquiry often requires dynamic, iterative processes that blend exploration of new ideas with the exploitation of promising leads. In The AI Scientist [73], an autonomous end-to-end pipeline automates key research stages, i.e., idea generation, experimental testing, and publishable outcome, thereby mirroring Herbert Simon’s decision-making cycle. This framework highlights how multi-agent systems can emulate the "explore-exploit" dynamic, though it also underscores the need for HAAC to overcome inherent limitations in isolation.

6.4.1 Echoing Simon’s Decision Cycle and Explore-Exploit Dynamics

Much like Herbert Simon’s classic diagram of iterative decision-making [74], The AI Scientist conducts a cyclical process that ranges from idea generation to outcome archiving. When viewed through a multi-agent lens, this cycle unfolds as an "explore-exploit" mechanism, balancing the generation of novel hypotheses with the refinement and formalization of validated ideas.

Mirroring Simon’s Decision Making Model
Open-ended scientific problems can be solved collectively by multiple agents, conforming to Simon’s decision making diagram and the general "explore-exploit" mechanism. In The AI Scientist [73], a fully autonomous end-to-end pipeline that generates, tests, and publishes machine learning research, a closed-loop process illustrated closely mirrors Herbert Simon’s classic decision-making cycle.

First, "Idea Generation" echoes Simon’s alternative generation stage, producing multiple research avenues evaluated for novelty and feasibility through LLM reasoning and automated literature checks. Second, the "Experimental Iteration" phase parallels implementation, as the system applies each idea in code, executes experiments, and collects results for subsequent reflection. Third, an "Automated Reviewing + Archive" step serves as selection, filtering out weaker proposals and retaining those with higher review scores. Finally, continuous feedback links these stages together, allowing each idea’s outcomes and paper reviews to inform future cycles, much as Simon envisioned iterative refinement in a dynamic decision-making process [75].

Multi-Agent Exploration of Novel Research Directions and Self-Corrective Exploitation
This same loop can also be framed as a multi-agent "explore-exploit" mechanism, a cycling between exploration (creation of new hypotheses) and exploitation (formal documentation, peer-review scoring, and iterative improvement). On the exploration side, the system’s LLM-driven brainstorming proactively searches for novel research directions, adapting or discarding them based on feasibility and self-assessed scores.

Once an idea is selected and developed, the exploitation side appears: The AI Scientist runs structured experiments, writes a formal LaTeX manuscript, and generates an automated conference-style review that refines findings and helps isolate the most promising breakthroughs. Through such exploitative filtering, the system prevents an endless proliferation of mediocre ideas while still capitalizing on unexpectedly strong results.

6.4.2 Overcoming Isolation Through HAAC

While The AI Scientist’s closed-loop framework illustrates how AI agents can advance research autonomously, its isolation from real-world expertise and emerging data poses key challenges. This subsection explores the limitations of such an isolated system and envisions an integrated approach that combines human insight with AI-driven automation.

Limitations of an Autonomous but Isolated Pipeline
However, a critical limitation of The AI Scientist lies in its relatively isolated nature, where no real-world human expert is "in the loop." While the system’s LLM can approximate certain forms of intuition via prompts based ’brainstorming’ from historical training data, genuine human insight, grounded in hands-on experience, updated knowledge of newly emerging research, and the capacity to collect fresh data in the physical world, remains absent, embodying restricted innovative theory construction due to ’data-belief asymmetries [50]. As a result, the AI’s discoveries are constrained to what can be tested via self-contained code and existing open-source experiments, limiting immediate applicability to broader scientific domains.

Envisioning Expanded Human-AI Synergy
Collaborations between human experts and AI agents could substantially broaden this framework, allowing real-time data gathering from physical labs, pilot field trials, incorporating the latest external developments that might not yet appear in any pretraining corpus, and infusing nuanced human judgment about the direction of scientific progress.

6.5 Constructivist Learning as a Basis for Open-Ended Scientific Discovery

"Discovery" belongs to ill-structured problem-solving tasks characterized by relatively ill-defined goals. When genuine discovery occurs, something new emerges, an insight or phenomenon not predictable with full certainty, that carries value or interest. Processes similar to those in learning systems can be harnessed to construct frameworks that foster new knowledge. Kolb’s and Rescher’s constructivist models exemplify this approach, offering cyclical structures that guide the development of ideas from formative observations to refined theories and methods. Such cycles align well with open-ended scientific endeavors, where each iteration can spark further questions and expansions of understanding.

6.5.1 Constructivist Models for Iterative Open-Ended Problem Solving

Two influential constructivist models illustrate how iterative processes can drive the evolution of scientific knowledge. Kolb’s cyclical framework emphasizes a progression from concrete experience to reflective observation and abstract conceptualization, culminating in active experimentation. Rescher’s two-cycle model, building on Piaget, differentiates between "why" knowledge and "how" knowledge, ensuring both conceptual coherence and practical applicability.

Kolb’s Experiential Learning Cycle
Kolb’s cyclical model of constructivist learning, grounded in the ideas of Lewin and Piaget, frames problem solving as a progression from concrete experience to reflective observation, followed by abstract conceptualization and active experimentation [76]. In this process, learners engage with tangible scenarios, critically reflect on outcomes, derive general principles or theories, and then adapt or refine these insights through further experimentation. Such a structured yet iterative approach offers a foundation for open-ended scientific discovery by enabling researchers to move fluidly between lived experiences, reflective observation, theoretical construction, and practical testing.

Because each new experiment or observation can spark further questions, the cycle never strictly ends, i.e., it perpetuates further exploration and hypotheses.

Rescher’s Two-Cycle Model for Why and How Knowledge
Rescher’s two-cycle model builds on Piaget’s work to offer a more intricate distinction between "why" knowledge and "how" knowledge, each requiring a separate cycle of conceptual assimilation and pragmatic correction [77]. While "why" focuses on the coherence and logical integration of emerging concepts, "how" emphasizes the operational methods and procedures applied to real-world tasks. This framework underscores the interplay of logic and praxis, and the associative dynamics, i.e., justification (the "why" cycle) and action (the "how" cycle).

This two-pronged approach ensures that scientists continually re-evaluate their theoretical assumptions and refine the practical methods used to test them. The interplay of conceptual justification and pragmatic feedback creates a self-correcting system, ideal for open-ended scientific pursuits where each new insight can redefine the questions asked and the methods applied.

6.5.2 Explore-Exploit Mechanisms and the Theory-Practice Interplay

Kolb’s and Rescher’s models both illustrate the interplay between exploring new possibilities and exploiting established insights, a dynamic that can be mapped onto the relationship between theory and practice. By emphasizing Piaget’s notion of the complementarity of action (praxis) and cognition, these constructivist cycles reveal how open-ended inquiry is sustained through iterative feedback loops.

Piagetian Emphasis on Praxis and Cognition
These two constructivist learning diagrams, well-suited for open-ended problem solving, underscore Piaget’s emphasis on the complementarity of affect (praxis) and cognition [78]: "Without a mathematical or logical apparatus there is no direct ’reading’ of facts, because this apparatus is a prerequisite. Such an apparatus is derived from experience, the abstraction being taken from the action performed upon the object and not from the object itself."

Explore-Exploit and Theory-Practice Dynamics in Kolb and Rescher’s Models
From Piaget’s perspective above-mentioned, we can abductively extract the fundamental "explore-exploit" mechanism and the "theory-practice" interplay highlighted in the preceding discussions. In Kolb’s experiential learning cycle, abstract conceptualization functions as a form of theory construction. When reflection on experience converges with abstract conceptualization, the result is an "exploit" phase, in which learners refine existing ideas by formulating more cohesive theoretical structures. At the same time, active experimentation can be viewed as the design of guided practice, while concrete experience represents the practical implementation stage, used to investigate unknown scenarios through testing. Taken together, concrete experience and active experimentation constitute the "explore" phase, where learners gather new insights and empirically probe the viability of their emerging theories.

In Rescher’s diagram, to "exploit" insights from the inner cycle, the outer cycle builds or refines "why" knowledge/theory as a correction for coherence. Meanwhile, the outer cycle "explores" the new theoretical assumption to feed the inner loop. Given the theory in the outer loop, the pragmatic correction from application is "exploited" to inform new methods and further "exploring" new "how" knowledge. Each nested cycle thus embodies "explore-exploit" dynamics for both "theory-practice" interplay and open-ended inquiry.

6.6 Deep Research Pioneering Human-AI Agent Collaborative Scientific Research

OpenAI’s deep research is an autonomous agent within for reasoning and structured research by iteratively browsing and analyzing content. While OpenAI hasn’t published a detailed schema, it almost certainly involves a planning phase (where the model outlines what to search for), a retrieval phase (using a web browsing tool to fetch information), and a synthesis phase. The architecture breaks down complex research queries into manageable chunks, suggesting a multi-step plan where the agent treats each chunk (subtopic) with focused searches. Multiple internal prompts or agent instances may be used: e.g. one to generate search queries, another to summarize findings, etc., all coordinated by the main agent. This effectively creates a multi-agent collaboration within one unified system, where the "agents" are different functional roles of the model orchestrated by the program logic. Notably, Deep Research’s architecture emphasizes source attribution and reasoning traceability, meaning it keeps track of which sources support each finding (this could be implemented via structured intermediate outputs or memory to store source-content mappings).

However, OpenAI’s deep research systems continue to exhibit instances of hallucination and may produce incorrect responses. Internal evaluations indicate that these systems often struggle to distinguish authoritative information from rumors and suffer from weaknesses in confidence calibration, failing to accurately convey uncertainty. Additionally, minor formatting errors in reports and citations persist. There is also an ongoing pursuit for enhanced agentic experiences to support asynchronous real-world investigation, operation, research, and execution.

7 Toward a Collaborative Epistemology and Knowledge Management Framework

7.1 Epistemological and Philosophical Foundations for Knowledge and Knowing Process

In grappling with how humans come to know and understand the world, scholars have offered diverse yet interwoven perspectives that emphasize the fluidity of knowledge and the complexity of its formation. From Descartes’ rationalist doubt to Piaget’s constructivism and Kuhn’s paradigm shifts, each philosophical stance highlights that what we take as "knowledge" is in constant evolution, shaped both by our innate cognitive structures and by our engagement with ever-changing phenomena. This section offers a concise exploration of these foundational theories, underscoring their shared theme of epistemic fluidity and the quest for coherence amid conceptual tension.

7.1.1 Rational Foundations and Practical Constructions of Scientific Fields

Historically, the quest to ground knowledge in reason has been central to Western philosophy, seeking to separate reliable insights from untested beliefs. At the same time, science has evolved into specialized disciplines more for pragmatic reasons than because nature is inherently partitioned. This interplay between rigorous inquiry and convenient categorization informs our modern understanding of how people unify diverse insights under a single epistemic umbrella.

Holistic Understanding and the Flexibility of Scientific Divisions
People always connect various aspects of understanding to form a comprehensive recognition of the objective world through their personalized epistemological processes, from which common laws of reasoning can simultaneously be observed. As suggested by Max Planck, the separation of science into distinct fields serves primarily as a practical construct arising from human convenience and the limitations of human intellectual capacity, while the actual boundaries between these fields are not inherent to nature itself [52].

Descartes and the Four Rules of Rational Inquiry
To establish a rational foundation for knowledge, Descartes [79] proposed methodical doubt, rejecting all beliefs that had not undergone rigorous rational scrutiny-including sensory perceptions, traditional authority, and even mathematical truths. Through this process, he arrived at the self-evident truth with absolute certainty: Cogito, ergo sum (I think, therefore I am), making rational existence the first principle of knowledge. His method follows four key rules: Accept only clear and distinct ideas (systematic doubt), break down complex problems (reductionism and analysis), proceed from simple to complex (systematic synthesis), and ensure completeness in reasoning (comprehensive review).

7.1.2 Innate Cognitive Structures and Constructive Interaction with Reality

Moving beyond strictly rationalist or reductionist frameworks, subsequent philosophers and psychologists illuminated the internal architecture of cognition. Whether viewed through Kant’s emphasis on fundamental categories or Piaget’s constructivist lens, these ideas share a belief in a feedback loop between the mind’s structure and the world, shaped by active synthesis and self-regulation.

Kant’s Synthetic A Priori and the Twelve Categories
Kant proposed that the knowing subject possesses an innate cognitive structure, which he termed "synthetic a priori judgments" These judgments are comprised of 12 pairs of categories, enabling the synthesis and organization of fragmented, unconnected sensory experiences into a coherent, generalized, and interconnected rational understanding [80]. Because all experience is organized by these mind-dependent structures, we can never reach the "thing-in-itself" (the noumenon) in a pure, unfiltered way. However, these categories apply universally and necessarily whenever humans experience anything, so they are not merely subjective whims.

Piaget’s Equilibration and the Mutually Shaping Process
From perspective of constructivist, though Piaget acknowledged the existence of the cognitive structure as well and its active contribution to knowing process, he argued that human cognitive structures do not rely solely on the external environment, nor are they existing in a pre-formed way. Instead, he emphasized that the cognitive structure shapes the process of understanding the objective environment, while the objective environment, in turn, influences and reshapes the subject’s cognitive structure [81]. This interaction is governed by an inherent tendency toward equilibration and self-regulation, meaning that the subject possesses an intrinsic mechanism for self-adjustment within the cognitive process.

7.1.3 Paradigm Shifts and Dialectical Synthesis of Knowledge

Knowledge formation does not proceed in a steady, incremental way. The history of science and thought is punctuated by leaps to new frameworks that resolve deep contradictions in older models. Kuhn’s paradigm shifts and Hegel’s dialectical sublation both point to friction, i.e., whether incommensurability or self-negation, as the fuel that propels understanding beyond the confines of established paradigms.

No Fixed Knowledge and the Impermanence of Paradigms
Knowledge is traditionally defined as justified belief and empirical hypothesis, with these beliefs and hypotheses being justified by data and evidence from an epistemic perspective. Kuhn’s perspective implies that there is no absolute or final knowledge; what we consider "true" or "scientific" is always relative to the prevailing paradigm [82]. Moreover, the frameworks we use are provisional, i.e., they are the most effective at a given time but are subject to replacement when they no longer explain emerging, even conflicting, evidence. Consequently, the derived beliefs and knowledge may become incompatible with the ever-evolving phenomena resulting from human interaction with the real world.

Antinomies Driving "Aufhebung" in Theory Building
When a phenomenon that defies existing knowledge is newly encountered, it cannot be regarded as the complete "thing-in-itself", we often classify it as a "known unknown" due to the first knowing attempt, distinguishing it from what is already understood. Yet in practice, such novelty is initially treated as though it fits within established categories—until deeper inquiry brings contradictions to light.

In the early stages of a new theory’s epistemic process, as we attempt to integrate the "known unknown," it frequently stands in antinomical tension with existing knowledge: the same phenomenon can lead to contradictory or even opposing judgments—exemplified by wave-particle duality or the shift from classical to relativistic conceptions of spacetime—precisely because the premises and scopes of each framework remain unclear and indistinct, making it difficult to unify them into an updated knowledge structure.

From a Hegelian dialectical perspective, these contradictions are not mere oversights in scope-setting; rather, they reveal partial standpoints that, when pushed to their limits, negate themselves and point toward a higher, more integrative viewpoint [83]. Although each standpoint’s premises and applicability may seem ambiguous, the resultant clash, once recognized, propels a sublation (Aufhebung) that preserves valuable insights from both sides while resolving their mutual exclusivity. In this way, tension spurs progress, culminating in a conceptual synthesis that expands rather than merely replaces earlier frameworks of understanding.

Kuhn and Hegel in Structural Transitions toward Higher Coherence
Both Kuhn and Hegel underscore that deeper progress emerges when recognized contradictions can no longer be resolved within the existing framework. In Kuhn’s terms, this renders the old paradigm untenable; in Hegel’s terms, it prompts the negation of the lower standpoint. Both depict a "leap" to a new organizing principle. However, Hegel explicitly integrates ("preserves") part of the old, whereas Kuhn at times sees old and new paradigms as "incommensurable." Even so, in practice, new paradigms typically retain some concepts or data interpretations from the old, albeit re-contextualized. In both approaches, tension or crisis is not a sign of mere error but the catalyst for a profound structural shift.

The friction that once seemed destructive becomes the condition for progress to a more encompassing perspective. Both highlight that progress involves redefinition of previous assumptions rather than mere additive growth. Each new stage reorganizes the entire landscape of concepts, methods, and aims. In both perspectives, the new stance doesn’t necessarily obliterate every element of the old. Instead, either by necessity (Kuhn) or by principle (Hegel), the new stage draws on or re-frames aspects of the old, even if the conceptual framework is profoundly changed.

7.2 Interplay of Knowledge Management, Practical Problem Solving, and Reasoning Techniques

Knowledge management and practical problem solving continually amplify each other: organized knowledge accelerates discovery, while problem solving refines and enlarges the knowledge base itself. Multiple reasoning methods, e.g., formal, dialectical, conversational, and narrative, further shape and enrich this interplay. Ultimately, practice grounds these theoretical approaches, ensuring knowledge remains adaptable to real-world complexities.

7.2.1 Dynamics between Problem Solving, Knowledge Management, and Reasoning

Mutual Enrichment of Problem Solving and Knowledge Management
Problem solving and knowledge management are deeply interlinked because each process mutually enriches the other. When we engage in problem solving, we delve into specific "how," "why," and "what" questions, thus deepening our understanding of the subject matter at hand. As we search for solutions, we refine our conceptual structures: we notice gaps, form hypotheses, test them, and either confirm or revise our assumptions. This cycle of iterative questioning and testing not only solves immediate problems but also generates new, context-rich knowledge that can be captured and organized through a knowledge management framework.

Conversely, structured knowledge management, where information is well-categorized, easily retrieved, and meaningfully linked, enhances problem solving by providing a readily accessible knowledge base. When confronted with a new challenge, a well-managed repository of how-tos, rationales, and experiential records allows solvers to rapidly apply or adapt existing insights.

Reasoning Drives the Transformation from Data to Knowledge
In the broader "knowing" process, problem solving thus becomes both a driver and beneficiary of knowledge accumulation: it propels inquiry and conceptual development, while simultaneously drawing on and expanding the knowledge that has been systematized. Reasoning acts as the connective tissue in this cycle, ensuring that the transition from merely "having data" to "knowing" is guided by purposeful exploration, rigorous testing, and reflective analysis.

7.2.2 Formal Reasoning as a Compressive Epistemic Framework

Leveraging Formal Logic for Prediction and Efficiency
