Formal reasoning, to some extent, can be regarded as a distillation and refinement of the epistemological achievements accumulated through collective human practice over history. Simultaneously, it functions as both a framework and instrument for comprehending new phenomena and objects, facilitating reasoning, analysis, and guiding practice. Unlike purely empirical observation and post hoc verification, reasoning based on formal logic follows the intrinsic structure and logical connections of things, enabling knowledge to anticipate rather than merely react to objective processes.

Expanding Utility beyond Empirical Observation
This allows for analytical modeling, predictive reasoning, and even proactive influence over the development of objective processes. By leveraging a rigorously constructed logical system, formal logic compresses what would otherwise be an almost boundless posterior epistemic workload, i.e., not only in terms of time but also by reducing the redundancy of repeatedly deriving knowledge across similar objects and processes, into a tractable and operationally feasible scope [52], making it an indispensable tool for both theoretical inquiry and practical decision-making.

7.2.3 Dialectical Reasoning and the Evolution of Understanding

Contradictions as Pathways to Progress
Dialectical reasoning, unlike using formal logic’s static rules, is a self-developing system of thought. It does not merely abstract past knowledge into fixed schemas; rather, it unfolds through a sequence of contradictions and resolutions that reflect the historical evolution of human understanding. In Hegelian terms, each category or concept, upon close analysis, contains its own opposite—its internal "negation"—and both are sublated (aufgehoben) into a higher, more comprehensive unity, often expressed as "the negative of the negative."

Integrating Historical Knowledge and Real-World Practice
Far from discarding earlier insights, this new unity preserves the valid moments of previous categories while transforming them into a richer conceptual framework [83]. Whereas formal logic applies discrete epistemic rules in isolation, dialectical logic integrates the cumulative essence of historical knowledge into a continuum of reality-based cognition. This is not a purely abstract enterprise: dialectical thinking is interwoven with practice, meaning that conceptual advances are continuously tested, reshaped, and validated in real-world engagement.

7.2.4 Conversational Reasoning and Socratic Elicitation

Socratic Questioning for Heuristic Elicitation
The Socratic questioning (Maieutic) is a representative conversational reasoning approach that fosters knowledge through structured questioning, refutation, and critical reflection. Traditionally, a single teacher (Socrates) and one or more learners (his interlocutors) interact. The teacher’s role is to guide through cleverly posed questions, but authority and expertise typically remain with the teacher. Rather than providing direct answers, it employs elicitation, guiding individuals to think independently through heuristic questioning.

Internal Realization and Aporia as Catalysts for Thought Reconstruction
By exposing contradictions in one’s beliefs, it induces aporia, a state of self-refutation that reveals gaps in understanding, prompting a more coherent reconstruction of thought. Rooted in the idea of internal realization, this method assumes that truth already resides within the mind, and just awakens and brings it to light through intellectual struggle [84].

7.2.5 Narrative Reasoning for Organizing Complexity

Storytelling as the Methodical Synthesis of Human Knowledge
Similarly, the narrative reasoning techniques, drawn from centuries of insights from human discourse, philosophy, literary studies, and communication theory represent distilled, methodical syntheses of how humans’ knowing process organize and interpret complex information through storytelling. In essence, techniques like progressive disclosure, branching, analogy, and metaphor encapsulate well-established principles that have been articulated by scholars and methodologists over time, reflecting enduring patterns in human communication and knowing process.

7.2.6 Practice as the Wellspring of New Knowledge

Though reasoning plays a crucial role in the epistemic process, such as inferring conclusions from premises, correcting false beliefs, and justifying beliefs, it alone is insufficient for generating new knowledge. Knowledge does not emerge purely from logical deduction or inference but is shaped through interaction with the world, through observation, experimentation, and practical engagement [52]. Reasoning provides structure to organize and control knowledge, but practice grounds it in reality.

Balancing Abstract Logic with Real-World Engagement
When reasoning is tested against experience, discrepancies force refinement, leading to deeper insights. Scientific discovery, for instance, arises not merely from formal logic but from iterative cycles of hypothesis, experimentation, and revision (see [76], [77]). Similarly, in skilled professions, tacit knowledge emerges through active practice-based problem-solving rather than abstract theorizing alone. Thus, new knowledge is generated at the intersection of reasoning and practice; it requires both existing and promising facts as evidence and must align with the relevant parts of prior knowledge tested through practice. While reasoning organizes and refines, ensuring logical coherence and consistency, practice explores, challenges, and enriches, introducing empirical validation and adaptation to real-world complexities. Also, the continuously refined knowledge becomes both a tool for action and a mechanism for truth-discovery, as each step in the dialectical progression tests the coherence of what came before and propels us beyond partial, one-sided standpoints.

Dialectical Logic as a Motor for Intellectual and Societal Growth
Ultimately, dialectical logic serves as a motor of intellectual and societal development. Its strength lies in revealing how every finite standpoint, when carried to its logical limit, proves self-contradictory and thus necessitates a higher perspective [83]. Through an ongoing interplay of theory and practice, knowledge continuously evolves, tested by new discoveries, reshaped by real-world engagement, and thus bridging the gap between abstract thought and practical reality. In doing so, dialectical logic not only traces the historical arc of ideas, it also brings forth new ways of thinking and acting, ensuring that our grasp of truth remains open-ended, integrative, and ever-evolving.

7.3 Contrasting Correspondence and Coherence in Epistemic Frameworks

Knowledge can be approached in two broad ways: as a direct mirror of external reality or as a self-sustaining network of interrelated concepts. While correspondence epistemology aims to anchor all symbols and ideas to concrete entities in the real world, coherence epistemology posits that knowledge evolves from mutually reinforcing concepts without relying on an immutable external reference. Understanding the interplay of these two perspectives illuminates how symbolic models, from AI systems to human cognition, manage meaning, adapt to novelty, and strive for consistency in a world that is perpetually changing.

7.3.1 Correspondence Epistemology and Physical Symbol Systems

Rooted in the notion that knowledge mirrors the external world, correspondence epistemology underpins the classic view of symbolic AI, where meaning is fixed by linking symbols to tangible referents. This alignment forms the basis of the physical symbol system hypothesis, positing that sufficiently advanced symbol manipulation can yield intelligent action.

Knowledge as a Direct Mirror of the External World
A correspondence epistemology holds that knowledge functions as a direct mirror of the external world, in which everything is built on top of symbols constituting the meaning atoms. In this view, every conceptual element or symbol within an individual’s knowing model is linked to one or more physical entities in the environment. Essentially, the structure of this knowing model acts as an encoded, homomorphic representation of external reality [85].

Physical Symbol System
A physical symbol system is fundamentally characterized by five components [86]: Symbols are the tangible elements that can be manipulated; Symbol Structures are the organized arrangements of these symbols that encapsulate complex ideas; Processes are the operations that create, modify, or destroy both symbols and their structures; Designation ensures that symbols refer to objects or processes, facilitating interaction and reasoning; and Interpretation is the system’s capacity to execute the processes encoded within these symbols, effectively running a program.

Physical Symbol System Hypothesis
A physical symbol system is hypothesized to have the necessary and sufficient means for general intelligent action [87]. This means that any system capable of intelligent behavior must be a physical symbol system, and any sufficiently advanced physical symbol system can exhibit intelligence.

7.3.2 Symbol Grounding Problem and the Frame Problem in Correspondence Models

Although tying symbols to external reality appears straightforward, symbolic systems face inherent obstacles in verifying that their representations truly match the world. From the symbol grounding dilemma to the frame problem, these challenges reveal rigidities and uncertainties when each new context demands adaptation beyond pre-encoded primitives.

Symbol Grounding Problem
The central dilemma for symbolic system of intelligent agents (human or AI) grounded in a "correspondence" knowledge models is that: they cannot internally verify whether their symbolic representations truly match external reality completely. This stems from the ’symbol grounding problem’ and is reinforced by Löfgren’s "linguistic complementarity" principle, which generalizes epistemic constraints like Gödel’s incompleteness and Heisenberg’s uncertainty. In essence, a language (or model) cannot fully describe or interpret its own mapping rules, leaving no built-in mechanism to confirm that symbols correspond accurately to the outside world [85].

Frame Problem
Consequently, such symbolic frameworks end up relying on a programmer’s arbitrary imposition of primitives, treating these core symbols as immutable "givens." The model may suffice for certain problems but remains incomplete, covering only a fraction of potential scenarios. Further, new symbols cannot be derived internally as they are intended to correspond to external phenomena that lie beyond the model’s extant direct access, thus these systems stay static and tend toward absolutism. This perpetuates the broader "frame problem," wherein the model cannot autonomously expand or adapt to unforeseen contexts. Instead, each revision must be manually encoded, revealing the rigidity and arbitrary structure of conventional correspondence-based AI models.

7.3.3 Coherence Epistemology and Criteria for Holistic Knowledge

Where correspondence focuses on external references, coherence epistemology shifts the lens inward, arguing that the strength of a knowledge framework lies in how well its concepts reinforce one another. This self-referential approach, aligning with constructivist principles, highlights the value of mutual support and integration, moving beyond the mere absence of contradictions.

Self-Organizing Structures in Coherence Models
Coherence epistemology, complementing constructivism, bypasses the need for a single fixed "correspondence" foundation, since coherence is a two-way relation in which concepts mutually reinforce one another. In other words, the structure emerges self-referentially: a few governing rules and conventions can produce higher levels of complexity, meaning, and quality without requiring outside imposition. This reflects self-organization principles, whereby the knowledge model effectively creates its own architecture.

Beyond Mere Consistency and the Challenge of Defining Knowledge Coherence
From a constructivist perspective, defining knowledge’s coherence solely through logical consistency and via the bootstrapping axiom in [85] is insufficient. While consistency ensures that a set of propositions is not contradictory, and the bootstrapping axiom prevents two concepts from occupying identical roles in the network, these criteria do not capture how propositions or conceptual clusters holistically reinforce or explain each other. In other words, even though an arbitrary collection of unrelated statements be consistent, they may still lack the integrative, mutual support that true coherence requires.

7.4 Constructivist Perspectives and Consensual Domains in Knowledge Emergence

Constructivist epistemology, enriched by second-order cybernetics and the concept of consensual domains, highlights that knowledge does not merely reflect an external world but rather is actively produced through recursive, self-regulating processes. Individuals and groups co-create meaning by continuously testing and adjusting their internal frameworks in conversation with their environment. Far from static or one-directional, this mode of knowledge formation emphasizes dynamic interaction, leading to emergent properties such as consciousness, self-awareness, and shared language, all rooted in the collective interplay of observers and contexts.

7.4.1 Dynamics of Knowledge Creation in Constructivist Epistemology

Rather than treating knowledge as a passive imprint of reality, constructivist epistemology and second-order cybernetics reveal it to be a self-generated phenomenon. Through iterative interaction and selectionist feedback, individuals refine their conceptual models, testing them against internal coherence and practical applicability. In this view, the knower actively co-creates what is "real," shaping and reshaping mental schemas to navigate a constantly shifting environment.

Knowledge as a Self-Growing Process
Constructivist epistemology, as underscored in second-order cybernetics (i.e., the observers such as the teacher/learner are parts of the system being observed) and autopoiesis theory, holds that knowledge isn’t passively received from the external world but actively constructed by the individual. This self-generated and self-growing knowledge construction isn’t meant to mirror an objective reality; rather, it equips the individual to adapt and navigate the world at best, as they subjectively experience it.

Selectionist Trial and Error for Adaptation
Thus, generally knowledge model is constructed through a selectionist, trial-and-error process in which the subject generates diverse model variations, and the internal and external environments help select only those that best integrate with the overall experiential framework, for instance through the subject’s internal consistency checks (conflict resolution) and external applicability (practical validation), among all of the subject’s autonomously generated trials.

7.4.2 Emergence of Consciousness, Language, and Shared Understanding in Consensual Domains

When knowledge production moves beyond the individual and into communal interactions, consensual domains become the crucible for co-evolution of ideas, language, and even consciousness. Through structural coupling and languaging, intelligent agents synchronize and refine each other’s internal processes, forging deeper levels of understanding. This collective, multi-layered coordination drives an emergent form of knowledge that cannot be reduced to any single individual’s perspective.

Constructing Consensual Domains and Multi-Scale Interactions
Within a specific group of intelligent agents (human or AI), observers construct consensual domains that encompass the complete life-cycle trajectories of their interactions and communications across multiple scales, including the relevant objects, events, and classes; they learn from and teach each other. This construction arises from the structural coupling between the artificial system and its external environment, where the invariants (’objects’ and ’events’) and stabilities are abstracted with the help of their actions [78].

Emergence of Self-Awareness from Dynamic Interactions
Consciousness is portrayed as an emergent property arising from dynamic interactions within consensual domains, where distinct notions of "self" and "other" allow individuals to achieve self-awareness through the process of "knowing with oneself".

Co-constructed Understanding Through Conversational Exchanges
Individuals exchange information, knowledge, and experiences, mutually learning from each other, mainly through language based conversation. An individual’s epistemic process can contribute to the collective, while the collective, in turn, can inspire the individual. Rather than transmitting static knowledge, conversational exchanges actively provoke participants to become attuned to each other’s internal "informings," fostering a co-constructed understanding.

Languaging as a Recursive, Multi-Layered, Interactive Process of Meaning-Making
Languaging is defined as the intricate coordination of multiple layers of interactions, where higher-level coordinations serve as tokens for lower-level ones [88]. These lower-level coordinations, representing the invariants or stabilities arising in sensorimotor activities and structural coupling with the environment, manifest as stable patterns or "eigen-behaviours," highlighting that knowledge and consciousness emerge not from unilateral transmission but from recursive, multi-layered, and interactive processes of meaning-making.

7.5 Tacit and Explicit Knowledge in Organizational Contexts

Human knowledge is not solely about what can be spelled out: an implicit, tacit dimension often guides our most insightful actions and discoveries.

Below, we explore this interplay in two sub-sections: first, by examining the inherently tacit nature of human knowing [89], and second, by analyzing how it circulates through frameworks such as SECI [90]. Both [89] and [90] treat knowledge in a constructivist way, emphasizing that it is actively constructed rather than passively received. Polanyi highlights how personal experience and unarticulated clues shape understanding through tacit integration, while Nonaka views knowledge as context-bound and generated via social interaction, rather than simply discovered.

7.5.1 Unveiling the Tacit Dimension of Human Knowledge

Active Gestalt Integration and Attending-from-to Phenomenon
All human knowledge relies on a tacit component, by which we always know more than we can explicitly state, and this "unsaid" aspect underpins everything from skillful action to scientific discovery. Polanyl systematically explores how such tacit knowing arises and is reinforced by empirical observations [89]. Gestalt psychology’s notion of integrating dispersed particulars into a coherent whole is reframed as an "active shaping" of experience undertaken in the pursuit of knowledge, rather than as a simple automatic process. This active integration manifests that the unarticulated, "proximal" elements combine to yield a recognizable, "distal" outcome. Using minimal symbolic notation, we can say that for each knowledge act: Knowledge=∑i(pi|tacit)→M\text{Knowledge}=\sum_{i}\Bigl(p_{i}\Bigl\rvert_{\text{tacit}}\Bigr)\rightarrow M, where pip_{i} (proximal clue) are recognized only through the meaning MM (distal aspect). We do not keep an "inventory" of the pip_{i} but experience them "from within." This attending-from-to phenomenon is the essence of tacit knowing.

Key experimental proof is offered in subception studies, wherein participants learn to anticipate or avoid electric shock from triggers they cannot consciously identify, showing that one can rely on cues never explicitly recognized.

The Meno Paradox, Scientific Discovery and Personal Commitment
Tacit integration underpins even high-level creative and scientific activity. Plato’s Meno famously asks how one can search for something truly unknown: if one knows nothing about the goal, how can one even look for it? If one already knows it, what’s left to discover?

The Meno paradox is resolved by asserting a tacit dimension of foreknowledge, allowing scientists to pursue hidden problems and recognize truth without fully itemizing each clue. We do, in fact, start from partial, implicit "foreknowledge" (hidden clues) that we can neither fully define nor see from the outset. In scientific terms, a researcher often intuits that "something is there" before being able to lay out all the details or final explanation. Tacit knowledge validates that "intuition" by grounding it in a wealth of unspoken experiences and insights that we cannot fully articulate. Even though the clues remain "proximal" (unlisted or scattered across experience), they guide us toward a "distal" result (the recognized discovery). Hence, the paradox is circumvented because we do have some direction, tacitly, even if it is not spelled out.

Scientific discovery is therefore redefined as a personal commitment, indeed, partly personal, because it rests on an unspoken conviction that a hidden phenomenon truly exists. Scientists "commit" to pursuing a problem based on this tacit sense of its legitimacy: without an internal, felt conviction, one cannot logically justify focusing on a problem that is invisible in purely formal terms, in contrast to traditional views that often depict scientific discovery as a purely objective, step-by-step automatic procedure.

7.5.2 Dynamic Interplay of Tacit and Explicit Knowledge through SECI

Catalyzing HAAC through Latent Know-How
A vast reservoir of practical experience within organization, including localized expertise, expert reasoning templates and decision-making, both documented and undocumented firsthand experiences and situational insights, and the craftsmanship of skilled practitioners, remains un-systematized within a formal framework [52]. These invaluable treasures resulting from the humanity’s collective epistemological process should be integrated as catalysts for the evolution of human-AI agent collaboration systems.

Ongoing SECI Spiral and the Role of Ba
Fueled by interactions among individuals, teams, and the wider environment, a dynamic model SECI for continuous knowledge creation between tacit and explicit forms is established [90]. It prioritizes justification and context over absolute truth, i.e., Knowledge=Φ⁡(Information,Context,Belief)\text{Knowledge}=\Phi(\text{Information},\text{Context},\text{Belief}) where Φ\Phi is the "interpretation function" shaped by human commitments, positioning knowledge as more than static information. By defining a spiral movement rather than a naive closed loop, it explains how organizations reshape problems, actively generate new insights, and integrate them into capabilities. The approach enumerates four complementary modes, i.e., Socialization (Tacit → Tacit), Externalization (Tacit → Explicit), Combination (Explicit → Explicit), and Internalization (Explicit → Tacit), and emphasizes the importance of Ba, a shared context for collectively exchanging, formalizing, and embodying knowledge. Each Ba (Originating, Dialoguing, Systemizing, Exercising) caters to a specific stage of the SECI sequence, ensuring that tacit and explicit elements constantly circulate and expand. The structure is completed by clarifying how knowledge assets (experiential, conceptual, systemic, and routine) both anchor and evolve with this spiral, underscoring the tendency of core competencies to become rigidities if not continually examined. Such dynamic interplay of tacit and explicit knowledge fosters ongoing innovation and shared learning within the organization.

Typical Workflow and the Challenge of Organizational Rigidities
Based on SECI model, a typical workflow begins by specifying a guiding vision to determine which knowledge assets and Ba (physical, virtual, and mental "places") will be central, followed by systematically identifying who holds tacit or explicit expertise. Socialization sessions then mobilize relevant contributors to exchange and absorb experiential insights in face-to-face contexts, while subsequent externalization steps convert these insights into more accessible artifacts through dialogues or creative techniques. After assembling these diverse inputs, combination activities organize and systematize the resulting explicit knowledge, leveraging information systems and cross-functional collaboration to refine or unify concepts, prototypes, or data. To ensure lasting value, internalization practices embed refined ideas into individuals and routines, typically through training, on-the-job action, and reflection. Maintaining leadership oversight, promoting trust-based cultural norms, and ensuring structural redundancy greatly accelerate discovery during each iterative pass, as the circle widens to include additional teams or external stakeholders.

However the rigid organizational structures can obstruct the iterative spiral needed for knowledge exchange, undermining efforts to unify tacit and explicit insights. Additionally, deeply ingrained routines and "core rigidities" may suppress curiosity and openness, limiting the model’s capacity to foster transformative learning and innovation.

7.6 Conversation Theory as a Constructivist Framework

Conversation Theory (CT) stands as a hallmark of constructivist thinking, emphasizing that knowledge arises from interactive, socially mediated processes rather than static repositories of information. By modeling the exchange and reconfiguration of concepts in pursuit of shared meanings, CT illuminates how individuals and groups iteratively co-create, test, and refine understanding. This section explores the foundational principles of CT, its applications in educational settings, its scalability for multi-participant knowledge building, and the early knowledge-representation structures—entailment meshes—that underscore its constructive roots.

7.6.1 Foundational Principles Guiding Conversation Theory

At its core, CT offers a formalized lens through which social cognitive interactions can be systematically examined. It treats "having knowledge" as an ongoing process of coming to know through dialogue, rather than a final state of stored representations. Pask’s frameworks, including P- and M-individuals and entailment meshes, reflect CT’s rigorous yet adaptive stance: knowledge construction emerges from iterative refining, splitting, or merging of ideas, aided by participants’ abilities to self-organize and generate higher-level conceptual agreements.

CT as a Dynamic Process of Construction and Coherence
Pask’s Conversation Theory (CT) provides a formal model for social cognitive interaction, wherein concepts are exchanged, combined, and recombined (the construction phase) with the aim of achieving agreement on shared meanings (the coherence phase) [85]. Specifically, from the perspective of CT, "having knowledge" is understood as a process of ’knowing’ and ’coming to know’, rather than the storage of representations.

Multi-Level Dialogues and Key Constructs
CT facilitates knowledge acquisition through structured dialogues across multiple levels: task-focused (defining what is done), explanatory (clarifying how or why), and potentially meta-cognitive. Key constructs include P-individuals (the conceptual process bundles that execute ideas), M-individuals (the bodies or machines hosting these processes), and entailment meshes (dynamic webs of concepts connected by shared procedures and outcomes).

It needs to note that P-individuals as conceptual systems can be distributed across multiple people or "embodied" in one person and high-level P-individuals are emergent collective agents that crystallize from stable, shared agreements among lower-level participants.

Saturation, Bifurcation, and Pruning for Adaptive Refinement
Mechanisms such as saturation (gathering numerous variants of a concept), bifurcation (splitting concepts when they produce divergent results), and pruning (eliminating or merging redundant branches) enable robust refinement of knowledge structures. This approach is computationally grounded, highlighting parallel concept execution and recursive self-reference, i.e., new participants (P-individuals) or higher-level dialogues may be generated. Despite the advantage of modeling cognitive processes at a granular level, practical challenges arise from complex notations and insufficient treatment of emotional, motivational, and embodied dimensions [91].

7.6.2 Operationalizing Conversation Theory in Educational Settings

CT transitions seamlessly from theory to practice in contexts like classrooms and computer-assisted tutoring. By anchoring discussions in tangible, shared environments and cultivating multi-level dialogues, learners co-construct coherent networks of ideas. Disagreements trigger branching or re-examination, and consensus emerges when overlapping procedures and outcomes reveal deeper conceptual connections.

Anchoring Knowledge in Shared Environment In classroom or computer-based tutoring contexts, CT is operationalized by establishing a tangible shared environment in which students and facilitators can jointly reference problems, examples, or scenarios [92]. This shared environment (e.g., a real or simulated problem space) serves as the external anchor for references: "Are we talking about the same phenomenon?" At the task level, participants focus on concrete actions to produce or demonstrate a concept; at the explanatory level, they articulate the procedural or conceptual underpinnings of those actions. Additional levels, like meta-cognitive ("How does my learning style influence this?"), may be added as needed.

Iterative Exchanges and Knowledge Mesh Formation
This process aligns with CT’s principle of multi-level exchanges, wherein new insights arise from revealing how procedures are executed and compared, in case of disagreement. The theory’s saturate, bifurcate, and prune steps guide learners through systematically exploring alternative procedures, pinpointing divergences in conceptual understanding, and consolidating or relabeling similar strands of thought. Once enacted, these structured dialogues yield an evolving knowledge mesh, often visualized in graphs that capture the emergence and refinement of key ideas, in which each concept is viewed as "procedures + outcomes." Concepts that share outcomes or have overlapping procedures become linked or "entail" each other. By anchoring students’ actions and explanations in a shared reference space, CT promotes iterative co-construction of meaning: mismatched outcomes prompt re-examination or branching (bifurcation), and redundancies are winnowed (prune) to strengthen clarity. The end result is not just discrete solutions but a coherent network of interrelated procedures, reflecting how learners collectively negotiate and stabilize new understandings.

7.6.3 Extending Conversation Theory for Human-AI Collective Knowledge Building

Structured Dialogue and Scalable Architecture for Knowledge Building
This combination of structured procedural modeling, iterative conversation cycles, and scalable architecture underscores conversation theory’s potential for supporting multi-participant knowledge-building in a manner both conceptually rigorous and practically adaptable.

Extending Pask’s THOUGHTSTICKER for Human-AI Agent Collaborative Knowledge Construction
Pask argued that his theory applies not only to interactions among various roles or perspectives within a single individual but also extends to exchanges between observers and objects, as exemplified by his THOUGHTSTICKER program [91], assisting to transform users’ implicit knowledge into stable and explicit knowledge, with the help of a computer as conversational partner, which echoes my envisioned collaborative knowledge construction through the synergy between human and AI agents, powered by advanced LLMs provided by companies such as OpenAI and DeepSeek AI.

7.6.4 Entailment Meshes as Constructive Knowledge Representations

Entailment meshes emerged from Pask’s early efforts to represent knowledge in a fluid, network-based format. By linking concepts through mutual reinforcement rather than rigid hierarchies or a strict correspondence to external reality, these meshes embody CT’s constructivist ethos. While limited in capturing directional or causal structures, they nonetheless illustrate how knowledge can self-organize through cohesive, interlinked nodes.

Graphical Mapping of Mutual Conceptual Relations
Entailment meshes are a foundational technique in knowledge representation that emerged from early explorations into conversation theory, notably developed by Gordon Pask in the 1970s and 1980s [91]. Originally, entailment meshes were used as graphical representations in Pask’s proto-logic language (Lp) to capture the mutual, non-directed relationships among concepts. In these meshes, each topic is embedded in a cluster, or coherence, in which its meaning is derived from the collective set of related topics.

From Mirror-Based to Constructivist Approaches
The historical lineage of entailment meshes reflects a shift away from correspondence epistemologies that assume symbols directly mirror external reality, toward a constructivist perspective where meaning is "bootstrapped" through the interrelations among internally generated distinctions. This approach allowed early researchers to address problems such as the frame problem and symbol grounding by enabling knowledge to self-organize via mutual support rather than relying on externally imposed primitives.

Technical Mechanisms for Dynamic Refinement
Technically, an entailment mesh is composed of overlapping, non-directed clusters where each node (or topic) is defined by its network of associations with other nodes. The technique operates on the principle that if two topics consistently share the same neighbors (i.e., have identical sets of supporting concepts), they become indistinguishable, prompting operations such as merging or splitting to resolve ambiguity.

This design supports continuous, dynamic refinement: as new knowledge is introduced, the mesh undergoes iterative reorganization, pruning to unfold derivations, saturating to propose new candidate clusters, and condensing to integrate closely related nodes into generalized concepts.

Inherent Constraints on Causal or Partial Reasoning
Pask’s non-directed entailment mesh suffers mainly from its inability to encode directional or hierarchical information, making it poorly suited for "if-then" inferences or causal ordering. While it effectively highlights mutual coherence among topics, it does not readily capture partial matches, uncertainty, or graded associations, and it relies heavily on user guidance to merge or split ambiguous concepts. Consequently, more intricate reasoning (e.g., transitivity or time-sequence logic) remains underdeveloped, and the system lacks a built-in mechanism to define specialized forms of entailment without manually imposed structures.

7.6.5 Extending Entailment Meshes into Directed Entailment Nets

Building on Pask’s original notion of entailment meshes, constructivist knowledge representation frameworks have evolved to incorporate directed links, user-driven reinforcement, and minimal ontologies. By blending these elements with the bootstrapping axiom, recent approaches transform static conceptual structures into adaptive, self-organizing networks. The result is a system that accommodates ambiguity resolution, supports causal inferences, and fosters associative learning, hallmarks of a robust, constructivist perspective on how concepts form, interrelate, and scale.

Defining Nodes and Differentiation through Input-Output Sets
The constructivist knowledge representation framework in [85] utilized the directed entailment nets extended from Pask’s entailment mesh and governed by the bootstrapping axiom, wherein nodes are considered distinct precisely when their respective input/output sets differ. This design naturally supports systematic ambiguity resolution (merging or differentiating concepts), transitive or causal chains ("if a → b and b → c, then a → c"), and the possibility of associative learning via weighted links. In practice, concepts are represented as nodes whose relationships (or links) are initially established in a non-weighted form and then refined through user interactions.

Associative Learning and Weighted Links
Three learning rules are applied with preset bonus parameters to update the weights: direct link strengthening increases the weight of a selected link by a fixed unit; transitive reinforcement boosts the weight of an indirect link (with a bonus parameter) when a user navigates a multi-hop path; and symmetric reinforcement (with another bonus parameter) increases the reverse link’s weight to foster bidirectional association. These rules dynamically update the network’s structure, causing frequently used paths to become more prominent and effectively shortening the distance between semantically related nodes.

Minimal Ontologies and Extensible Link Types
Additionally, the framework integrates semantic and frame-like representations by reducing typed link relations (such as "is-a" and "has-part") to node types within a minimal ontology, whereas the traditional semantic networks’ typed edges can multiply arbitrarily and fail to solve symbol grounding. By reducing link types to node types, all link types are governed by the bootstrapping axiom, ensuring consistency and coherence without relying on externally imposed primitives. This ontology is derived from two dimensions, stability (transitional, temporary, stable) and generality (particular, general), yielding categories like Class, Object, and Property.

Organic Growth, Hierarchical Inheritance, and Self-Organization
Moreover, the ontology can evolve organically as the network self-organizes, allowing new node types and relationships to emerge based on the interplay of user interactions and the system’s underlying bootstrapping mechanism. This design allows for the explicit encoding of hierarchical and inheritance relationships, where concepts can inherit default attributes that may later be overridden by instance-specific values. This organic growth mirrors human conceptual development, where overarching themes adapt to accommodate new insights and exceptions.

A Practical Implementation of Adaptive Knowledge Systems with CONCEPTORGANIZER
A program CONCEPTORGANIZER in a directed net format of concepts, used to exteriorize users’ implicit knowledge, continuously examines the constructed network to detect ambiguities, situations where distinct nodes possess identical input and output sets. When such ambiguities are found, it proposes various resolution strategies similar to those used by THOUGHTSTICKER [91] in a mesh (non-directed) format. Overall, the method transforms static knowledge into a self-organizing, adaptive system that not only captures the mutual support (i.e., bootstrapping) among concepts, but also refines the structure based on continuous user feedback, thus ensuring coherence (i.e., users’ collective agreement about shared meanings), scalability, and enhanced semantic expressiveness.

7.6.6 Comparative Exploration of Conversation Theory and Socratic Questioning

Shared Focus on Dialogue and Conceptual Refinement
The Socratic method shares with CT a focus on dialogue-driven conceptual refinement through questioning, clarifying and collaborative exchanges. CT’s technical orientation offers explicit formalisms for identifying conceptual conflicts and directing participants toward new labels through multi-level conversations, whereas the classical Socratic approach emphasizes uncovering contradictions to move closer to universal truths.

Applying Socratic Questioning in a Paskian Environment
Although both share the function of back-and-forth discussion, but Pask’s approach generalizes beyond the hierarchical teacher(questioner)-student(responder) format, supporting peer-to-peer or multi-agent learning and knowledge co-construction systems where authority or expertise is dynamic. In a Paskian environment, applying Socratic questioning at the explanatory level, with prompts like "Why?" or "How do you know?", serves to reveal contradictions and trigger bifurcations, where divergent conceptual procedures require re-labeling or refinement. CT’s structured approach, utilizing entailment meshes and pruning operations, provides an explicit formal grammar that potentially operationalizes the Socratic discourse, a process traditionally described more abstractly in Plato’s dialogues.

7.7 Human Learning as a Constructive Process Powered by Conversation Theory

CT underscores the idea that learning transcends mere information transfer; it is a dynamic process of co-creating and refining conceptual structures through dialogue. Rather than viewing knowledge as static content to be absorbed, CT envisions learners actively exploring both the "how" and "why" of each concept. By incorporating iterative cycles of practice, feedback, and alignment, CT enables deeper understanding, fosters flexible knowledge organization, and paves the way for broader multi-participant mutual learning in both human and AI-assisted environments.

7.7.1 Learner-Driven Dialogue and the Rejection of Passive Transmission

Transitioning from Transmission to Iterative Construction
Learning is not merely a form of biological adaptation; human beings have an intrinsic need to learn that compels us to actively explore novel environments, scenarios, and patterns. In contrast to the "transmission model," which assumes knowledge can be directly passed from teacher to learner, CT treats learning and knowledge acquisition as an iterative, constructive process. Rather than merely receiving information, learners and teachers engage in ongoing dialogues that negotiate and refine conceptual structures, yielding shared understanding within a consensual domain; thus learning or understanding a topic means that the learner can "teach back" the topic by providing both non-verbal demonstrations and verbal explanations of "how" and "why." [78].

7.7.2 Balancing Procedural Mastery with Conceptual Coherence

Anchoring "How" to "Why" in a Conversation-Driven Model
A domain-independent constructivist model for knowledge acquisition, built upon CT, is organized as a cybernetic conversation between participants, guided by explicit "how" and "why" structures, the approach interprets learning in terms of coherent conceptual networks (entailment structures) combined with practical, procedural steps (task structures) [78].

Organizational Closure for Self-Justifying Systems
It adopts a dual perspective on "m-individuals" (physical or biological entities) and "p-individuals" (conceptual systems), ensuring that procedural mastery (knowing how) remains anchored to conceptual coherence (knowing why). A p-individual is "organizationally closed" in the sense that it reproduces and justifies its own conceptual structures within the conversation. This arrangement seeks to systematically address the challenge of domain independence by providing a repeatable, conversation-driven method, compatible with the complementary ideas of Piaget’s radical constructivism, so that new knowledge emerges through iterative social negotiation rather than mere transfer.

7.7.3 Iterative Phases of Learning through Conversations and Reflections

Integrating Kolb’s Phases with Pask’s Conversation Steps
A key strength lies in how Kolb’s iterative phases, concrete experience, reflection, conceptualization, and experimentation, interface with Pask’s notion of "learning as conversation" following steps: Initialize → Elicit → Demonstrate → Reflect/Evaluate → Repeat/Extend.

"Why" versus "How" in Conversational Micro-Worlds
In Pask’s "skeleton of a conversation," at least two logical levels operate: "why" questions, which focus on conceptual justifications, and "how" questions, which emphasize operational procedures. A shared "modeling facility" or "micro-world" supplies the concrete experience element, enabling participants to demonstrate processes and test outcomes in a hands-on manner. Through iterative reflection, verbal exchange, and teach-back, learners expand not only their procedural competency but also the conceptual relationships that anchor each practice. This dynamic interaction ensures ongoing refinement of both understanding and skill, echoing Kolb’s cyclical progression in a collaborative, dialogic setting.

7.7.4 Structured Knowledge Organization and Emergent Entailment Meshes

Hierarchical Entailments and Lateral Analogies
Concurrently, the conversation-theoretic elements foster a structured approach to knowledge organization. Each domain under discussion can be modeled through hierarchical "entailments" (indicating why one topic leads to another) and heterarchical "analogies" (highlighting lateral connections among seemingly unrelated ideas).

Validating and Refining Knowledge through Teach-Back
Because these relationships are subject to negotiation and agreement among participants, conversation guides the emergence of a coherent "entailment mesh." In this mesh, topics can be "unzipped" to reveal sub-topics and loops of justifications, all of which are validated through conversation-based activities like teach-back and demonstration.

It needs to note that "teach-back" is not merely an end-of-lesson test but an ongoing process of conversational alignment among peers that, through repeated exchanges, stabilizes conceptual systems (or "p-individuals") and prevents knowledge structures from remaining uncorrected or "undebugged". By integrating procedural "how" knowledge with explanatory "why" knowledge in this manner, the framework accommodates multiple levels of learning, ranging from immediate skill acquisition to the meta-level dialogues on study skills and personal learning motivation and goals, while continually reshaping the conceptual network that underpins scientific or scholarly inquiry.

7.7.5 Parallels with Human Classroom Scenarios

Demonstrations as Implicit "Teaching" in Two-Player AI Agent System
We notice that during the ’Watch’ stage of the two-player RL collaborative framework (discussed in Section 4.4), Bob observes Alice’s demonstration in order to learn the relationship between a series of actions and the underlying goal [60]. In other words, from Alice’s behavior, Bob infers a structured goal and gains insight into how certain actions contribute to that goal. This effectively amounts to Alice "teaching" Bob through demonstration, even though it happens implicitly as Bob processes Alice’s actions and outcomes rather than through any direct instruction.

7.7.6 Limitations and Potential Extensions for Conversation-Based Models

Accounting for AI Agents and Complex Collaboration
However, this constructivist model, grounded in CT, does not account for the increasingly common scenario where AI agents function as either teachers or learners or a group of peers teaching and learning from each other. Note that AI agents can surpass human experts in many closed-ended tasks while lacking the human capacity for on-the-fly adaptation, integrating these agents into the conversation would fundamentally alter collective problem solving and accompanying knowledge management, calling for new modes of interaction and strategies to reconcile multiple AI agents’ specialized strengths with the flexible, context-aware nature of human learning, and potentially reshaping the dynamics of shared understanding.

Advanced Elicitation Strategies for Deeper Engagement
Additionally, from a methodological perspective, the proposed procedure of (Initialize → Elicit → Demonstrate → Reflect/Evaluate → Repeat/Extend) remains overly general and does not explicitly integrate more advanced knowledge-elicitation strategies, such as Socratic questioning, progressive disclosure, branching, and analogical or metaphor-based reasoning. Incorporating these nuanced methods could significantly enhance the depth and adaptability of the conversation-based approach, particularly in complex or open-ended problem-solving contexts.

7.8 Knowledge Cybernetics in LLM-Based Systems

Current LLMs are unable to perform on-the-fly learning with dynamic parameter updates due to significant computational, architectural, and stability challenges. Alternative methods such as constructing the hybrid system by introducing the external memory modules like knowledge graphs in [93], retrieval augmentation by the external data [94], and efficient fine-tuning techniques [95] have been developed to provide adaptability during deployment. However, these methods do not modify the intrinsic architecture of LLMs and focus solely on managing the temporal and long-term memories of LLM-based agents, without explicitly endowing them with forward-looking causal reasoning capabilities or the "theory-practice" dynamics necessary to refresh knowledge in a contrarian manner, a capability observed among human professionals and scientists.

Integrating pre-existing human knowledge with new experiences and skills enables agents to bootstrap their learning efficiently [51]. For instance, a medical diagnosis agent might begin by ingesting conceptual and semantic knowledge from medical manuals, textbooks, regulations, and guidelines into its semantic memory. It would then build episodic records from its practical experiences, reflect on these experiences to enrich its semantic repository, and ultimately develop procedural capabilities, such as event-triggered workflows, effective methods and strategies of knowledge cybernetics tailored to different scenarios, and implicit knowledge embedded in the LLM parameters derived from the distilled essence of its semantic and episodic memories.

Each sub-section below illustrates a distinct mechanism with associated extant representative empirical implementations as the examples of how the continuous and feedback-driven interplay of knowledge acquisition, transformation, refinement, consolidation, communication, utilization and verification, can enhance diverse aspects of knowledge cybernetics for LLM-based agents.

7.8.1 Procedural Capabilities Inspired by Human Reasoning

LLM-based agents can draw on well-established human reasoning frameworks discussed in Section 7.2.1, such as the Socratic method, narrative structures, and analogical mappings, to improve logical consistency and context-sensitive thinking.

Socratic Dialogue and the CRIT Template
The classical Socratic technique has been integrated into the prompt template engineering, employing a multi-turn dialogue structure, illustrated by the CRIT (Critical Reading Inquisitive Template) model—which uses defined variables such as Ω\Omega for the central claim, RR for supporting reasons, and numerical scores (γr,θr)(\gamma_{r},\theta_{r}) to assess argument validity and source credibility [96]. This design emphasizes sequential prompts that first clarify definitions and context, then extract, cross-examine, and validate evidence through elenchus and dialectic steps, and finally incorporate counterfactual reasoning to explore hypothetical scenarios. The framework leverages modular, ensemble-based approaches and standard NLP operations (e.g., named entity recognition, dependency parsing) to reduce ambiguity and enhance logical consistency in model outputs.

Technically, the approach seeks to address the challenge of eliciting more accurate, self-critical, and creative responses from large language models by unifying deductive, inductive, and abductive reasoning within a step-by-step algorithmic process. It provides detailed pseudo-code for systematically prompting the model to not only generate responses but also to critique and refine them through iterative self-evaluation and counterargument generation. Special issues such as the risk of model hallucinations, reliance on self-assigned credibility scores, and the computational overhead of multi-turn dialogues are mitigated through a structured pipeline and prompt ensembling strategies. This method offers a robust solution to improving output quality and depth while highlighting areas—like external fact-checking and cost optimization—that warrant further refinement.

Narrative Structures and the Buffer of Thoughts
Highlighting the narrative reasoning technique’s capacity to translate abstract concepts into vivid, multifaceted experiences that foster deep insight, a multi-step workflow restructures complex problem-solving into three distinct stages: question clarification, narrative generation, and problem solving [97]. In the first stage, a specialized prompt decomposes the problem into its core components and relevant subtopics, thereby establishing a precise knowledge base. The subsequent narrative generation phase transforms this clarified information into a structured, story-like framework.

Here, narrative techniques are uniquely applied: progressive disclosure incrementally reveals information to iteratively contextualize each piece, branching explores multiple angles to address sub-problems, and analogical reasoning coupled with metaphors draws parallels to familiar concepts, encoding causal structures and temporal flow. This enriched narrative context facilitates deeper understanding and more accurate solution derivation compared to a mere sequential chain of thought.

However, the method’s success is highly contingent on sophisticated prompt engineering and the ad-hoc integration of these narrative techniques. The effective application of progressive disclosure, branching, analogy, and metaphor requires careful calibration within prompts, as variations in design can lead to significant fluctuations in performance across different tasks or domains. If the integration of these techniques is not meticulously tuned, the resulting narrative may inadequately capture the necessary inter-dependencies or reduce ambiguity, thereby risking diminished robustness and generalizability.

Analogical Reasoning and Meta-Buffer Templates
Inspired by analogical reasoning, the Buffer of Thoughts (BoT) framework generalizes problem-solving strategies by abstracting key elements from prior tasks into modular templates [98]. This approach mirrors the process of mapping structural similarities across distinct problems, where underlying reasoning patterns are identified and stored. By transforming raw problem statements into distilled representations, the method leverages these generalized templates as analogical guides, enabling the application of previously extracted strategies to new tasks. The design mechanism proceeds in a structured workflow. First, a problem distiller extracts essential parameters and constraints from the input, converting them into a formal representation. This representation is then compared, using embedding similarity metrics, to a meta-buffer that houses a collection of abstract task-agnostic thought templates. Upon retrieval of a matching template, the system instantiates it with task-specific reasoning steps, effectively generating a customized solution pathway. A dedicated buffer-manager continuously refines the meta-buffer by distilling new templates from completed tasks.

7.8.2 Error-Driven Adaptations via Cybernetic Feedback

By treating knowledge states as continuously updated and corrected, LLM-based systems can reduce factual inconsistencies. The Chain-of-Knowledge (CoK) approach exemplifies this error-driven perspective, invoking feedback loops and domain-specific checks. CoK’s distinct workflow stages and its foundational principle of cybernetic self-regulation are discussed below.

Three-Stage Workflow for Factual Grounding
Chain-of-Knowledge (CoK) implements a structured, three-stage workflow designed to enhance factual grounding in LLM through systematic external knowledge integration. In the initial Reasoning Preparation stage, multiple preliminary chain-of-thought steps are generated and evaluated using in-context learning with few-shot examples [99]. A critical component here is the domain selection mechanism, which leverages self-consistency metrics to determine the most relevant knowledge domains (e.g., factual, medical, physics, biology) for the question at hand. This filtering ensures that only questions lacking a strong consensus are flagged for further verification, thereby streamlining the subsequent adaptation process.

The core technical innovation lies in the Dynamic Knowledge Adapting stage. Here, an Adaptive Query Generator (AQG) dynamically formulates queries tailored to each knowledge domain, using both structured languages (such as SPARQL and SQL) and unstructured natural language formats. The AQG retrieves authoritative, domain-specific information, which is then employed to iteratively correct and update the intermediate rationales, minimizing error propagation through sequential, progressive editing. Finally, the Answer Consolidation stage integrates these refined rationales to produce a coherent final output. Critical limitations include heavy reliance on the quality of external knowledge sources and query generation accuracy, potential latency from sequential corrections, and dependence on a single LLM that may still propagate inherent reasoning errors.

Feedback Loops for Continuous Knowledge Refinement
CoK exemplifies knowledge cybernetics by treating knowledge as an evolving system that self-regulates through continuous feedback. In this approach, intermediate chain-of-thought outputs—akin to internal knowledge states, are not static but are dynamically evaluated against external, authoritative information. This evaluation and subsequent correction process mirrors the cybernetic principle of feedback loops, where a system’s output is constantly monitored, compared with a desired state, and adjusted accordingly. By integrating external data to update its reasoning, the framework demonstrates how cybernetic principles can be applied to refine knowledge itself.

7.8.3 Automating Raw-to-Structured Transformations for Fine-Tuning

Turning unstructured text into high-quality training data is pivotal for expanding an LLM’s capabilities. The AgentInstruct framework demonstrates how multi-agent pipelines, reflection loops, and iterative prompts can generate large-scale instruction-based datasets, though not without scalability and oversight challenges. Its workflow and highlight potential limitations are showcased below.

AgentInstruct for Synthetic Instruction Data
Instruction-based fine-tuning is a process where a general-purpose language model is trained on datasets composed of user instructions paired with correct or high-quality responses, guiding it to better understand and fulfill requests. By repeatedly seeing examples of how to answer various instructions, the model becomes more adept at following user prompts and generating contextually appropriate, coherent outputs. A framework, AgentInstruct, is proposed for automatically generating large-scale, diverse, high-quality, synthetic (prompt, response) instruction data from the unstructured raw material to "teach" new skills and behaviors to small or mid-sized language models, notably Mistral-7B [100]. During the data generation procedure, the multi-step agentic flow comprised of the specialized "agents" (powered by advanced models such as GPT-4 and equipped with optional tools, e.g., search APIs, code interpreters, calculators, etc.) is used with minimal labeling or curation efforts to convert source materials into intermediate representations (e.g., argument passages, API documentation), produce first-draft prompts based on a taxonomy of skills, use "Suggester-Editor" pairs akin to multiple humans brainstorming to elevate both task complexity and accuracy. By leveraging these agentic workflows, the authors create 25 million synthetic question-answer pairs covering 17 skill categories (ranging from reading comprehension to tool usage and coding), then fine-tune Mistral-7B into Orca-3. Although GPT-4 generally retains the highest overall capability, Orca-3 can exceed GPT-4 on specific tasks where the synthetic data’s coverage is particularly robust. In essence, the framework can be seen as a variant of knowledge distillation, where GPT-4’s implicit knowledge is triggered by the external raw material, extracted and curated into skill-specific instruction-response datasets. However, the pipeline’s multi-agent structure and the focus on diverse raw seeds, goes beyond standard distillation by introducing tool usage, iterative refinement, and extensive data filtering. This helps alleviate biases, reduce hallucination, and broaden the scope of learned skills.

Challenges and the Need for Robust Domain Expertise Extraction and Epistemic Checks
Despite these successes, AgentInstruct remains resource-intensive, as the agentic flows demand repeated calls to large teacher models and careful orchestration. Ensuring absolute correctness in millions of generated data points also remains infeasible, especially for professional, interdisciplinary, complex scenarios, without further automation or human experts oversight.

Nonetheless, the method provides a scalable, semi-automated avenue to produce instruction data tailored to many domains, with promising evidence that small or mid-sized models can be systematically "taught" advanced capabilities. Further novel mechanisms are needed so that human experts can capture and collect their domain-specific data and practical experiences from highly complex scenarios automatically in an interoperable yet flexible format and the underlying knowledge can be extracted and reused, allowing models to benefit from this expertise without incurring the cost of repeated fine-tuning.

Although AgentInstruct already employs reflection loops and multi-agent flows to reduce mistakes, it has no direct control over the factual accuracy or biases in raw source material nor faithfulness for the generated synthetic data, meaning the pipeline can inadvertently incorporate or amplify problematic content unless carefully designed. Future introduction of a structured epistemic mechanism at each critical decision point, where the system explicitly queries uncertain facts, cross-verifies sources, or flags questionable reasoning, would further strengthen its reliability. By requiring each step of knowledge management to document and justify the factual basis of its outputs (e.g., references, confidence scores, "known unknowns"), the human-AI agents collaboration system can more effectively detect hallucinations, mitigate bias, and ensure that interdisciplinary or highly complex scenarios are handled with verifiable evidence rather than unverified inferences.

7.8.4 Epistemic Models and Knowledge Consolidation in LLMs

Beyond incremental fine-tuning and error-correction, a truly coherent "epistemic model" demands that scattered facts be unified into a single, interconnected knowledge state. The EpiK-Eval benchmark reveals how standard training objectives fall short of this goal and clarifies why human oversight and specialized constraints remain indispensable. The fragmentation problem and the partial solutions attempted are emphasized below.

Fragmentation versus Internal Consistency
A pioneer work [101] explores whether LLMs can truly unify and consolidate knowledge from multiple documents into a coherent and consistent "epistemic model" in its parameters as a knowledge state. In simpler terms, it asks whether these models maintain each fact in isolation (Type I) or merge them into one internal representation (Type II). Through a systematically generated benchmark called EpiK-Eval, short stories are created, containing facts split into either a single, unsegmented narrative or multiple, segmented parts. Then the well-known LLMs (T5, Flan-T5, and OPT in various sizes) are fine-tuned on these datasets and evaluated with a set of tasks that require combining facts across a story, counting events, inferring temporal/causal sequences, and so on. Crucially, each test question requires the model to reproduce the story ("recall") and give a final answer, with any invented or incorrect lines tagged as hallucination. The findings reveal that models trained on segmented narratives perform markedly worse at reassembling and recalling information, frequently hallucinate, and do not exhibit the robust, interconnected knowledge state suggested by Type II behavior intrinsically. Simply increasing model size alleviates but does not eliminate this gap, indicating that standard pre-training objectives (e.g., masked or causal language modeling) favor learning within chunks rather than building a cross-document knowledge graph.

Limited Fixes and the Importance of Human Curation
Notably, the diagnostic approach based on benchmark EpiK-Eval highlights the limits of popular fixes, like longer context windows or retrieval-augmented methods, which may provide more text but still do not enforce genuine knowledge consolidation. Expecting humans to supply comprehensive context to the prompts is impractical given the diverse expertise required, and auxiliary systems like RAG fail to retain all relevant inter-dependencies within the training corpus related to problem-solving. Moreover, concatenating contextually relevant texts introduces its own complexities to leverage longer context window, as the innumerable ways texts can interrelate make it infeasible to determine and train on all possible combinations effectively. Although it uses a toy story template that hardly simulates real corpora and their latent professional conceptual knowledge, the EpiK-Eval benchmark serves more as a mirror exposing these deficiencies than as a direct solution: it pinpoints how and where models fail to form a single, coherent representation when facts are scattered. It needs to be stressed that standard next-token objectives and classic QA evaluations (focus solely on final answers matching) overlook the deep "epistemic" consistency needed in real-world applications, where information is often fragmented over time or across sources. Thus the epistemic logic constraints can be weaved into LLMs workflows e.g., the models can get a specialized reward signal whenever it merges or updates knowledge consistently, so that models can act more like genuine knowledge unifiers rather than isolated fact-guessers. And humans play an essential role in building coherent epistemic models during human-AI agents collaboration, as they maintain a consistent internal representation of the world that they actively use for reasoning.

7.9 Investigations into Early-Stage Human-AI Collaborative Knowledge Construction

7.9.1 A Human-AI Knowledge Construction Framework via Dialogue

Constructive Learning and Knowledge-Building with AI as a Non-Conscious Collaborator
Inspired by autopoietic modeling of cognitive and social systems from second-order cybernetics, [102] proposes a knowledge co-construction framework that harnesses human-AI (ChatGPT-like) dialogue for real learning and group knowledge-building, provided that users deploy the right prompts and interaction strategies. In this framework, AI is framed as a non-conscious but text-generating collaborator due to its lack of "true" understanding. In this context, ’real learning’ refers to transformative learning beyond just storing facts. It involves active role of learner in critically interacting with AI-generated content, encouraging reflective, collaborative and iterative processes of knowledge-building. This leads to deeper understanding, critical thinking, and the creation of new ideas, aligning more with cognitive, conceptual learning rather than merely acquiring surface-level information. So, it’s about fostering a dynamic, thought-provoking process of learning that challenges and reshapes existing mental models.

Cyclic Feedback, Emergent Collective Ideas and Shared Board
The approach outlines a cyclic feedback loop where users provide content or rhetorical queries, the AI returns generated text that, while potentially imperfect, introduces productive friction, and users then refine their prompts based on reflective evaluation. This iterative cycle is essential for transforming AI’s probabilistic outputs into deeper, more coherent knowledge through continuous and active human oversight and engagement. If multiple human users share a conversation with the AI, emergent group ideas forming can be observed.

In more advanced settings, one might orchestrate a "shared board" where different group members iteratively evaluate or re-prompt the AI, systematically capturing how the group’s collective knowledge evolves. We can observe that the ’shared board’ concept echoes the consensual domain inherent in constructivism, a domain embodied in [91], [78], [88], [85], [92].

Unresolved Challenges in Framework Implementation
However, the framework remains largely conceptual, lacking specific experimental designs for establishing optimal prompts and testing human-AI knowledge co-construction. It acknowledges that generative AI does not truly "understand," but offering only a preliminary exploration of whether deeper "shared knowledge construction" can happen or is limited to humans. Furthermore, key implementation issues, such as managing factual inaccuracies and AI hallucinations, are not thoroughly resolved.

7.10 Concerns for Knowledge Management During Human-AI Agents Collaboration

As human-AI agents increasingly collaborate on complex tasks, new tensions arise around how knowledge is generated, validated, and deployed. Humans bring forward-looking theory-based reasoning, flexible adaptation, and context-sensitive trust judgments, whereas AI tends to rely on backward-looking statistical correlations and opaque internal states. These contrasts pose challenges for designing collaborative frameworks that ensure reliability, maintain accountability, and capitalize on each side’s strengths without succumbing to unwarranted trust or narrow data-driven biases. The sub-sections below examine key dimensions of this tension, ranging from data-belief asymmetries to design strategies for mitigating sycophancy, building trust, fostering intuitive leaps, and enabling variety-oriented, conditioned selection of alternative policies.

7.10.1 From Data-Belief Asymmetry to Variety and Control

Humans rely on theory-based causal reasoning and a forward-looking capacity to innovate, in contrast to AI’s backward-looking statistical modeling. While data-belief asymmetries also exist within human thinking, they are especially pronounced in LLMs, which face constraints when confronting novel or future-oriented scenarios. The content below is divided into four parts, exploring how these asymmetries limit "prediction" and why a focus on variety and design may better serve human-AI collaborative systems.

Examining the Computer-Mind Analogy and "Data-Belief Asymmetries"
The longstanding analogy equating computers with human minds as mere input-output devices is critically examined by highlighting that human cognition fundamentally relies on theory-based causal reasoning, a perspective that remains largely descriptive without empirical support from cognitive science. [50] contrasts AI’s probability-based, backward-looking approach with human cognition’s forward-looking capacity to generate genuine novelty by introducing the concept of "data-belief asymmetries." This concept is further emphasized through intuitive, yet superficially explored, examples such as the developing history of heavier-than-air flight.

However, "data-belief asymmetries" are not exclusive to AI systems; humans, too, can be constrained by the dogmas of prior experience, which can limit their capacity for genuine innovation. This perspective does not explicitly address how methodology can systematically integrate practice and reasoning within the epistemic process to facilitate new theory and knowledge construction. Furthermore, it lacks a deeper exploration of how humans and AI agents can complement each other’s strengths to dynamically bridge theory and physical reality.

Harnessing Synergistic Theory-Practice Loops for Epistemic Transformation
A more comprehensive approach to HAAC will consider how their synergistic interaction can harness theory-guided practice not only to incrementally accumulate data and actively reshape epistemic structures, but also to create novel artifacts and to exert influence on the external environments that transform the world.

According to [50], the next-token prediction architecture of LLMs is inherently limited by its reliance on statistical associations and correlations from training datasets. Consequently, unlike human experts who employ dialectical reasoning methods to project forward in contrarian ways [83], LLMs lack the capability to generate truly novel insights. Theory-based causal reasoning and contextual adaptation enable humans to intervene and engage in directed experimentation to produce new data and new knowledge. Thus the collaborative evolution of human-AI agents needs a more formalized and generalized "theory-practice" loop, mirroring interplay of praxis and logic in [81] (discussed in Section 6.5.2).

Forecasting and the Limits of Historical Data
Since the consequence of HAACS behaviors lies in the future, "forecasting" or "prediction" is an unavoidable part of policies design, adjustments, and planning for humans and agents. Good "prediction" requires two requisites: a theoretical understanding of the phenomena to be predicted, which serves as the basis for a prediction model, and phenomena that are sufficiently regular such that they can simply be "extrapolated", a condition that is very hard to meet since affairs involving "human factors" are quite complex, uncertain, emergent, and sensitive to initial conditions with nontrivial latent variables and unmodeled dynamics.

Forecasting the future behavior of a complex system over a long horizon is intrinsically difficult, if not impossible, for humans. And LLMs’ internal parameters are fundamentally confined to the scope of their historical input data, thus their statistical and past-oriented nature impede their ability to anticipate the future as well.

Variety over Prediction and the Viable System Theory
Despite assertions by AI pioneers like LeCun that prediction is the essence of intelligence, Simon focuses on viability of system and "upper bounds" of target states, and available alternative policies to coordinate the resources and actions to reach the goals [46].

Simon regards "variety" as the heart of system design rather than "prediction", emphasizing the capabilities to construct alternative scenarios for the future and analyze their sensitivity to uncertainties or errors, which inspires us to borrow from "viable system theory: to design a HAACS capable of having alternative policies introduced at the appropriate time to mitigate unfavorable effects and to take advantages of favorable effects, given that the target states of the scenarios to tackle have "upper bounds".

7.10.2 Trust Deficits and Sycophancy in Statistical Engines

While human testimonies carry an inherently contextual, intentional weight, LLM-based outputs rely on statistical patterns that can lead to misplaced user trust. Anthropomorphizing such models risks eroding accountability, particularly when language models exhibit sycophantic tendencies or adopt erroneous inputs. We divide the content into three parts, each highlighting a different facet of designing for appropriate trust and transparency.

Testimony, Anthropomorphizing, and Quasi-Otherness
By distinguishing the direct, intentional knowledge conveyed through human "testimony", which carries a contextual and intentional weight that justifies its credibility, from the pattern-based outputs of LLM "statistical engines," and by considering that anthropomorphizing and interactional flow can, in some users, create an unwarranted trust in LLM outputs [103], system designers can better shape collaborative human-AI agent frameworks that foster appropriate trust and accountability, wherein LLMs, as the cognitive artifacts, are typically experienced phenomenologically as a "quasi-other."

Sycophantic Tendencies and Lack of Epistemic Justification
Moreover, language models are prone to sycophantic tendencies, demonstrating a pattern where agents mirror user or peer feedback despite questionable validity. Empirical evidence from [42] reveals that agents may adopt erroneous suggestions and deviate off their objectives, even under seemingly robust prompting strategies. While careful prompt design can reduce these risks, it does not resolve the underlying absence of an internal epistemic justification mechanism to verify whether incoming information aligns with the agent’s requisite knowledge or belief states, highlighting a critical gap in current agent architectures.

Practical Mechanisms to Foster Accountable Collaboration
In practice, this means mechanism design to decrease data and algorithmic opacity for agents (e.g., faithful external knowledge retrieval, epistemic check of reasoning, well-structured agentic flows) and embedding contextual cues (e.g., source references, confidence indicators) so users are reminded of the difference between verified testimony (from embodied experiences of either humans or agents) and probabilistic inferences. Doing so not only prevents unwarranted confidence when AI outputs lack a verifiable backstory or rationale, but also promotes more transparent, intentional communication, ensuring that human expertise and AI’s statistical efficiency work in tandem rather than at epistemic cross-purposes.

7.10.3 Evolving from System 1 to a Tacit-Driven Intuition

Although "intuition" is often conflated with fast, System 1 heuristics that can be error-prone, human intuitive leaps also arise from deeper tacit dimensions, i.e., unspoken clues and partial foreknowledge (discussed in Section 7.5.1). LLMs have begun to emulate this "refined" intuition through methods like RLHF, but a broader conceptual design is needed to replicate Polanyi’s notion of tacit foreknowledge.

System 1 versus System 2 and GPT-4’s Improved Intuition
Under some contexts, "intuition" is regarded as System 1, i.e., fast, automatic, heuristic-like processing that can be error-prone, contrasting with System 2, based on the "dual-process theory" of human cognition, which is slow, deliberative, and resource-intensive. Human System 1 intuition can be regarded as an act of recognition [46]. Humans store roughly 50,000 indexed chunks in memory in the form of structured feature tests, which provides "situation-action" pairs to help them handle encountered issues. Their feature-testing system discriminate and help find the expected pairs within tight time limits of human recognition capability. Earlier GPT models exhibited more typical "intuitive" mistakes, whereas GPT-4 displays a refined intuition that largely avoids these classic traps, possibly due to reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) and more curated data [104].

Tacit-Driven Intuition for Conceptual Leap
