However, note that this usage of "intuition" (fast, automatic, System-1-type responses) differs from the view that human intuition during scientific discovery serves as the initial direction inspired from the proximal thinking clues that trigger active experience integration and eventually lead to correct answers or novel scientific discovery [89]. Though Polanyi’s framework remains largely conceptual, it points toward designing AI systems that replicate intuitive leaps, detecting and pursuing hidden problems via partial but meaningful "tacit foreknowledge," similar to the Meno paradox resolution. In HAAC, such tacit-aware architectures could amplify human researchers’ creativity and complement strictly algorithmic methods.

7.10.4 Customized HAAC Architecture for Domain Experts

Surpassing the Constraints of Extant Knowledge
The rapidly evolving nature of real-world problems demands capacities that go beyond pattern recognition driven by historical data and knowledge, including a forward-looking intuition, contrarian causal reasoning, and on-the-fly experimentation, i.e., capacities that today’s LLMs-based agents do not inherently possess. While AI agents excel at augmenting decision-making in repetitive, closed-ended tasks, they struggle in unpredictable or unseen scenarios that require re-contextualizing domain-specific knowledge and continuously recalibrating beliefs against a shifting reality, echoing "explore-exploit" dynamics preliminarily discussed in Sections 4.1, 6.4, 6.5 from different aspects.

High-Quality Specialized Data Constraints and Intrinsic Hallucinations Costly constraints on specialized, high-quality training data compared to the vast low value-added general data, due to privacy considerations, paywalls, or siloed organizational policies, further exacerbate LLMs’ limitations of high dependency on data. Even when advanced prompt engineering and external knowledge bases are employed, these models remain prone to "hallucinations" and misalignment, underscoring how purely data-oriented solutions cannot replace the nuanced expertise and contextual judgments cultivated by human professionals in areas like medicine or general scientific research.

Customized Research Assistant Architecture of HAAC for Copilot
To bridge these gaps, HAAC must prioritize complementarity rather than substitution. A modular, "personalized" research assistant architecture, rather than a monolithic, one-size-fits-all "general" system discussed preliminarily in Section 6.6, will copilot and allow domain experts to iteratively supply high-quality, context-specific, real-time data including complex reasoning templates, refine models through guided practice. As contradictory findings accumulate and complex, ad hoc problems, and edge cases arise in the workplace or research communities, it becomes evident that humans must retain a guiding role, iteratively intuiting which new data and experiences to gather via theory-guided experimentation, how to build new theory and frame emergent insights, and when to challenge the model’s assumptions or incorporate specialized and private knowledge silos.

Epistemic Justification and Real-World Validation
Also HAAC needs to perform epistemic checks at each stage of reasoning of a series of granular "blocks" ranging from exploring novel domain knowledge, verifying retrieved knowledge, to maintaining consistent rationales across dialogue, communications and general interactions.

In addition, knowledge in HAAC requires continuous scrutiny under real-world conditions to reveal hidden contradictions or incomplete reasoning, ensuring that knowledge consolidation proceeds without sacrificing validation in practice or ignoring emergent physical phenomena. By embedding theory-building and reflective iteration into the workflow, human and agents ensure that LLM-based systems stay aligned with ever-shifting realities, harnessing the best of both worlds: AI’s computational reach and humans’ intuition, creativity, and contextual acuity.

8 Revisiting Meta-Synthesis as a Stepping Stone for Open Complex Human-AI Agent Collaboration Systems

Meta-synthesis, historically developed as a "from qualitative to quantitative" approach, offers valuable insights for tackling open complex giant systems by combining expert knowledge, empirical data, and theoretical constructs. In modern contexts, however, AI agents equipped with LLMs can play an increasingly substantial role, complementing or sometimes surpassing human capabilities. While the original framework integrates human specialists in a collaborative "discussion hall" as an early-stage cyberspace, extending meta-synthesis to incorporate advanced AI agents as active players requires adaptations in collective problem solving, decision-making, knowledge management, system design and modeling practices, tasks planning, and iterative consensus-building.

8.1 Foundational Qualitative Approaches and Knowledge Types in Meta-Synthesis

Meta-synthesis initially emphasizes the qualitative underpinnings of complex problem-solving, highlighting how diverse forms of qualitative knowledge, ranging from empirical observations to theoretical insights, can be systematically integrated and eventually transformed into quantitative results. This focus on qualitative reasoning and knowledge representation sets the stage for tackling the intrinsic uncertainties and multifaceted interactions in open complex systems.

The Qualitative to Quantitative Paradigm
Tsien introduced the "meta-synthesis" methods as an exploratory "from qualitative to quantitative" methodology for open complex giant system [56]. It organically integrates expert groups, data, diverse sources of information, and computer technology, while also synthesizing scientific theories from various disciplines with human experience and knowledge. Together, these elements form a cohesive system. Specifically, it proposes the associated "cyberspace" as discussion hall for human experts from different disciplines with the help of information technology. The successful application of this method relies on fully leveraging the synergistic strengths of this integrated system.

Knowledge-Controlled Inductive Methods for Practical Problem-solving
Problem-solving in the real world is carried out using knowledge-controlled inductive methods rather than precise quantitative procedures, as most knowledge is empirical and cannot be described with absolute precision [56]. A knowledge type system is essential for representing various kinds of knowledge in real-world scenarios, such as book knowledge, domain-specific knowledge, empirical knowledge, and common sense knowledge, in a form that can be processed and interpreted by a computer.

Qualitative Modeling and Reasoning
Typically, qualitative physics concepts and model-building methods are used to establish qualitative models, which serve as a foundation for studying qualitative reasoning. Qualitative model-building encodes deep underlying knowledge, focusing only on trends of change such as increment, decrement, and invariance. Qualitative reasoning, in turn, operates on these qualitative models to understand or predict system behavior. A brief discussion on component-centered, constraints-centered, and process-centered qualitative physical systems, which are explainable and predictable, can be found in this publication [56]. For an open and complex HAACS, qualitative methods are more suitable for its knowledge type system rather than the strict quantitative mathematical models used in formal systems.

8.2 From Empirical Hypotheses toward Iterative Consensus and Model Refinement

Building on qualitative foundations, meta-synthesis advances to the stage of constructing empirical hypotheses and testing them through iterative modeling and expert consensus. This phase underscores the importance of refining models, aligning them with real-world data, and navigating the complexities of expert collaboration. Despite offering a structured process, the methodology also highlights gaps in addressing discrepancies between theoretical models and dynamic practical realities.

Empirical Hypotheses and Expert Consensus
Professional studies and practices in scientific research and artificial system design often involve empirical hypotheses about means or methods to address practical problems. These hypotheses are typically derived from findings and conclusions of previous studies, i.e., qualitative knowledge such as cause-effect relationships that cannot be proven true or false with the rigor of mathematics. These empirical hypotheses often stem from researchers’ beliefs and intuitions as well. Reference models, based on the practical experience and verified knowledge of studied systems from experts, are then constructed, incorporating governing variables and parameters from the complex interconnections.

Through simulations or experiments using these models, along with quantitative calculations and analyses based on collected data, and following repeated verification and validation, conclusions and consensus are reached among experts. These conclusions represent the most accurate insights attainable at the current level of understanding of reality, reflecting quantitative knowledge built upon a foundation of qualitative understanding [56].

Integrated Model Construction, Simulation, Analysis, Optimization and Iterative Consensus Formation
As exemplified, the meta-synthesis problem-solving process begins with experts from the concerned domains (simulated by some LLM-based multi-agents system’ experts experts recruitment stage [42], [48], etc.), and system engineers analyzing the problem by leveraging their expertise and experience. They identify the core issue, make qualitative assessments (empirical hypotheses) about potential solutions, and define the problem within a system framework. This includes determining boundaries, state variables, environment variables, control variables (policy variables), and output variables (observation variables). This initial step establishes the foundation for system modeling by defining its concept, requirements, and functions, similar to the process transforming the targeted concrete systems to the conceptual systems [67].

System modeling employs mathematical or logical models to represent the structure, function, and input-output relationships of the real system. This model reflects the behavior of the actual system and relies on both theoretical methods and empirical and statistical data. Using these models and computer simulations, the system’s reactions to various inputs, dynamic characteristics, and future behaviors are analyzed, while concerns about real-time connection between the physical and virtual systems and all lifecycle stages are complemented in [105]. This process, known as systems analysis, allows researchers to study the system and identify optimization strategies to achieve the desired outcomes.

The optimization step aims to determine the best, near-optimal, or satisfactory policies [46] or strategies to improve system performance. The quantitative results derived from simulations and analyses are reviewed and discussed by experts to ensure reliability. If the results are found to be questionable, the model is revised, parameters are adjusted, and the process is repeated until consensus is reached among experts (similar iterative consensus formation process simulated in LLM-based multi-agents system among experts can be found in [42], [47], [48], [39], [72]). Once experts agree on the model’s reliability, conclusions and policy recommendations are finalized, supported by both qualitative descriptions and quantitative evidence. This ensures a scientifically grounded basis for decision-making, moving beyond mere conjecture.

Remaining Gaps in Dynamic Real-World Integration
However, during the theory-building process to convert empirical hypotheses, assessments, and conjectures into quantitative knowledge as consensus at best, preliminary meta-synthesis methods still lack an explicit mechanism to guide experts in performing necessary practices and experiments meanwhile to address potential discrepancies between models and real-world scenarios in an evolving epistemic process. Although these methods emphasize the cyclic dynamics between modeling, simulation and analysis, expert discussions, and decision-making, this gap remains, requiring dynamic incorporation of new data, information and experiences from practice.

9 Towards Open Complex Human-AI Agents Collaboration Nets

9.1 A Preliminary Ontology for Distinctive Agenthood

Reevaluating Agenthood Through Non-Interchangeable Identity
The essence of an "agent" must involve a clearly delineated, non-interchangeable identity. Intuitively, when examining current single-agent or multi-agent configurations, where individual components such as memory modules, LLM-based reasoners, or tool sets are highly modular, there appears to be no genuine uniqueness distinguishing one agent from another. A specific agent can be replicated, and its components interchanged across different instances, suggesting these entities do not qualify as “true” agents in the way humans do.

Humans possess spatio-temporal identification: we humans can only act in one place at a time, inheriting memories and behavioral patterns continuously, in a manner that is not merely modular. Our functional subsystems exhibit latent yet uniquely correlated structures that are absent in current AI-based agent designs. Although these AI agents can operate tools to affect the physical world, they lack an entity conferring genuine uniqueness.

So, how might one construct a parallel form of "uniqueness" within digital agents, something akin to human wholeness with its strong interdependence among internal subsystems? The organ for memory in a human cannot be simply removed while retaining full reasoning and tool-use capability; yet, this sort of modular swapping is possible in AI agents. One might counter that LLMs already contain internal, persistent memories that enable basic reasoning even without external memory. But in humans, removing external or sensory-based memory systems (to isolate "internal" memory) without impairing normal functioning is not straightforward, if not impossible.

Therefore, the fundamental question emerges: how do we define, and what theoretical criteria or frameworks can we employ, to categorize and formalize concepts like "uniqueness," "wholeness," and "autonomy" for humans, agents, human collectives, and multi-agent systems? This naturally transitions us into discussing the broader landscape of agentic AI and AI agents.

Mapping the Four Pillars of an Agentic Ontology
We propose a robust ontology of "agenthood" hinges on four conceptual pillars, i.e., ’Identity’, ’Wholeness’, ’Autonomy’, and ’Continuity’. Identity highlights an entity’s self-maintenance and non-interchangeability, drawing on ideas of autopoiesis of second-order cybernetics to contrast humans, whose singular "self" endures despite biological changes, with LLM-based agents that can be copied or forked at will. Wholeness focuses on how deeply subsystems are integrated: human cognition is tightly coupled (memory, emotion, reasoning and even physical states for embodied cognition interweave inseparably), whereas many AI agents rely on modular, replaceable components. Autonomy differentiates self-generated human goals, rooted in biology and social context, from AI agents whose objectives typically derive from user prompts or preset performance targets for specific tasks. Finally, Continuity underscores that humans live a single, spatio-temporally anchored existence absorbing external information all the time, while AI agents may run on multiple servers or be paused and resumed, complicating the notion of a unified personal history.

These four pillars form the basis for a formal ontology of agenthood that can be used to evaluate or design artificial entities. Practitioners may ask: does an agent exhibit unique identity that cannot be trivially merged or replicated? Are its core functions (e.g., memory, reasoning) so interwoven that removing one undermines its entire existence? Do its goals arise from within, or are they externally imposed? And is the agent’s trajectory anchored in a continuous timeline, or can it be cloned and parallelized without fracturing its identity? Addressing these questions pushes us beyond surface-level descriptions, forcing designers and researchers to specify precisely where along each dimension an AI agent stands compared to human-like singularity. In this way, the ontology doubles as both theoretical lens and practical tool.

Practical Strategies for Deeper Human-Like Uniqueness
For those seeking to create digital agents with deeper "human-like" uniqueness, several strategies emerge. Immutable identity anchors, such as cryptographic ledgers, can ensure copying an agent results in a distinct new entity rather than a seamless clone. Strong embodiment constraints, enforcing a single computational environment, can foster continuity and limit casual replication. Systems that support self-maintenance and self-regulation approximate autopoiesis, letting agents adapt or repair themselves without external "module swapping." Finally, bounded perception-action loops ground each agent’s unique experiences in a singular "world," such that any trivial duplication of its personal history disrupts the agent’s continuity. Though such measures complicate engineering, they underscore the profound difference between mere plug-and-play software and truly integral, singularly continuous agenthood.

9.2 Representing Agent-Level Collaboration via Petri Net

Dilemma of Agent Modeling: "Ship of Theseus" and Fluid Boundaries
Much like the "Ship of Theseus" paradox, where planks are replaced over time, causing us to question whether it remains the ’same’ ship, defining an agent becomes tricky when its modules are swapped or reconfigured. Traditional multi-agent models often assume a stable boundary around sensing, decision-making, and acting components, treating each agent as a discrete, autonomous unit. But edge cases abound: a "two-headed" agent with dual LLM cores sharing resources can act as one cohesive unit or as two separate agents, depending on how we group or label its internal processes.

Similarly, fluid boundaries in reconfigurable cognitive architectures defy strict partitioning; the agent can share modules with the environment or with other agents in ways that challenge the classical notion of self-contained autonomy. These prevalent methods, ranging from purely task-focused definitions (e.g., grouping by function) to intentional approaches (e.g., assigning beliefs, desires, and intentions), highlight the ongoing dilemma: does an agent remain "itself" under continuous reassembly of internal components, or should we define it differently each time the boundary shifts?

Adaptive Interface Dynamics in Goal-Oriented Systems
A goal-oriented adaptive system focuses on the "interface" between its "inner" and "outer" environments, achieving its goals by adapting the former to the latter through "interface" [46]. Although the inner environment (akin to hardware) is relatively simple, the system’s complexity emerges from the richness of the outer environment. A thinking human being is such an adaptive system: an individual’s goals define the interface between their inner and outer environments. With memory stores in play, human behavior reflects the characteristics of the outer environment in light of a person’s goals, revealing only a few limiting properties to enable a person’s thinking. Thus, the apparent "complexity" of human behavior over time reflects the "complexity" of that external setting.

Adopting Simon’s Interface-Oriented View
To transcend this dilemma, Simon’s interface-oriented approach offers a powerful guiding principle: rather than fixating on an agent’s internal composition, one focuses on its boundary of interaction with the environment. From a systems perspective, we can treat all internal states and modules, however many heads or reconfigurable sub-parts they possess, as belonging to a single "artifact," provided they share a coherent external "interface" for exchanging information, matter, or energy. Under this framework, the places and transitions of Petri nets define how the agent’s internal states are coupled and how the agent exerts influence on the outside. Whenever a module remains within the boundary, it is "internal." If it can be directly accessed by external forces publicly [51], it becomes part of the environment. This interface-oriented method gracefully handles "Ship of Theseus" scenarios: no matter how many planks (modules) are replaced, so long as the overarching interface and its capacity to control or be controlled, i.e., self-regulate, remains coherent, we can still call it the same agent.

9.2.1 Modeling Multi-Agent Systems with Petri Net Formalisms

Ad-Hoc Approaches and Their Limitations
In the multi-agent implementations discussed in Sections 3.5, 3.6, and 4, the interplay between agents is often described through ad-hoc, empirical approaches that omit the explicit and detailed accounting of how information, matter, and energy flow within and among agents. These implementations typically focus on high-level behaviors (e.g., whether agents cooperate or compete to achieve tasks) but rarely capture the precise transformations and transfers underpinning such behaviors. As a result, crucial elements, like the actual resource constraints in each agent, the energy costs of communication, and the storage, dissipation, or conversion of matter, remain hidden or approximated in ways that limit both explanatory depth and predictive power. When these approaches do try to account for resource flows, they often do so superficially, aggregating them into generic "cost functions" or "utility metrics" that only approximate or partially capture the underlying processes.

Without a formal foundation, these ad-hoc methods risk producing fragmented, inconsistent, or non-generalizable results. For instance, the same basic modeling architecture might be used across different interaction scenarios without ensuring that core resource-flow principles (e.g., conservation of matter or the transformation of energy into work) are consistently upheld. Moreover, concurrency, synchronization, asynchrony, parallelism and sequentiality as fundamental aspects of multi-agent communication and coordination, tend to be treated in an implicit manner, leaving potential conflicts or race conditions underexplored. This patchwork approach also complicates comparative analysis across different benchmarks, since each one might incorporate its own arbitrary assumptions about resource handling, message passing, and agent "states."

A Formal Framework with Petri Net Formalisms
In contrast, Petri net-based formalisms offer an explicit and rigorous way to model these dynamics. By specifying which "places" (states) store information, matter, or energy, and which "transitions" transform or exchange these resources, Petri nets capture the structural and causal details of multi-agent interactions. This enables systematic analysis of properties such as deadlocks, resource bottlenecks (modelling bounded rationality [46] explicitly), or synchronization issues, i.e., properties that may remain opaque or undiscovered in less formal modeling frameworks. Furthermore, Petri nets allow for easy extension and clear modularization, ensuring that each agent’s internal conversions (information, matter, and energy) among inner modules can be clearly described at the same time as the collective interplay emerges from the transitions, whether shared or privately owned, that occur among agents. The final framework will serve as not only a more precise representation of the system’s mechanics but also a robust foundation for comparing and contrasting different multi-agent approaches in a consistent, theoretically grounded manner.

In Petri nets, "tokens" flow through transitions according to certain rules. It’s relatively straightforward to extend the token colors so they represent or carry different "substances" for HAACS: information tokens (e.g., messages, data, knowledge); matter tokens (e.g., physical resources); energy tokens (e.g., consumable energy capacity); note that each transition can then transform tokens of a certain type into tokens of another type, capturing the "interplay" of information, matter, and energy occurring in the processes of [68]. And the built-in concurrency and the rich analysis techniques behind Petri nets can be utilized to reason about the properties such as reachability, liveness, synchronization, and resource usage.

9.2.2 Interface-Oriented Human-AI Agent Collaboration in Petri Nets

An agent sustains itself by upholding a dynamic interface, i.e., its boundary, through which it exchanges information, energy, or matter with the outside, mirroring the essential information-energy-matter processes to support living systems in [67]. Even being idle without imposing control on the outside, the agent must preserve its own integrity via processes akin to autopoiesis or autogenesis. Analogically, a computational agent "lives" in RAM when inactive and may be recycled once its threads complete, but as long as it retains the internal capacity to maintain itself, it remains an autonomous entity.

The overall HAACS is represented by a colored Petri-net:

𝒞​N=(P,T,A,Σ,κ,Pre,Post,M0),\mathcal{C}N=(P,T,A,\Sigma,\kappa,\mathrm{Pre},\mathrm{Post},M_{0}), (1)

where PP is a finite set of places. TT is a finite set of transitions. AA is a finite set of arcs connecting places and transitions (input and output arcs). Σ\Sigma is a global (or multi-sorted) color universe, i.e., the union of all color types that might be used (e.g., "information," "matter," "energy," etc.). κ:P→2Σ\kappa:P\to 2^{\Sigma} assigns each place a color set κ⁡(p)⊆Σ\kappa(p)\subseteq\Sigma; tokens in place pp must belong to κ⁡(p)\kappa(p).

Pre\mathrm{Pre} and Post\mathrm{Post} define how tokens flow: Each arc p→tp\to t or t→pt\to p has an associated arc expression that describes how many tokens (and of which colors) are produced/consumed. For simplicity in matrix form, we can store integer counts if we treat color matching externally. In more advanced definitions, Pre⁡(p,t)\mathrm{Pre}(p,t) or Post⁡(p,t)\mathrm{Post}(p,t) can be functions from color sets. M0M_{0} is the initial marking, specifying how many tokens of each color reside in each place initially. A marking MM is thus a function M:P→ℳκM:P\to\mathcal{M}_{\kappa}, which tells us the multi-set of colored tokens in each place.

Ownership of Transitions and Places Partition
We partition the entire net among nn agents {A1,…,An}\{A_{1},\dots,A_{n}\}, plus an environment EE, plus a human HH, which can be extended to a group. Instead of having a separate "interface transition" class, each transition t∈Tt\in T is owned by exactly one entity:

Owner:T​→​{A1,…,An,E,H}\text{Owner}:T\textrightarrow\{A_{1},\dots,A_{n},E,H\} (2)

Note that the transitions ownership is essential for supervisory control. If Owner​(t)=Ai\text{Owner}(t)=A_{i}, agent AiA_{i} controls that transition. If Owner​(t)=H\text{Owner}(t)=H, then the human decides if/when tt fires, subject to the marking and color constraints. If Owner​(t)=E\text{Owner}(t)=E, it is an environment-driven transition. Similarly, each place pp belongs to either an agent AiA_{i}, the environment EE, or the human HH. For instance, PH⊂PP_{H}\subset P are the human-owned places (storing tokens representing human knowledge, tasks, decisions, etc).

A transition can consume or produce tokens in places belonging to different agents (or environment or human), but responsibility for enabling that transition is assigned to a single owner. The boundaries between agents, the environment, and humans are represented by transitions whose input and output places belong to different entities. By default, all input places originate from the same entity, and the boundary transitions (interfaces) are owned by the entity from which the input places originate. This avoids the confusion of separate "boundary transitions" blocks, because any boundary-crossing transition simply belongs to whichever agent (or environment) can trigger it.

Each place pp is assigned either to an agent’s internal set PiP_{i} (indicating that the place "belongs" to agent AiA_{i}) or to the environment PEP_{E} or to the human PHP_{H}. A place can still contain tokens that move in or out via transitions owned by other agents, thereby realizing "boundary crossing." Thus we have:

P=(⋃i=1nPi)∪PE∪PH,T=(⋃i=1nTi)∪TE∪TH,P=\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}P_{i}\right)\cup P_{E}\cup P_{H},\ \ T=\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}T_{i}\right)\cup T_{E}\cup T_{H}, (3)

Reorder PP to group places as (P1,…,Pn,PH,PE)(P_{1},\dots,P_{n},\,P_{H},\,P_{E}), and reorder TT to group transitions as (T1,…,Tn,TH,TE)(T_{1},\dots,T_{n},\,T_{H},\,T_{E}). The incidence matrix CC (of size |P|×|T||P|\times|T|) breaks down into blocks as follows:

C=(C1,1⋯C1,nC1,HC1,E⋱Cn,1⋯Cn,nCn,HCn,ECH,1⋯CH,nCH,HCH,ECE,1⋯CE,nCE,HCE,E).C=\begin{pmatrix}C_{1,1}&\cdots&C_{1,n}&C_{1,H}&C_{1,E}\\ \vdots&\ddots&\vdots&\vdots&\vdots\\ C_{n,1}&\cdots&C_{n,n}&C_{n,H}&C_{n,E}\\ C_{H,1}&\cdots&C_{H,n}&C_{H,H}&C_{H,E}\\ C_{E,1}&\cdots&C_{E,n}&C_{E,H}&C_{E,E}\end{pmatrix}. (4)

If Ci,j≠0C_{i,j}\neq 0, it means that transitions in TjT_{j} (owned by AjA_{j}) affect places in PiP_{i} (owned by AiA_{i}). The environment is simply regarded as "agent EE" from this matrix viewpoint. Each block Ci,HC_{i,H} shows how human-owned transitions THT_{H} produce or consume tokens in agent AiA_{i}’s places PiP_{i}. Similarly, CH,jC_{H,j} shows how agent-owned transitions TjT_{j} affect the human’s places PHP_{H}.

MIMO Transition and "Collaboration Boundary"
Consider a multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) transition tt that has arcs from places in {Pi}\{P_{i}\} (agent AiA_{i}) and from {Pj}\{P_{j}\} (agent AjA_{j}), etc., and produces tokens into places across these same or other agents. In a simple "single owner" scheme as Eq. (2), we’d assign a transition tt to exactly one agent. But that can be awkward if multiple agents must collaborate for tt to fire (e.g., each must provide a resource or confirm readiness). For example, a transition tt that transfers "energy" from agent A1A_{1}, "task info" from agent A2A_{2}, and outputs combined results to both. Firing tt therefore has multi-agent preconditions and multi-agent effects.

Instead of forcing single-agent ownership, define a special set of collaboration transitions Tcoll⊆TM​I​M​OT_{\text{coll}}\subseteq T_{MIMO} that is incorporated into the original TT in Eq. (3). For any t∈Tcollt\in T_{\text{coll}}: Inputs: tt may consume tokens from places {Pi1,Pi2,…}\{P_{i_{1}},P_{i_{2}},\dots\}, belonging to different agents. Outputs: tt may produce tokens in those same or other agents’ places. Collective Enabling: All relevant agents, i.e., those that supply tokens or must authorize their use, must "agree" or enable tt to fire. The incidence matrix in Eq. (4) is thus extended to

CM​I​M​O=(C1,1⋯C1,nC1,collC1,EC1,H⋱Cn,1⋯Cn,nCn,collCn,ECn,HCH,1⋯CH,nCH,collCH,ECH,HCE,1⋯CE,nCE,collCE,ECE,H).C_{MIMO}=\begin{pmatrix}C_{1,1}&\cdots&C_{1,n}&C_{1,\text{coll}}&C_{1,E}&C_{1,H}\\ \vdots&\ddots&\vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\vdots\\ C_{n,1}&\cdots&C_{n,n}&C_{n,\text{coll}}&C_{n,E}&C_{n,H}\\ C_{H,1}&\cdots&C_{H,n}&C_{H,\text{coll}}&C_{H,E}&C_{H,H}\\ C_{E,1}&\cdots&C_{E,n}&C_{E,\text{coll}}&C_{E,E}&C_{E,H}\end{pmatrix}. (5)

a column block C∗,collC_{*,\text{coll}} is reserved for collaboration transitions. Each column in that block corresponds to a single collaboration transition tt, and the row entries indicate how the tokens from each associated agent’s places are consumed or produced. For each collaboration transition tt, define an ownership set formally as:

Owners⁡(t)⊆{A1,…,An}\operatorname{Owners}(t)\subseteq\{A_{1},\dots,A_{n}\} (6)

That indicates which agents must participate in or consent to tt. This is more general than single-agent transitions than that in Eq. (2). A transition tt fires in a concurrency step if all agents in Owners⁡(t)\operatorname{Owners}(t) enable it, and the marking (token distribution) satisfies all input arc constraints (including color checks) across each agent’s places.

For supervisory control, if a control matrix Γ∈{0,1}|T|×n\Gamma\in\{0,1\}^{|T|\times n} is used, then for any t∈Tcollt\in T_{\text{coll}}:

Γ⁡[t,i]={1,if ​Ai∈Owners⁡(t),0,otherwise.\Gamma[t,i]=\begin{cases}1,&\text{if }A_{i}\in\operatorname{Owners}(t),\\[2.84166pt] 0,&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases} (7)

At run-time, each agent AiA_{i} follows a local policy σi\sigma_{i}. A collaboration transition tt becomes enabled if all σi\sigma_{i} for i∈Owners⁡(t)i\in\operatorname{Owners}(t) allow it, in addition to satisfying the marking constraints.

9.2.3 Decoupling Computation and Control with Interpreted Petri-Nets

We extend the colored Petri-net presented in Eq. (1) to the interpreted Petri-net so as to unify: (1) token-based coordination (with optional guard logic), capturing interactions occurring in boundaries between agents and environment, and (2) data-processing/state updates (global or agent-local), capturing the internal logic of each agent and state variables of the global system. This yields a two-level design:

- Level 1: Petri net structure (places, transitions, arcs) for concurrency and synchronization, including "boundary" interactions between agents.
- Level 2: Interpreted state variables (data updates), handled by each transition’s "operation" and guard conditions.

The approach generalizes neatly to systems (modeled in Section 9.2.2) with either single-owner transitions or collaboration transitions (multi-owner), as well as colored tokens for message- or resource-passing across boundaries. Although earlier studies (e.g., AutoGen [41] discussed in Section 3.5.1) have reported empirical designs that exhibit similar decoupling design, our formalism is independently developed and provides a rigorous theoretical framework for separating computation and control. In contrast to the ad-hoc approaches described in previous work, our method systematically delineates the two aspects, thereby extending the insights initially observed.

Global and Local Data Variables Computation and Updates
An interpreted Petri net (IPN) extends a basic net (P,T)(P,T) in Eq. (2) with a collection of data variables that can be: (1) global variables: 𝐗𝐠=(x1,…,xm)\mathbf{X_{g}}=(x_{1},\dots,x_{m}) shared by all agents, (2) local variables: each agent AiA_{i} may keep a local vector 𝐗𝐥i=(xi​1,…,xi​ki)\mathbf{X_{l}}_{i}=(x_{i1},\dots,x_{ik_{i}}). When a transition fires, it can read and write these relevant data variables based on the assigned permission associated. The net effect is that the IPN has two "layers": "Petri Net Layer" (concurrency, token flow, enabling transitions) and "Data Layer" (each firing updates or checks data variables).

Thus we concatenate 𝐗𝐠\mathbf{X_{g}} and 𝐗𝐥\mathbf{X_{l}} to get XX. Provided a guard Gt​(X,γ)G_{t}(X,\gamma), i.e., a Boolean condition referencing XX (data variables) and, optionally, γ\gamma (the colors of tokens on the input arcs, if colored tokens matter).

9.2.4 Stepping Semantics and Conflict Resolution

In discrete-event settings for system expressed in Eq. (1), a "step" can be a set of transitions firing simultaneously (or in rapid succession). We represent the count of how many times each transition fires in a concurrency step by a vector:

δ⁡(τ)∈ℕ|T|\delta(\tau)\in\mathbb{N}^{|T|} (8)

where δ​(τ)​[t]=k\delta(\tau)[t]=k means transition tt fired kk times in this step. Mk+1=Mk+CM​I​M​O​δ​(τ)(k),M_{k+1}=M_{k}+C_{MIMO}\,\delta(\tau)^{(k)}, (10)

Per-Agent Stepping Δ​Mi\Delta M_{i}
If Pi⊂PP_{i}\subset P are the places owned by agent AiA_{i} (indexed accordingly), we extract the relevant rows from CM​I​M​OC_{MIMO} in Eq. (5) to obtain the sub-block Ci,∗C_{i,*}. Then,

Because each transition has a single owner, "boundary" interactions appear as nonzero off-diagonal blocks Ci,jC_{i,j} for i≠ji\neq j.

For IPN that extends system in Eq. (1), an update Δt\Delta_{t} for a concurrency step in virtue of the total firing vector (9) that modifies XX is:

Δt:X′←ft​(X,γ).\Delta_{t}:X^{\prime}\leftarrow f_{t}(X,\gamma). (12)

Where γ\gamma captures the colors of tokens on the input arcs of transitions if colored tokens matter, and ft​(X,γ)f_{t}(X,\gamma) are update functions within the transitions. The updated data for agent AiA_{i} is given by

Xi′=Xi⊕{Δt​(X,γ)|t∈Ti∪Tcoll​ fired in this step and ​t​ updates ​Xi},X_{i}^{\prime}=X_{i}\oplus\Bigl\{\,\Delta_{t}(X,\gamma)\;\Big|\;t\in T_{i}\cup T_{\text{coll}}\text{ fired in this step and }t\text{ updates }X_{i}\Bigr\}, (13)

In practice, one might require transitions updating the same variable to be mutually exclusive or define a merging function.

Agents Interactions Across Boundaries (i.e., Interfaces)
Internal transitions TiT_{i} that read/update only XiX_{i} (plus possibly some global variables) and consume/produce tokens solely in PiP_{i}. For an agent AiA_{i} whose places are output of boundary and collaboration transitions, the single-input single-output (SISO) and single-input multiple-output (SIMO) boundary transitions, as well as MIMO collaboration transitions, may consume tokens from multiple other agents’ places (and possibly human and environment places) and may read or write data variables in XiX_{i}.

If a transition belongs to a single agent AkA_{k}, then that agent has the final authority on its enabling. If a transition belongs to the "collaboration set" TcollT_{\text{coll}}, each agent with a resource or data stake must enable it. This distinguishes an agent’s "internal" net sub-structure from the transitions that cross boundaries to other agents, the human or the environment. Through the boundary transitions, the agents can synchronize (e.g., handshake or protocol transitions) to cooperate, and compete for the same resource, leading to transitions that represent resource locking or conflicts.

9.3 Achieving Cognition and Meta-Cognition via Execution-Level Sub-Nets Coordination

The cognition and meta-cognition capabilities, mainly discussed in Section 3.4 and 3.8, can be achieved through modelling the necessary transitions and places for meta-cognition and basic inference operations and coordinating the execution-level sub-nets.

Petri Net Modeling of the Sense-Plan-Act Loops
Based on discussions of LLM-based AI agent through a cybernetic lens in Section 3.4, goal-seeking adaptive agency is generalized into basic "sense-plan-act" (SPA) loops, with additional advanced functionality modules that can be plugged in, such as learning, self-explanation, criticism, reflection, and self-reflection. The Petri-net representation for SPA loops allows concurrency of "sense," "plan," "act," and additional tasks (like learning or reflection) within one agent.

First the SPA loop is decomposed into smaller major sub-tasks, such as: (1) Sense: acquire data from environment; (2) Plan: interpret data, identify and orchestrate tasks, make decisions; (3) Act: execute the selected decisions by interacting with inner modules, other agents, human and environment; and the optional (4) Learn: update long-term memories such as internal parameters of model, etc. Then each sub-task is modeled as a sub-net, and the basic diagrammatic description of places (PP) and transitions (TT) for these sub-nets is as follows (note: this description is extendable and provided solely for demonstration purposes):

- Sense Sub-Net: SensingReady—a place with a token when the agent can initiate sensing; DoSense—a transition that fires to collect data; NewDataAvailable—a place that gets a token once sensing completes.
- Plan Sub-Net: StartPlanning—a transition that consumes token from NewDataAvailable once data (including tasks) is ready; PlanningInProgress—a place that holds the "work in progress" state; FinishPlanning —a transition that produces the planning output; ActionReady—a place with a token that indicates an action can now be triggered.
- Act Sub-Net: InitiateAction—a transition that consumes token from ActionReady; ActingInProgress—a place that represents the system carrying out the action; CompleteAction—a transition that returns token to SensingReady (closing the loop), or to some environment or human places to model state changes for environment and human explicitly.
- Learn Sub-Net (Optional): this sub-net could be plugged in the SPA loops to run in parallel, and might be triggered by a token from NewDataAvailable or ActionReady (i.e., learning as an internal action planned in [51]) or both; LearningReady—a place that receives tokens indicating new info is available to learn from; PerformLearning—a transition as a learning step that updates long-term memory of agent such as the internal parameters of LLM model; LearningDone—a place to hold the completion marker and possibly it sends signals back to SensingReady or PlanningInProgress to inform the agent’s updated model.

A simple sense → plan → act loop can be extended into a more sophisticated net by explicitly representing each phase as sub-nets with places and transitions. Because Petri nets can hold multiple tokens in different places at once, the agent can "sense" again or "learn" while it is still "acting," provided we allow appropriate transitions and do not enforce strict resource conflicts that block concurrency, which is something basic finite-state machines or simple cyclic loops in [51] cannot do as neatly. For more refined models (involving real-time constraints or continuous variables), timed or hybrid Petri nets can be used.

Extending SPA Loops with Epistemic Justification and Explore-Exploit Mechanisms
To demonstrate the modularity and flexibility of Petri nets in modeling interactions and coordination within the internal modules of individual agents and among the agents (including humans), epistemic justification and "explore-exploit" mechanisms are modeled as sub-nets running simultaneously with the main SPA path by branching token flows between the main SPA path and these new sub-nets in both directions.

For epistemic justification mechanism, each agent maintains or uses certain pieces of knowledge (rules, norms and policies, beliefs, partial observations, etc), epistemic justification verifies whether that piece of knowledge or belief is valid, consistent with the environment, or accepted by other agents and human. We must capture both the agent’s own internal check (intra-agent) and any collaborative verification among multiple agents (inter-agent), conforming to the conventions in Eq. (5). Thus Epistemic Justification Sub-Net is created to focuses on verifying new or updated knowledge. For "explore-exploit" dynamics (preliminarily discussed in Sections 4.1, 6.4, 6.5 from different aspects), during "exploration" phase: humans (or specifically designated "explorer" roles assigned to AI agents) generate or refine new knowledge/rules when novelty or anomalies arise; during "exploitation" phase: AI agents apply known (verified) knowledge or routines to handle routine tasks, stabilizing the system; note that the epistemic justification sub-net ties into this dynamics by ensuring that newly explored knowledge is validated before entering the "exploitable" knowledge base. Thus Explore-Exploit Sub-Net is modeled to coordinate how the agent alternates between exploring new knowledge and exploiting known rules. We have the two new sub-nets within an individual agent as follows:

- Epistemic Justification Sub-Net: (1) Intra-Agent Epistemic Justification: within each agent’s Petri net, there exists a set of places storing that agent’s current knowledge and rules (e.g., Rule Repository for an AI agent, or Human Known Solutions for a human expert), the new or modified knowledge claims are placed here in a "Provisional" form initially; the transitions for epistemic justification consumes a Provisional Knowledge token plus any required data (observations, prior knowledge, test results) from other places, optionally the transitions might require an Energy token (representing cognitive or computational effort to perform verification), and the transitions produce either Validated Knowledge (if the verification passes) or Refuted/Requires Further Inspection tokens (if the check fails or is inconclusive) which may require further processes to gather data from the theory-guided experimentation controlled by another sub-net to create; the transitions from other sub-nets can loop back to an Exploration place with New Data token, prompting the agent refine or test the knowledge further; if validated, the token moves into a separate place representing Exploitable Knowledge, making it available for routine use. (2) Inter-Agent Epistemic Justification: when multiple agents must confirm or align on knowledge, an agent posts a knowledge claim (e.g., "I believe solution X is valid for scenario Y") to its place associated with its collaboration transition Multi-Agent Verification Transition, complying with Eq. (5); the claim token references (or "carries") the relevant knowledge content. This transition can fire only if each relevant agent contributes a consent or review token. Each agent’s local sub-net checks the claim (possibly generating more internal tokens or feedback transitions). If all agents produce Agreement tokens, the knowledge claim is validated at the inter-agent level (becomes Common Knowledge or Shared Verified Knowledge). If any agent produces Disagreement or Doubt the token is diverted back to the original claiming agent’s exploration net for revision or deeper testing.

- Explore-Exploit Sub-Net: this sub-net has exploration and exploitation places and associated transitions. Within Exploration module, if a piece of knowledge is found wanting (internally or collectively) and promising based on the tacit clues (more details in Section 7.5.1), the system triggers a new exploration cycle to discover, refine it or generate alternatives; its transitions trigger when novelty or anomalies appear in the agent’s input and might generate new knowledge claims (placed in a Provisional Knowledge place). Within Exploitation module, only validated knowledge is used by the exploitation transitions, ensuring that the AI agents or the humans do not rely on unverified or faulty claims during routine tasks; its transitions consume a Validated Knowledge token plus a Task token (assigned by others or self-generated, based on agent roles or load balancing) to produce an Outcome typically representing some successful operation or a result for the environment, which will be archived to the Episodic Memory module.

9.4 Three-Layered Petri-Net Architecture of HAACS

To synthesize all the phenomena, aspects, requirements, features, methods, functionalities, and identified issues discussed above during HAAC, a three-layered Petri-net architecture named Hierarchical Exploration-Exploitation Net (HE2-Net) is constructed for the open complex human-AI agents collaboration system, as below that combines meta-level orchestration, organizational-level management, and agent-level sub-nets, each agent sub-net containing its internal sense-plan-act, explore-exploit, epistemic justification, etc. This design allows system designers to (1) control or reconfigure higher-level structures (like which agents collaborate or which "explore vs. exploit" policy is active system-wide), (2) manage agent-level concurrency and resource sharing, and (3) detail each agent’s internal sub-net for final execution. It is rational to use multiple layers of Petri nets (or hierarchical net constructs) so that each layer addresses a different scope of control and configuration. We can conceptualize the system as three nested (or stacked) layers briefly:

- Meta-Level governs large-scale organizational policies, e.g. whether the system is in "explore-heavy" or "exploit-heavy" mode overall, how resources are globally allocated, or whether certain agent sub-groups should merge or split. It can potentially reconfigure the organizational-level Petri net structure (adding or removing agent interactions, changing supervisory rules, etc.).
- Agent-Level (mainly discussed in Section 9.2) controls the internal and organizational interactions among agents. Each agent is represented by a high-level Petri net that manages the agent’s modes and concurrency constraints (e.g. sense-plan-act concurrency, learning concurrency, resource limits, etc). This net ensures that, for instance, the agent can only do so many tasks in parallel, or must occasionally run an "epistemic check" after a specific number of new knowledge claims.
- Execution-Level (mainly discussed in Section 9.3) represents the agent sub-nets beneath each agent-level net, they are more fine-grained sub-nets to execute the specialized functions (e.g. detailed sensors, communication with other agents, meta-cognition modules, advanced learning modules).

Hence, from top to bottom: Meta-level = global reconfiguration or big switches. Agent-level = each agent’s core concurrency and synergy with the system. Execution level = specialized sub-nets that do the real tasks once the agent-level transitions enable a specific sub-task. Each layer tackles different concerns. The meta-level deals with overall "who does what, in which global mode," the agent-level deals with concurrency and resource usage per agent, and the execution sub-nets implement the final details (like step-by-step sensor data handling). From perspective of organization theory, the meta-level can "load" or "unload" certain agent-level modules or shift them into new modes, akin to flipping big "organizational" or "policy" transitions. Meanwhile, the agent sub-nets proceed with day-to-day concurrency as usual. The collaborative problem solving (more details in Section 6) and knowledge management (more details in Section 7) among human and AI agents who balance exploration and exploitation can be modeled and analyzed formally using the HE2-Net; Note that during collaborative problem solving conditions such as multiple concurrent subgoals (differences) and the synchronization of subgoals and operators can be modeled, and elaborate models of these processes will be constructed in future work.

Concurrent Execution of Multiple Sub-Nets
Note that the multiple sub-nets can run concurrently. While a hierarchical Petri net often models a sub-net as a "module" that runs to completion before control returns to the higher-level net, we can instantiate multiple such sub-nets in parallel. In practice, this is achieved by allowing multiple tokens to invoke the sub-net independently, so each instance processes its task concurrently, and then later re-joins the main net when it completes (or reaches a designated intermediate state).

For example, an agent might have a "Sense-Plan-Act" module that, upon receiving a token, launches an instance of the Act sub-net. If new tasks arrive before the previous instance finishes, additional tokens can concurrently trigger further instances of that sub-net. This is analogous to multi-threading in software where several tasks run in parallel and later merge their results back into the main process. In short, hierarchical Petri nets can be designed to allow concurrent execution of multiple sub-net instances, as long as the design permits multiple tokens (or "threads") to be active simultaneously.

Rationale for Hierarchical Design
The hierarchical structures and multi-level interactions widely present in the open complex system, as discussed in the Section 5.1.3, apply to our hierarchical design of HAACS. Regarding scope separation, each layer tackles different concerns. The meta-level deals with overall "who does what, in which global mode," the agent-level deals with concurrency and resource usage per agent, and the execution sub-nets implement the final details (like step-by-step sensor data handling).

If everything were jammed into a single Petri net, we’d quickly face an unwieldy global net with thousands of places/transitions. By layering, each net stays simpler and focuses on its domain. Moreover, the meta-level can "load" or "unload" certain agent-level modules or shift them into new modes, akin to flipping big "organizational" or "policy" transitions. Meanwhile, the agent sub-nets proceed with day-to-day concurrency as usual.

We might imagine an even higher "universe-level" net that decides whether the meta-level net is active or not, etc. If the system is extremely complex (like multiple organizations of agents), a 4th layer that orchestrates multiple meta-level modules could exist. But typically, "meta-level for reconfiguration + agent-level concurrency + specialized sub-module for detailed operations" is enough.

9.5 Achieving Adaptive Agency Through the Lens of Second-Order Cybernetics

9.5.1 Two Feedback Loops in the Three-Layer Design Aligned with Second Order Cybernetics

In the three-layer Petri-net architecture, we have: (1) Execution-Level Feedback Loop: each agent has a sense-plan-act (SPA) and other local feedback loops across execution-level sub-nets controlled by the agent-level; SPA is the standard "cybernetic" loop, e.g. the agent senses the environment, processes the data, makes decisions and acts, then sees the result and adapts further. (2) Meta-Level Feedback Loop: the meta-level Petri net monitors the agent-level behavior (e.g., performance metrics, resource usage, "how well the concurrency is working," or "are agents exploring vs. exploiting effectively?"); it can reconfigure or override the agent-level sub-nets such as merging agents, changing concurrency tokens, toggling explore/exploit modes, etc.

The meta-level loop is explicitly controlling the agent-level Petri net, which in turn controls the execution-level sub-nets, mirroring a self-referential or higher-level control-of-control loop in terms of second-order cybernetics. Specifically, this architecture aligns with second-order cybernetics as follows: (1) Meta-Level Observes and Adapts: the meta-level net doesn’t merely watch passively; it acts to reconfigure the agent-level net’s concurrency or resource tokens, and even merges/splits entire agent sub-nets. This is reminiscent of the "observer in the system" viewpoint: not only does the higher-level net observe the whole system, it is also an integral part of it, modifying the rest of the system’s control loops. (2) Self-Reflection: if the system is designed to allow the agent-level net to send "performance tokens" or "resources utilization" up to the meta-level net, it effectively has a self-reflective loop, i.e., the system is generating data about how well it’s controlling itself, feeding that data to a higher-level loop that rewrites/improves the lower-level loop in real time. (3) Evolving Boundaries: the second-order cybernetics often discusses how the system boundary can shift or how the observer can become part of the system. In our multi-layer approach, if the meta-level net decides to merge or split agent sub-nets (e.g., assign a long-term memory module to an agent, which belongs to another agent originally; combine two agents into one, etc), that changes the boundary among the components of agents and the identifications of the agents. This is very much in the second-order flavor of "the control system changes its own boundaries dynamically."

9.5.2 Synthesizing Biological Cybernetics, Multi-Scale Goals, and Evolving Boundaries

Unpacking Autopoiesis and Autogenesis
Coined by Maturana [106], autopoiesis refers specifically to a system’s capacity to continuously regenerate itself through internal interactions and processes, maintaining its organizational identity. It involves clear boundary maintenance that distinguishes the entity from its environment, while autogenesis refers to the self-initiated development, self-organization, and emergence of structural complexity. Autogenesis emphasizes developmental processes and self-driven evolution within a system’s boundary. A boundary defines the distinction between the system (agent) and its environment. In autopoietic systems, maintaining this boundary is fundamental to identity. An agent in Section 9.2 can be configured to exhibit autopoiesis, it autonomously maintains its boundary, continuously rebuilding itself from within.

Embodying Purposeful Agency with BDI
Each agent defined in Section 9.2 is an adaptive goal-oriented system with two levels of goals with different time scales: (1) externally assigned (ad-hoc) goals are temporary, situational tasks dictated by the environment, other agents or higher-level authorities like the humans. These are tactical and context-dependent, like immediate task assignments; (2) internally maintained (long-term) goals (Desires, Intentions) are strategic, stable, and identity-defining. These reflect deeply rooted aims, often aligned with personal identity, professional role, or long-term vision, akin to a professional profile, career orientation or organizational loyalty [46] in human terms. In other words, an agent isn’t just an executioner of tasks but a purposeful, identity-driven entity.

Inspired by the belief-desire-intention (BDI) model of human practical reasoning [107] as a way of explaining future-directed intention, each agent has (1) beliefs: internal representation of its own state, boundary conditions, environment, and historical knowledge; (2) desires: stable preferences or overarching aims, analogous to values or long-term interests of humans. These could reflect the self-maintaining organizational closure emphasized by autopoiesis, maintaining an identity over time; (3) intentions: the specific commitments an agent adopts to satisfy its desires. Intentions translate abstract desires into concrete courses of action. They reflect the agent’s active choice in navigating its complex environment.

Harmonizing Autopoiesis and Autogenesis with Exploitation and Exploration
Agents achieve genuine adaptability by continuously balancing identity maintenance with adaptive transformation, thriving amid dynamic complexity, through an elegant interplay of autopoiesis and autogenesis that addresses the perpetual tension between stability (identity preservation) and adaptation (boundary-expanding growth). Specifically, agents are defined along two dimensions: structural stability (autopoiesis), which ensures continuity, maintains internal integrity, short-term efficiency, and stable boundary management (exploitation) by using known strategies and resources including existing structure and functions; and structural adaptability (autogenesis), which fosters innovation by actively incorporating external resources (energy, matter, information) to evolve internal structures and drive emergent self-growth (exploration). This exploitation-exploration dynamic not only mirrors the classic trade-off observed across multi-scale, diverse systems but also endows agents with genuine purposefulness, enabling them to proactively shape their own evolution with human-level meaningful intentionality and deliberate action.

Evolving Boundaries through Splitting and Merging Agents
Complexity and openness discussed in Section 5.3 supports modelling the HAACS as fluid and nested: one agent can consist of nested sub-agents (sub-systems), each potentially autopoietic. This nesting suggests that agency is inherently multi-scale, hierarchical [68], and recursive. Agency emerges from interactions, thus the notion of boundary is contextually defined and observer-dependent, what constitutes an "agent" at one scale may simply be a subsystem or even environment at another. Boundaries can shift, evolve, and adapt. However, merely "cutting" an agent apart physically or computationally does not guarantee maintaining independent agency unless each part has internal organizational autonomy and closure.

- Dividing into Sub-agents: if we take an autopoietic, autogenetic agent and conceptually divide it, each resulting sub-agent could only maintain genuine "agency" if it, too, retains the capacity for autopoiesis and autonomy, i.e., each sub-unit must retain a capacity for autonomous identity preservation, boundary maintenance, and self-production. Without that, it becomes merely a functional module or subsystem, not truly an independent "agent."
- Merging into Larger Agents: merging multiple agents implies integration of boundaries into a new meta-boundary. From a cybernetic perspective, this forms a new system identity, a higher-order autopoietic agent, if and only if it establishes a coherent organizational closure and self-maintenance at the new level, i.e., the larger agent as an integrated system needs to achieve a new autopoietic boundary, a distinct organizational identity, and emergent autonomy above and beyond the sum of the parts.

In practice, there might be meta-level places that count how many tasks are in the system, or measure concurrency load. If two or more sub-nets (originally thought to belong to separate agents) cannot function independently or be strongly coupled, i.e., they share so many places or transitions that they always fire in lockstep, whether to "merge" or keep "split" these sub-nets upon crossing a threshold concurrency measured in real-time depends entirely on the system’s design goals and resource-management philosophy, e.g., "do you want to distribute their functions by modelling them as separate agents with heavy synchronization or a single larger agent with multiple internal sub-tasks?" Some architectures merge multiple small agents during high load to unify knowledge or resources, reducing inter-agent communication overhead (centralizing control in one "super-agent"), then split again when load is low to eliminate unnecessary overhead. Others do the exact opposite, splitting under heavy load to increase parallelism, offload heterogeneous sub-tasks, or specialize sub-agents (like differentiation in [68]), and merging only when tasks are sparse and homogeneous. The key is to decide which strategy, centralization vs. distributed parallelism, best serves the needs under varying load conditions, since both approaches can be valid in a reconfigurable setting of HE2-Net.

Driving Agent-Level Self-Organization through Meta-Level Transitions
A special order place can be defined to reconfigure the HE2-Net mainly controlled by the meta-level. It represents a global or higher-level state of the system, akin to an "order parameter" in enslaving principles of synergetics discussed in Section 5.3. Its marking determines which "meta-transitions" (the structural changes to merge/split agents and associated sub-nets, reconfigure the collaboration flows among agents, etc.) become enabled. By tracking a system-wide condition in just a few such places, we can effectively let these "order places" drive major reconfigurations, thereby "enslaving" the rest of the net’s local details to the new global arrangement.

Self-organization can be achieved, and the reconfiguration can be emergent (rather than orchestrated by an external supervisor), we can define additional meta-level transitions or control policies that cause the "order transitions" to become enabled under certain macroscale conditions. For instance, the pivotal communication structure constructed by "Criticize-Reflect" method in [39] are analogous to the macro order parameter tipping the system into a new organizational mode, and its strategy can be modeled and refined further formally and analytically in our framework. Hence, the firing of these "order" relevant transitions effectively enslaves the rest of the Petri net’s structure to the newly emerging global pattern, mirroring Haken’s principle.

9.6 Summary

Building on the critical insights gathered, we envision a next stage of theoretical and applied research founded on an open complex human-AI agents collaboration framework, supported by a Hierarchical Exploration-Exploitation Net (HE2-Net) and inspired by Tsien’s meta-synthesis principles.

In this future direction, AI agents become customized research assistants, interacting with human experts to tackle open-ended scientific investigations and complex real-world scenarios. A central aspect is orchestrating multi-level "explore-exploit" mechanisms, in which collective reasoning, advanced search strategies, and dynamic adaptation can flourish across an evolving problem space. Co-construction of knowledge, anchored by robust epistemic justification, will ensure that newly generated insights or methods integrate seamlessly with existing theories or domain expertise. Moreover, integrating qualitative (e.g., emergent team behaviors or dynamic role assignments) with quantitative modeling (e.g., matter-energy-information flows) is key to bridging organizational theory, traditional HCI studies, and social science with engineering rigor. By systematically enabling multi-tasking alongside a spectrum of different collaboration modes, ranging from clearly demarcated teamwork to profound symbiosis, this open complex framework underpins the study of emergent behaviors and non-equilibrium dynamics, thereby tackling evolving environments and exploring novel collaborative forms. Ultimately, the HE2-Net approach equips us to model, simulate, analyze and refine advanced human-AI agent systems that transcend ad-hoc coordination, aiming toward an authentic co-evolution of human cognition and AI functionality for sustained, deeply integrated symbioses.

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:
